item.title: The Met’s Orientalism Exhibition Puts Edward Said on Display—and His Critique Aside - ARTnews.com
item.description:
I have been teaching a graduate seminar on Orientalism and representation at MIT for the last 34 years. Centered around Edward Said’s 1978 book Orientalism, the course examines the ways fraught relationships between the “West” and the “Orient” have been represented across different media since at least the Renaissance. Every two years, as I prepare to teach the seminar anew, I ask myself whether it might be time to shelve the subject, which has become so mainstream and seemingly overanalyzed. And every two years, something happens on the world stage that convinces me it’s still necessary.

This year, in addition to the rising racism against Muslims and Arabs in European and American political discourse; the vilification of Palestinians, Yemenis, and Iranians in Western media as their homelands are being destroyed; the suppression of Muslim rights in Modi’s India; and the continuing erasure of Muslim identities in Myanmar and China, an exhibition enigmatically titled “Orientalism: Between Fact and Fantasy” has reaffirmed the urgency of Said’s critique of Orientalism as a “Western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient.” I will be teaching the seminar again next fall.

The exhibition, on view at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York until February 28, is the latest in a succession of exhibitions devoted to Orientalist art mounted around the world over the past three decades. As such, it introduces little material that has not already appeared in similar contexts, highlighting celebrated 19th-century Orientalist painters, principally Jean-Léon Gérôme (1824–1904) and Osman Hamdi Bey (1842–1910), among orientalizing 19th-century vases, plates, lamps, and ewers; old photos of “Orientals” and the Orient; and a number of representations of bashi-bozouks, the general term Europeans used to designate the unruly and reckless irregulars in Oriental armies.

Yet, to my mind, its most ingenious maneuver is the way it manages to circumvent nearly half a century of sustained criticism of Orientalism without openly challenging that criticism. Indeed, it even enshrines the first hardcover edition of Said’s Orientalism, with its famous cover reproducing Gérôme’s The Snake Charmer (1879), as a fetish object in a glass case alongside three Turkish helmets without incorporating its arguments into its texts. The rest of that gallery is largely devoted to dissecting Gérôme’s controversial painting, explaining where the artist might have found his visual sources.

A TELLING OMMISSION transpires at the entrance connecting the museum’s Islamic galleries to the Orientalist exhibition, where the arrangement, to my eyes, suggests considerably more than the wall text explicitly states. Two glass cases flank the opening. On the left is a copy of Pascal Coste’s Architecture arabe: ou, Monuments du Kaire, mesurés et dessinés, de 1818 à 1826 (1837–39); on the right, a volume of the monumental Description de l’Égypte, the multivolume encyclopedic survey (published between 1809 and 1829) that was produced by the army of scholars and scientists who accompanied Napoleon’s ill-fated invasion of Egypt (1798–1801). Together, the volumes invoke one of the exhibition’s principal themes: In the 19th century, Orientalism produced knowledge. Yet the critique—“knowledge is power”—on which Said, following Michel Foucault, insisted, goes unmentioned.

Meanwhile, the two paintings hanging above the cases make that power relationship unmistakable to the attentive viewer. Painted by Gérôme more than 60 years after the failure of the invasion and more than 40 years after Napoleon’s death, they belong to a series of hagiographic representations of Bonaparte in Egypt. One depicts Napoleon on horseback surveying Cairo, the city he conquered, from the ramparts of its Citadel. The other shows him defiantly confronting the Sphinx. Taken together, the paintings proclaim French dominion over Egypt’s present and past, precisely the ambition underlying Napoleon’s first colonial venture into the Orient.

That they were painted around the time of the contentious renegotiations between Ismaʿil Pasha, Egypt’s ruler (1863–79), and the French-dominated Suez Canal Company, headed by Ferdinand de Lesseps (1805–94), may be more than coincidental. Those negotiations culminated in an inequitable compensation settlement imposed on Egypt through the arbitration of Napoleon III, who regarded the canal as a prestige project for the Second French Empire. Gérôme’s resurrection of Napoleon I’s Egyptian campaign, at a moment when France was consolidating its economic and political influence over Egypt, had a charge that would hardly have escaped his contemporaneous French audience. None of this historical context, however, is mentioned in the exhibition.

If France’s imperial ambitions in Egypt were primarily financial and economic exploitation, its colonization of Algeria was considerably more direct and brutal. Following the invasion of 1830, French armies spent decades attempting to suppress Algerian resistance, most prominently that led by Emir ʿAbd al-Qādir al-Jazāʾirī, represented here in a melancholy photographic portrait taken in 1860 by the Parisian firm Mayer & Pierson. The caption cryptically states that he “was the spiritual and military leader of Algeria following the French invasion of the country in 1830” and that “hoping to end his people’s suffering, he surrendered in 1847, living as a prisoner in France.”

What precisely was the emir doing as a leader? Who was responsible for his people’s suffering? What circumstances compelled him to surrender, and why was he subsequently imprisoned? The caption hints at these questions without answering them, leaving me wondering how a visitor unfamiliar with the history of French colonialism could possibly make sense of such evasive formulations, which transform a protracted struggle against conquest into an almost inexplicable sequence of personal decisions and misfortunes.

In reality, in 1843, French forces launched a surprise attack on his smala, the mobile encampment that housed his family and followers. The raid caused numerous casualties, including noncombatants; resulted in the capture of members of the emir’s household; and led to the seizure of his possessions and library while he was absent.

THE PAINTER ACCORDED the greatest prominence and most profuse praise in the exhibition is Osman Hamdi Bey, a member of the Ottoman ruling elite who was born in Constantinople, educated in France, and served as director of the Imperial Museum. He also led several archaeological expeditions in the Arab provinces of the empire, and, most significantly for this exhibition, emerged as the foremost Ottoman practitioner of Orientalist painting. Over the past three decades, largely Turkish scholars have elevated him into the paradoxical figure of an anti-Orientalist Orientalist, an artist supposedly capable of overturning the conventions of a genre whose techniques and subjects he enthusiastically adopted.

But the contrast between his and Gérôme’s paintings and themes hardly amounts to a critique of Orientalism. Hamdi’s major paintings are often cerebral, enigmatic, and resistant to straightforward interpretation. Some, such as The Tortoise Trainer (1906) and The Mihrab (Genesis) (1901), neither included in the exhibition, border on the insulting in their treatment of Islamic sensibilities. Others, including his various depictions of reading emirs and young women, examples of which are on view, are celebrated for reversing a familiar Orientalist trope: The supposedly indolent and ignorant Orientals are shown instead as learned individuals absorbed in books. Between these opposites stand his depictions of urban life in Istanbul and Bursa, praised by the curators as “vibrant,” “dynamic,” and—most perplexingly—“modern.”

This last characterization stopped me in my tracks, particularly as I examined Hamdi’s celebrated At the Mosque Door (1891). The painting depicts groups before the portal to the Muradiye Mosque in Bursa (1425–26). Hamdi-like figures, dressed in various forms of traditional attire, are scattered across the scene: a seated mendicant, a sheikh, a man apparently preparing for ablution, and perhaps a vendor of books and calligraphic panels. Several figures resemble Hamdi himself; this is a recurring feature in his paintings. But the most incongruous, indeed awkward, elements of the composition are two groups of women: Two stand on a stone porch to the left of the entrance, and four ascend the steps toward the mosque. Elegantly dressed in fashionable Ottoman entaris, several carrying delicate parasols, they appear to have been transposed from a leisurely promenade in a park to the threshold of a mosque. Nothing in their demeanor or the composition convincingly suggests that they are entering the building, participating in its activities, or even particularly interested in their architectural surroundings. They seem less integrated into the setting than inserted into it.

The exhibition label declares that Hamdi’s portrayals of Islam and the mosque as public space “emphasize daily life and articulate a sense of authenticity and modernity.” Is it the women theatrically approaching the mosque, perhaps, who are the source of the authenticity and modernity found in the painting? Their presence would have been unusual given the social norms of the time.

I could not help recalling the photographs that circulated not long ago on social media of Afghan and Iranian women strolling through their cities in short skirts during the 1970s, presented as incontrovertible evidence that these societies had once been “modern,” before the imposition of stricter dress codes by the mullahs and the Taliban. In these images, modernity is reduced to a woman’s appearance and freedom of dress, abstracted from the political, economic, and social conditions in which she lived. Might Hamdi Bey’s clumsily staged women, and the exhibition’s enthusiastic reading of them, be reproducing a similarly reductive understanding of modernity? More fundamentally, why should the insertion of fashionable women into an otherwise straightforward Orientalist painting make it modern?

I left the exhibition with the disquieting impression that Orientalism, as Said defined and critiqued it, is being expertly resurrected, aesthetically rehabilitated, and intellectually retrofitted for our troubling times of suspicion, intolerance, and rejection of the different other. Far from confronting the ideological premises of Orientalist representation, the exhibition seems to render them newly respectable under the ostensibly neutral rubrics of artistic achievement, historical curiosity, and knowledge production. That this rehabilitation should occur at a moment when the peoples once objectified by Orientalism are again subjected to dehumanization, dispossession, and violence makes the exhibition’s evasions all the more troubling—and the critique of Orientalism all the more necessary.

item.title: Discovering John Baer, an Untrained Master Photographer - Hyperallergic
item.description:
On a recent Saturday at The White Loft, a gallery on the Lower East Side, Andrew Baer showed me a 1938 Leica Model III. His father, John Baer, acquired the camera from a captured German soldier in 1945 while he was deployed to Germany in World War II. He took his first shots in Wetzlar, home of the Leica headquarters, where he happened to be stationed. What followed was a decade of obsessive picture-taking, a quotidian quest through post-war Europe and midcentury New York, the wondrous results of which remained largely unknown until 2021. These photographs sat untouched for decades, until John died in 1994 and Andrew discovered three boxes in a damp corner of his father’s basement. 

A selection of black-and-white images, hanging unframed on the Loft’s walls, showed what he discovered — a series of Baer’s experiments in looking. In Europe, he captured people among the ruins of war; in New York, he studied shadows on Stuyvesant Town, asphalt pavers engulfed in smoke, intimate moments between friends in Bryant Park, street scenes taken from the fire escape of his fifth-floor walkup on Second Avenue in the East Village. The first image I noticed, “Rainy Day Reflections,” showed a slice of sunlight stretching across Lexington Avenue, a pedestrian caught midstride, whose umbrella mimics the manhole cover.

item.title: Johanna Hedva Keeps Doom in Her Mouth - Hyperallergic
item.description:
"Age seven, I stepped barefoot on a slug in the front yard … I will never forget the way my spine shivered and I knew I was in an unknowable presence and I felt my foot never afterwards be clean. Was this God?" This is a perfect origin story for Johanna Hedva's writing. The Korean-American artist’s sentences shine as blades ground sharp against the void, writing with a mystic orientation to life — mystic but not mystical. The union with otherness here is no easy one. As Hedva says, "I can only use language like fated and chthonic and words that try to reach into the ontological fact that we're ancient and we're fucked." Because "hope, uplift, and transcendence are not to my taste."

For those of us who attend to it closely, and who refuse to leave it alone, life is long. One's relation to it is never not broken, worn, frayed, sullied. It is what can "not be fixed but only endured." Hedva asks, "For people like me, what kinds of spirituality deal with this, not as a salve for the friction but the music made from it?" There's a space for kinds of art, ritual, magic, writing which gesture toward a knowledge that is strictly impossible but at least knows it’s impossible. Hedva again: "I want to hear the voice throw itself against the silence, keep making noise against the asphyxiating black sauce of cosmic noiselessness."

Hedva's work has accumulated a following. As she puts it, "I began to notice that a murder of wayward girls, misfits, freaks, and orphans was circling behind me." The most interesting people, of course. The words that drew them are compiled in My Knife Collection and Other Subjects of Desire (2026), offering her writing in a range of forms: fiction, essays on artists ranging from Tracey Emin to Mire Lee, and short pieces that read a bit like fairytales, but not the Disney kind. There are no happy endings or easy exits for Hedva; "I did not know how I was going to bear this life."

item.title: The Young Women Who Prefigured the Hudson River School - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The Hudson River School, founded by Thomas Cole’s academic style of landscape painting, emerged around the 1830s, but what if I told you that the first distinctly American art movement was actually produced by women decades earlier? Women and girls of New England in the 18th and 19th centuries made landscape scenes in needlework, oil, and watercolors, filling rolling hills with wildlife and dotting harbors with soldiers in red coats. 

This work, and the proposition of its unappreciated preeminence, is the subject of a new exhibition, Locating Girlhood: Place and Identity in Early American "Schoolgirl" Art, at the American Folk Art Museum. “Schoolgirl” art became a collecting category by the early 1950s and is still used in the art market today. By placing the term in quotation marks, the museum hints at an understanding of its “belittling connotations” and instead favors “girlhood embroidery” or “student artworks.” 

Faith Trumbull is perhaps one of the best-known artists in the exhibition. At a young age, she developed highly technical skills in painting and drawing at a finishing school, incorporating embroidered silk thread, gouache, and mica flakes into her panels. In a 1754 needlework, brown and yellow leaves recall late autumn in New England. The water appears frosty, glittering white as cows stand knee-deep and shivering. The work achieves such a fine degree of realism that it is mystifying how the artist completed it at just 11 years old.

item.title: Words Can Kill in Cj Shaw’s Art - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Cj Shaw’s four large compositions on view in a quiet farewell, let it kill you at Weatherproof are a sort of neo-noir, projecting the enigmatic paranoia of the brooding outsider anti-hero. The main actors are words — cropped, angled, and scattered — surfacing between layers of translucent expressionist markmaking, and functioning simultaneously as subject, message, and abstracted form. 

Take “Braz” (2026): perhaps short for “Brazil”, the upside-down lettering spans the entire canvas with purple and yellow contours. Beneath, or perhaps above it (it’s hard to tell), a smattering of other words and phrases appear, varying in obfuscation through layering and gestural brushwork. Nonexhaustively, there’s “Blue,” in diagonal block letters; “Am something,” a half-statement that forms a “V”; and “In time you will know what it’s like,” the Joker-esque phrase broken in two that runs across the top and bisects the canvas diagonally in a pale Impact font.

item.title: Russia Is Erasing Memories of the Gulag and Reframing Stalin’s History - ARTnews.com
item.description:
All over Russia, memories of the Soviet Union and its former dictator Joseph Stalin are being manipulated to tell a new story by the government of President Vladimir V. Putin. An investigative report by The New York Times details how the horrors of Gulag camps are being reframed to depict the Soviets as the victors of World War II and the fight against Nazism. Russia is also using the memory of WWII to act as an extension of its fight against Ukraine.

Efforts to rewrite the story of Russia were already in play before the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022. Notably, Memorial, an organization dedicated to memorializing the camps, was dissolved and labelled an “extremist organization” by Russia’s Supreme Court, forcing the group to move its operations abroad. Memorial was also awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022.

The Gulag was established by Vladimir Lenin in the late 1910s and early 1920s, but Stalin was the one who expanded the operation from the 1920s to the early 1950s. Nearly 1.5 million people were imprisoned in the Gulag and died from extreme cold, starvation, disease, and intense labor. Monuments that preserved its painful history are now being erased or censored. Examples include the shuttering of Moscow’s Gulag Museum earlier this year and the disappearance of at least 26 memorials dedicated to Gulag victims since 2022.

Additionally, in the summer, a Gulag memorial plaque was removed from the Arctic village Yur-Shor, and more symbols of the Gulag are starting to vanish. Under the power of the Kremlin, Russia is undergoing its own modern-day “digital gulag,” according to the Independent. To wit, a mandate now requires that all new digital devices be equipped with the messenger app Max, launched last year by the Russian tech company VK, which allows Russia’s Federal Security Service access to materials from the app.

item.title: German Museum Transforms Permanent Collection Galleries into Gym to Attract Youth - ARTnews.com
item.description:
We’ve seen dance and musical performances in museums, as well as yoga classes, but a full array of gym equipment and gear? Beginning earlier this month and running through February 21, 2027, the Kunstpalast in Düsseldorf, Germany, has set up weight machines, mats, treadmills, ellipticals, and all manner of gym equipment in its permanent exhibition galleries, so that visitors can work out beside the historic and contemporary artworks, reported the Times of London. Whether or not participants are able to take in the art hanging in front of them while bench pressing, is anyone’s guess, but the idea has its fans, some of whom show up to the museum appropriately dressed in workout clothes.

What artworks do these health-conscious visitors get to enjoy while sweating away? The program titled “Gym. Fit with Art” unfolds across 20 stations beside the museum’s collection of over 800 works, which span pieces by Peter Paul Rubens to Gerhard Richter. It was conceived as a tribute marking the centenary of the GeSoLei, which was the largest trade fair held during the Weimar Republic, which was also dedicated to health.

“We want to target people who might prefer going to the gym rather than a museum on weekends,” and this particularly includes younger audiences, said Alina Fuchte, who has led the project. To wit, “the museum is transforming its collection into an extraordinary fitness circuit,” states the museum website. “Instead of just strolling from painting to painting and admiring the art, visitors will soon be able to get active,” it adds. The endeavor is sponsored by TARGOBANK in cooperation with Technogym, which makes fitness equipment, according to the website.

“Anyone who would rather simply take in the art is equally welcome,” continues the website. This, however, begs the question of whether that simple act may be tough to do while standing beside someone jogging on a treadmill in front of large busts of Johann Wilhelm, Elector Palatine, and his wife, Anna Maria Luisa de’Medici, per just a few examples of the works on view.

One visitor, Kai Heimes, 25, tells the Times of London, “It’s cool to work out in the collection,” and if it feels “awkward” for some, “I don’t think it’s a big deal,” he added.

However, another, Moritz Rossmanith, 40, admitted to being “a bit confused by it all.” Rossmanith was visiting from Rome, and thought it was “very strange to see kids holding thick barbells while there’s old Italian art on the wall.” Children are reportedly the biggest fans of the gym gear.

As for bringing water bottles to the museum-gym, given that many other museums sternly scold visitors for taking covert sips of water inside art galleries, that rule doesn’t seem to apply here.

“Coming here and realizing this is also a space for me, I can feel comfortable here, I can be free here, I can try new things—that, for me, is the first step,” said Fuchte.

Did we mention there is also a range of scheduled fitness classes at the museum? You can sign up here.

item.title: Final Report Details Minor, But Visible Damage to the Bayeux Tapestry Following Trip to the British Museum - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A final report released by France’s ministry of culture yesterday details where the Bayeux Tapestry sustained some minor damage following its transfer from Normandy to the British Museum, reports Le Figaro.

While the overall state of the nearly 1000-year-old tapestry was deemed “satisfactory” by the eight conservationists and experts working in France and England, who co-authored the report, they found there were “two zones of fiber breakage,” new folds and tensions, as well as “very small” damage that appeared in areas that were already weakened, prior to the voyage. News of an initial condition report about the tapestry showing some damage made headlines in September, but this is the first time a final copy has been seen by the media.

ARTnews has reached out to France’s Ministry of Culture for a copy of the report, which was not shared via press release or posted on its website, as is customary with public announcements.

In other details, translated from the French news story, experts reportedly observed that “a red wool thread in an embroidered area and another from the linen background cloth have undergone a slight progression.” Additionally, they spotted “slight folds and pockets,” as well as areas of tension in the embroidery and its linen support. For the latter, the tapestry’s horizontal display, in contrast with its previous vertical hang, should help fix the stretching issue. The report also warns of areas to watch closely, particularly on the tapestry’s return trip to France in July 2027. These include several more pronounced folds, areas of wear, and a broken thread.

The authors, who conducted their report in July and August, added that it’s not possible to know precisely when the changes occurred within the time span of the tapestry’s transfer from Bayeux to its current display in London. Additionally, they noted that this last check, including additional, highly detailed photographs of the artifact, is the most complete review of the tapestry to date. It was compared with two less thorough assessments made in 2020 and 2025.

“We now know the condition of the tapestry as never before, which will be useful later on,” said Delphine Christophe, general director of heritage in France, speaking to Le Figaro. She added that the overall assessment, despite the noted damage, proved “exceptional,” given the fragile tapestry’s roughly 230-foot length and 20-inch height.

The loan of the tapestry was heavily criticized in the months leading up to the handoff, due to risks of harming it. But after three failed attempts to secure a loan, it was ultimately made possible thanks to a carefully controlled ground transportation plan that was designed to eliminate almost all vibrations, aided by the political will of French President Emmanuel Macron. The latter was intent on making a strong diplomatic statement of friendship with the UK. In exchange, France will receive the Sutton Hoo archaeological ship burial and the Lewis Chessmen set from the British Museum. However, as Le Monde’s Roxana Azimi pointed out, “the Sutton Hoo treasure does not resonate at all with the French public,” and the French people “are getting objects that are certainly valuable, but not very impressive.”

As for the Bayeux Tapestry, it is believed to have been made in Canterbury following the coronation of William the Conqueror as king of England in 1066. It tells his side of the Norman Conquest, which was one of the most pivotal moments in English history. Meanwhile, British Museum director Nicolas Cullinan responded frankly to Azimi’s point in Le Monde. “Yes,” he said. “It’s very hard to beat the Bayeux Tapestry.”

item.title: Rachel Whiteread Has Designed the 2027 Brit Awards Trophy - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Dame Rachel Whiteread, who was the first woman artist to win the Turner Prize in 1993, has been selected to design the 2027 Brit Awards trophy. The trophy has previously been designed by the likes of Damien Hirst, Zaha Hadid, Es Devlin and Anish Kapoor.

The trophy will be bestowed upon musicians nominated for the prestigious award ceremony taking place on February 27, 2027. Each trophy takes inspiration from the image of Britannia, a tall, elegant female figure that personifies Britain. For her design, Whiteread has inverted the statue, exposing its silver lining with punched holes throughout. “I exposed the interior of the statue—as an artist would do with their music,” said the artist in a statement. “I accepted the invitation to design next year’s Brit Award trophy, as I saw this as a natural extension of my work—to continue to celebrate and recognize British art and creativity, and to have an opportunity to apply my own perspective within such an iconic British cultural institution.”

Whiteread said she also agreed to design the statue in an effort to safeguard arts and culture, which she described as being “under very real threat.” “The Brits have celebrated musical creativity and artistry for decades now. We have some fantastically creative musicians who have produced music that lays their souls bare, provides hope in times of darkness, or speaks directly about a moment in time,” she added.

In designing the trophy, Whiteread joins a prestigious list of other artists who have given the statue new life: Dame Peter Blake, Tracey Emin, Vivienne Westwood and Yinka Ilori. In 1997, Whiteread became the first woman to represent Britain at the Venice Biennale, and in 2001, she became the third artist to have her work placed on the Fourth Plinth in Trafalgar Square, which took the form of an inverted resin recreation of the plinth.

item.title: ‘The Book of the Human Body’ Surveys 2,000 Years of Remarkable Anatomical Inquiry - Colossal
item.description:
As long as humans have been around, we’ve been curious about existential questions like, Why are we here? And how do things work? That goes for our own bodies, too. But in our era of modern science and medicine, it’s difficult to imagine a time when physicians weren’t familiar with all of the bones in the skeleton, how a baby grows inside a womb, or how the cardiovascular system works. Even the profession that comes to mind when we think of a doctor didn’t really emerge until the past few centuries. During the medieval period, barber-surgeons were the primary medical practitioners (yes, the people who cut hair also conducted surgeries).

As medicine morphed into a scientific and intellectual pursuit, academies cropped up starting in the late 1700s, such as the College of Philadelphia—the first medical school in the U.S.—and the Edinburgh School of Surgery in Scotland. Ethics were, let’s say, malleable. In Edinburgh, a legal shortage of fresh cadavers used for study in the early 1800s spawned a shady underground trade in bodies, many of which were dug up from new burials in the dead of night. And then there were the famous serial murders committed by William Burke and William Hare, who cashed in by selling well over a dozen of their victims’ corpses to anatomist Robert Knox for use during his lectures. Suffice it to say, some scholars really wanted to understand our innards.

Slated for release in January, The Book of the Human Body delves into the art and science of anatomy, disease, reproduction, and more. Published by TASCHEN, the two-volume set compiles more than 950 images from over 75 rare books and manuscripts from around the world. From ancient analyses to medieval studies to modern diagrams, the anthology surveys the breadth of eras and cultural influences that have shaped our understanding of our physical selves.

Authored by medical historian Richard Barnett, the book celebrates universality and unquenched curiosity. Despite sleeping, breathing, and walking around in our bodies every day, we are often still mystified by much of what makes them work. Throughout history, that sense of wonder has remained constant. Barnett says, “Whatever they might represent, whatever they might express, these extraordinary images have lost none of their power to shock or captivate, to teach or inspire.”

Illustrations include a silk manuscript dated to 168 B.C.E., discovered in a tomb in southern China, which features 44 figures engaged in exercises of “self-cultivation,” plus excerpts from Andreas Vesalius’s anatomical atlas, Fabrica, published in 1543. “In all of these examples, the illustrations stand out not only as objects of medical understanding, but as conspicuous works of art in their own right,” the publisher says.

Pre-order your copy on Bookshop.

item.title: Celebrating the OverlookedLegacy of Violette Cornelius - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
In 2003, Nederlands Fotomuseum received several suitcases containing thousands of negatives, slides, contact prints and documents. They belonged to Violette Cornelius (1919-1998), one of the first women of her generation to become a professional photographer. Whilst Cornelius was a respected figure within the Netherlands during the 20th century, having established herself in architectural and reportage circles, this donation – made by her son – shed a whole new light on her prolific career. “We were astounded at the scale and quality of the work we encountered, for which no place had yet been reserved in the canon of Dutch photography,” says Curator Loes van Harrevelt. Now, the museum seeks to redress the balance, finally giving this overlooked trailblazer the attention she deserves. This winter, Violette Cornelius Rediscovered opens in Rotterdam.  The show is the culmination of an extensive study of her life and work, featuring over 200 pieces and coinciding with the publication of her first-ever monograph.

Cornelius was born in Jakarta but trained at the Nieuwe Kunstschool art college in Amsterdam, growing up amidst a mix of cultures. It was in the Netherlands that she discovered the Bauhaus and its ideas, becoming part of a network of graphic designers and visual artists based in the city. During WWII, Cornelius was an active member of the artists’ resistance, helping to produce forged identity documents. Her documentation of this period is now listed in UNESCO Nederland’s Memory of the World register. After the war, as a member of the GKf photographers’ association, Cornelius made pictures of buildings alongside photojournalism for influential books. The publication Letter op straat (1956) was one of the highlights of her career, exploring urban typography and street lettering, whilst her reportage on displaced Hungarian people and the Hoogovens steelworks in IJmuiden made her a well-known name.

In 1964, Cornelius began to travel the world. She journeyed to the Tellem caves in Mali with her Leica camera, and recorded the social impact of rapid urbanisation across India, Iraq, Peru and Yemen in both black-and-white and colour. These international assignments were almost entirely overlooked for many years, but now form a focal point of the presentation at Nederlands Fotomuseum. They are displayed alongside prints that demonstrate her mastery of different genres, from still life studies made at Nieuwe Kunstschool – including a standout depiction of an egg on a plate – as well as portraits of models during a fashion show and a distinctly Bauhaus shot (think Lucia Moholy) of a private residence designed by architect Jo van den Broek in Rotterdam. Elsewhere, other images offer insights into the lives of young people in the Dutch Reformed Church, as they dance the twist and Cornelius presses the shutter.

Despite her role as a pioneer of her profession, Cornelius has not received the same recognition as her male peers. Rediscovered seeks to address this, with curator van Harrevelt delving into her archive and tracking down work that had ended up in other collections – part of Nederlands Fotomuseum’s wider goal of “preserving and studying photographic legacies and making them accessible to the public.” The exhibition draws on an archive of 40,000 black-and-white negatives, slides, vintage and contact prints, alongside documents, dummies, objects and a small library. Together, these materials offer a fuller picture of an artist whose contribution to Dutch photography has remained undervalued for far too long.

Violette Cornelius Rediscovered is at Nederlands Fotomuseum, Rotterdam, until 28 February.

nederlandsfotomuseum.nl

Words: Eleanor Sutherland

Image Credits:
1. Emmy Andriesse, Violette Cornelius, Amsterdam,1938–1939. Special Collections, Leiden University Libraries.
2. Still life with egg on a white plate, Amsterdam, 1939. Study assignment for the Nieuwe Kunstschool. © Violette Cornelius / Nederlands Fotomuseum.
3. Models during a fashion show by designer Dick Holthaus, Amsterdam, 1961. © Violette Cornelius / Nederlands Fotomuseum.
4. Private residence designed by architect Jo van den Broek, Kralingseweg, Rotterdam, 1953. © Violette Cornelius / Nederlands Fotomuseum.

The post Celebrating the Overlooked<br>Legacy of Violette Cornelius appeared first on Aesthetica Magazine.

item.title: Carroll Dunham Calls His Filthy Formalism “Abstraction with a Hard-On” - ARTnews.com
item.description:
I thought it best to confess up front that I was still forming an opinion about his work. Carroll Dunham took that like a gentleman. He is familiar, he made clear to me during ourranginginterview, with the two main camps of interpretation about his potty-mouthed paintings and drawings: 1) that he is a high formalist with an ear for the unconscious seldom rivaled since Surrealism, and 2) that he is a simple vulgarian.

“I’m lucky people even want to write about my work,” Dunham said. “I made the paintings. They can say whatever they want.” At 76, Dunham is thin, likable, and frank. He has a sharp, deadpan face framed by transition lenses and Beckettian white hair. When we spoke in his studio in Connecticut, he wore a silk suit in the shade of gray-green the French call caca d’oie, the shirt buttoned only in the top half, cholo style, with chunky sneakers in the same shade.

The spacious upstairs had been given over to small abstract sculptures he was making out of aluminum sheeting with assistants. It was July, and Dunham was between two capstone surveys of a long career. A show of his drawings spanning 1974 to 2024 had recently come down at the Art Institute of Chicago, while curators at the Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami, were finalizing a survey of his paintings from 1983 to the present for December. It was the kind of summary moment an artist is lucky to be alive for.

Since the ’90s, Dunham’s best-known pictures have starred carefully framed cartoon penises, vaginas, and anuses in varying states of specificity, usually attached to the bodies or the faces of humanoids engaged in sex or violence. This scenery belongs to a tradition of ridiculous bodily extremes, from Greek vases to Thomas Rowlandson to Gustave Courbet to Nicole Eisenman. His style, meanwhile, belongs to the black outlines and dropped-in colors of cartoons. That graphic clarity seems to ask us to read his bodily subjects loud and clear, without any of the technical seduction of peers like Lisa Yuskavage or John Currin.

Although his loud and lusty scenarios committed no real transgression (Peter Saul took care of that in the ’60s, then Robert Mapplethorpe in the ’80s), what may genuinely surprise the uninitiated is the academic remove that characterizes the writing about Dunham. His work is discussed—and discussed primarily by those born before 1975—almost exclusively in the specialist language of form or space or paint application, with little reference to the subject matter. It seems that the writers in Camp 1 understand the shock factor that attends men dildoing their rectums with pistols, or angrily ejaculating on each other from enormous penis-noses, as ammunition against the claim that subject should dictate one’s opinion of a painting. As if to deny the charge of prudery, some of them describe moments of rapture. On a Dunham painting made between 2006 and 2012, of a giant woman spreading her anus and vagina above a landscape like a parade float, the artist Paul Chan wrote of feeling transported: “When I entered the room where it hung [at the Whitney], I gasped. The painting was at once exuberant, provocative, and entrancing. It literally took my breath. I quickly glanced at the other people in the room. Was anyone else having an asthma attack looking at this?”

Representing Camp 2 are John Yau (The Brooklyn Rail, 2007: “Saul is an iconoclast and Dunham is a wannabe.”) and a young man in a basketball jersey I met at the Chicago show. This man was examining a pencil scribble from 2020 of a fist clasping an erection, the balls parted and meatus shaped like a teardrop. I asked him what he thought, and he said, “I feel like I’m being pranked.”

Dunham walked me to the “other studio,” a smaller room reserved for painting, where acrylic tubes lay neatly on a table in gradients, labels down. A canvas he had just finishedstood on sawhorses. It showed a man with long black hair down on all fours in a sculpture studio. The painting is called Looking for Something, and its protagonist’s pants are on the floor. His skin is white, and a woman, who is purple, kneels behind him, her head thrown back in a wail or moan. With her hand, she does something to the man’s ass that is not visible to us. In the foreground, another purple person, a Peeping Tom, watches them through a window. Nine of these most recent “Sculptor” paintings, from about Covid to now, were to go up at the Matthew Brown gallery in Manhattan in September as a sort of appetizer for the Miami show.

I asked where these recent purple/white folks come from. “They come from my work,” Dunham explained. “And I don’t mean that to be glib. They really do. So to even answer that question, I would have to go, ‘Before I was doing these paintings, I was doing these paintings, then these paintings,’” he continued, miming with his hands successive leaps into the past.

BORN THE FIFTH IN A line of Carrolls to a Connecticut poultry farmer who turned to real estate, Dunham went to Phillips Academy (Andover), class of 1967. The sculptor Mel Kendrick was his roommate. “Tip was doing Rapidograph drawings,” Kendrick recalled as we spoke by phone, using Dunham’s nickname. “Almost hippie drawings, very fine sketches.” (Of “Tip,” Dunham said, “It’s a WASP thing.”) Kendrick also recalls Dunham’s appetite for science fiction. (Face-down on his studio table, I spotted James L. Cambias’s Darkling Sea.) Dunham took darkroom classes. In the school’s literary magazine, his finely exposed photograph of a pouting and rotund lady in a playground swing illustrates a poem by Anthony Grafton, the historian-to-be. “Anything he did, he always had a touch,” Kendrick said. “Tip is very specific. And that’s something I don’t know if people know about his paintings, even now.”

After a year at the University of Rochester, Dunham followed Kendrick to Trinity College, in Hartford, where they worked in a small studio art department. “That meant smoking a lot of dope and reading Artforum,” said Dunham. On weekends, Dunham and Kendrick would drive down from Connecticut in Dad’s (Carroll IV’s) pickup truck, Kendrick recalled, to sample the new galleries in Soho—Bykert, Paula Cooper, Sonnabend, OK Harris—and to feast on spaghetti and jug wine at the apartment of their Trinity teacher Terence LaNoue.

LaNoue made almost three-dimensional combine paintings with poured latex and molds. He “was a great teacher, but I always had a kind of resistance to what he was making,” Dunham said. “And I’ve been that guy. I know that I’ve had good experiences between students and me where it really didn’t have to do with them being that turned on about my work.” Dunham never followed, either, in the footsteps of the artist with whom LaNoue installed him for a formative internship. Dorothea Rockburne produced—and still does, at 97—large, clean panes of paper or vellum, lined geometrically or coated in graphite. But the two got on, and still do. “Brighter than almost anybody around,” Rockburne said of him by phone.

What attracted Dunham was the planning implied by Rockburne’s planes—she taught him and Kendrick “how to handle a T-square and other basic things,” she said. He was also drawn to the repetitious text paintings of Mel Bochner (who lived with Rockburne), and to the heaps of raw material arranged by Barry Le Va and by Richard Serra. On graduating, he moved into a loft on Thomas Street shared with Kendrick and Peter Wheelwright, the architect. His 1970s and ’80s in New York were “isolation lite,” he told me. Dunham was part of no scene, he said, but befriended the photographers of the so-called Pictures Generation, and married one: Laurie Simmons. For seven years he worked in a frame shop, then for another seven at Time magazine, as a layout artist, all the while plotting his entrance into the art world.

DUNHAM’S ’70s ART BEGAN with single-line squiggles on canvas or paper. Some are elegantly coiled springs, while others resemble long strings dropped to the floor, their loops filled with ground colors of fast-drying casein or acrylic. He debuted with them at Artists Space in 1981, the Chicago survey was their first time on view since. Rockburne sees little of herself in Dunham’s famous later work. “It had that kind of [Sol] LeWittian, instructional aspect,” said the artist John Newman, another Dunham confederate from those days, by phone. “In the ’70s, drawing was sort of raised to a new place,” Newman explained, “as a much more immediate and idea-oriented kind of territory that wasn’t so laden with the history of painting and sculpture.”

The string-loops soon became blobs. When Dunham found the lid of a shipping crate on the street, around 1980, and used that for his surface, the almost sculptural grains and knots of the plywood veneer became guidelines for even more specific and conflicting blobs all mashed together—amoebas, geysers, wilting donuts, kinked tubes, beans, ripples, Froot Loops—in palettes ranging from medical textbook to clown paint. It is with these plywood paintings that the Miami survey begins. From 1984 to ’88, they appeared in three shows at the Baskerville + Watson gallery, with the middle show limited to monochromes.

“When the veneer things came out,” Newman recalled, it was amazing. “Think about the first time you ever read James Joyce. You really had to step up to it, participate in it. It was new information.” The art dealer David Nolan “hated them” at first, he said by phone: “I thought these garish, psychedelic colors were just there to shock me, and I just wasn’t interested.” But after a while, he began “to peel away the layers and see how they’re put together. And once I understood that, I thought, Oh God.”

The third show sold out before even opening, scoring acquisitions by the Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney, and the Brooklyn Museum. Dunham quit his magazine job. Gestural painting had been deemed safe again by young galleries, and although Dunham used a brand of biomorphism that didn’t quite fit with the headliners—Basquiat, Baselitz, Schnabel—he was made. Instead of buying up pallets of plywood and sticking safely to what worked, however, Dunham pivoted again. By the ’90s, his veneer paintings migrated to stretched linen, this time as single forms. They began to elongate into screaming fish-lipped mouths, nugget bodies, wincing faces, and undeniable penises. “They weren’t until they were,” Kendrick said of these organs. Nolan noticed them, too. But since they were untitled, Nolan said, “I thought he was avoiding what was right in front of our noses. They are bodily explosions. Come on.”

DUNHAM HAD BEEN PLENTY aware. He described the ’90s work to me as “abstraction with a hard-on.” But he seemed as bewildered as I about its origin. He spoke with plainness about sex and aggression as if he were a social worker, treating his own work as a sort of passive conduit for those realities. This tone did not seem to me like an act. I asked if he had tried to be provocative with his art, then or now. He said no: “It doesn’t interest me very much … The entire enterprise was provocative.” He spoke of Duchamp’s urinal.

Into the new century and his large survey at the New Museum in New York from 2002 to 2003, which was his last show of that scale until this year, his canvases begin to carry entire buildings and shiploads, colonies and planets full of hateful little nugget people with their penises, guns, and hideous gourd breasts. The exceptions from sex—lumpy tree scenes and landscapes—became the transgression. From there, he went more humanoid. In the past 20 years, his nuggets have grown up, first into suited G-men with fedoras and angular suits, then into cleanly clarified cartoon nudes, their globe buttocks outlined in elegant black and set in plain landscapes or rooms. They wrestle, fight, bathe, masturbate, copulate, and blind each other. They examine their gaping anuses, their big labia like bike tubes, and their nipples like air-hockey pushers.

These characters occupy about half the Miami paintings. In one, Horse and Rider (My X), 2013–15, a woman holds her arms up in a “Why me?” pose on the back of a horse. The lines of her reach continue south into a stand of flowers and a broken tree branch, dividing the canvas into a perfect X, which Dunham has left visible in pencil beneath the paint. At the geometric center is the woman’s anus, as if to say “Look here.” Just beneath, the horse’s anus gapes, too. He turns back at us with a look like “Excuse you.” (No human or humanoid, however, has eyes in a Dunham work.)

Dunham said of this X composition, “I was very excited when I figured out that that would work.” He explained: “It’s two layers of truth. There’s the subject and whatever that requires to be plausibly rendered.” (He counted “breasts, genitalia, asshole, some notion of limbs, and hair.”) “Then the geometry of the canvas has this other kind of truth, and the two things have to become one thing.” And the woman? “I honestly do not remember why I thought it would be interesting to put a woman on a horse in the paintings.” He thought. “It’s nice to have a black dot in the center of a painting. And it’s even nicer when that black dot is a woman’s ass, you know?”

Nolan was the only one I spoke to who saw strategy in Dunham’s turn to hyper-figuration. He saw the artist “dealing with his own demons or faults about the world.” But he described the work as Dunham did, composition-first. “If you try to forget there’s a face in there, the compositions are very strong.” He advised me to view the paintings upside down, pointing out convincing similarities to Aztecan decoration and adding that recently he, Nolan, had refused to sell one—for a lot of money—until the potential buyer flew to New York to see the shapes in person. “That is a problem with the younger generation. They will lose all of the subtleties.”

WHAT DOES THE YOUNGER generation think? The Miami show this winter (and the Chicago catalog forever) will give them the chance to see Dunham’s career as a single entity and to decide if the evolution of blob to aggression to anus stands up to the hindsight of a more literally minded era. In the purple alien characters on view at Matthew Brown this fall, from the series Dunham calls “Studio on Another Planet” (2022–26), one was hard-pressed not to read a narrative about artists at work in a culture that will misunderstand them: a solitary white male surrounded by voyeurs (critics? dealers? posterity?) as he quietly molds his clay on their land, incurring their sinister attentions. In the last of those canvases, Finished (2019–2025), the aliens have had enough. They’ve dragged the artist outside and are now quartering him to death.

“You’re not supposed to get it,” Newman said of Dunham’s pictures. “Art is about having an experience.” Newman speaks, Darwin-like, of Dunham’s characters emerging from the primordial soup of the plywood paintings. “Younger people probably don’t know the early work. And I actually think if they did, it would help them understand his later work better.” In my conversations with Camp 1, I began to wonder if there has ever been a generation more permissive, more game, than the one that had Dunham as a sort of living symbol of egress: out of the hermetic tasks of Minimalism, through pure shape, into a future where human fictions of any extreme can live without excuse or embarrassment. And I began to envy them.

I asked Dunham if he believed pure abstraction existed. He said yes, adding, “And I think that when I started my work, I was doing it. And then I think at a certain point I realized that it fascinated me to try to add some really literal aspects of just being a human being incarnated, or incarcerated, however you think about it, in a body.”

But I didn’t fully buy Dunham’s hermetic account of his own work as “always in some way self-referential.” There seems to be plenty of lived Artist v. World in his pictures and posture, and plenty of visual breadcrumbs leading to the culture at large. I asked, for instance, which cartoons he watched with his two children, who were born in 1986 and ’92. His eyes widened. “Ren & Stimpy was good,” he said of John Kricfalusi’s unhinged and influential program. “But the masterpiece of ’90s cartooning as far as I’m concerned was Angry Beavers,” which he watched with his son. I was fishing. The affinities between Dunham’s ’90s work and the prevailing depravities of Nickelodeon and Cartoon Network are inarguable; and in those affinities, a new generation may see homage to the last golden age of a truly transgressive child-absurd.

Speaking of his younger child, Dunham flashed back: “He came into my studio a lot. He would pick up on things I was drawing and then he would draw stuff of his own that was kind of like that. So I got a lot of, you know, 6- and 7-year-old energy coming back at me about my own work.” Dunham smiled. “It definitely encouraged a certain kind of energy. It’s very sweet to think about actually.”

item.title: Batima Zaurbekova’s Textiles Meld Traditional Kazakh Techniques with Modernist Influences, Defying Easy Categorization - ARTnews.com
item.description:
How does an artist sustain five decades of artistic production while remaining faithful to her cultural heritage? For Batima Zaurbekova, one of Kazakhstan’s most respected artists, the answer seems to be an unrelenting commitment to her craft. “You can’t be lazy,” the 80-year-old artist told me during a recent conversation.

That maxim is borne out in “Threads of Heritage,” a retrospective of more than 80 works at the Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts in Almaty, Kazakhstan. Her largest exhibition to date, it features the textiles she is known for as well as drawings and paintings. Curated by Alina Fedorovich, a curator at the Museum of Moscow, the exhibition traces a career in which tapestry becomes both a repository of cultural memory and a vehicle for artistic reinvention.

Rooted in traditional Kazakh textiles, her practice is also shaped by the influences of modernist painting and music, moving fluidly between abstraction and figuration and in turn, defying easy categorization. Her tapestries hold seemingly disparate influences, transforming traditional motifs into a distinct visual language. Ornamental Rug (1969), for example, revives motifs associated with horses, spiritual symbolism, and petroglyphs depicting mountain goats. Completed just after her graduation and the earliest work in the exhibition, Ornamental Rug provides a recognizable reference to the country’s landscape via the distinctive horns of the wild argali, a local mountain goat, while distilling these forms into rhythmic, stylized arrangements. The work’s title foregrounds the relationship between ornament and abstraction, suggesting how decorative forms can become a vehicle for modernist experimentation.

Zaurbekova grew up in the mountainous Zhambyl region of Kazakhstan, where textile-making was part of everyday life. She remembers watching older women create syrmak, traditional felt rugs, and kurak-korpe, patchwork quilts meaning “stitched from scraps.” Neighbors gathered to work, sing, cook, and share food, embodying the Kazakh tradition of asar, in which a community joins forces to help a household undertake a task, be it making a carpet or building a home.

Textile-making was as much a social practice as a technical one, transmitting skills and cultural knowledge across generations. This collective spirit is evoked in In the Yurt (1985), a weaving in which a maternal figure presides over the dastarkhan, the table prepared for guests. The yurt, a traditional felt dwelling associated with Kazakh nomadic life, becomes a symbol of hospitality, family, and belonging. Its ornaments merge with the surrounding figures, establishing a visual language equally rooted in the formal and the domestic.

In her youth, Zaurbekova had alternative ambitions for herself. “I really loved music, so I wanted to become a musician,” she recalled. However, her seamstress mother encouraged her to pursue painting instead. She is equally accomplished in oil painting and tapestry, and occasionally the same image is translated in both mediums.

Nevertheless, music has remained central to Zaurbekova’s life and practice, in which her visual compositions are animated by repetition, variation, and rhythm—the basic structure of music. This way of working is best observed in one gallery showing three works, each titled Composition and made in 1980, 2019, and 2024. Their stained-glass aesthetic, contrasting color planes, and rhythmic linear forms evoke Henri Matisse’s celebrated “Jazz” series. Undulating figures and vegetal motifs merge within an ornamental field, dissolving the distinction between figure and ground.

“Threads of Heritage” is being exhibited in dialogue with the museum’s collection of Kazakh decorative and applied art. Traditional felt objects, carpets, and ornaments establish the historical context out which Zaurbekova’s work emerges, while the installation reinforces the relationship between inherited forms and contemporary expression. Here, custom-built walls reference the architecture of the Khoja Ahmed Yasawi Mausoleum, an important historical monument whose forms recur in the artist’s imagery, like the monumental Antiquity (1993). The display also evokes the balbal, ancient stone monuments that connect contemporary life with earlier cultures.

The exhibition’s largest gallery showcases Zaurbekova’s technical mastery and evolving visual language. Each tapestry offers a dazzling array of color that boggles the mind. How, exactly, does she coax such subtle gradations from a seemingly limited collection of threads? “Selecting the right colors is a big part of the work—and it takes me a long time,” Zaurbekova explained. During the Soviet period, artists often dyed threads by hand, painstakingly creating transitions from darker to lighter shades. Although commercially produced threads from Belarus expanded her palette in the 1990s, Zaurbekova has continued to experiment, combining those threads and ones she has dyed to create colors all her own. “Kazakhstan, our land, is very rich, and this is represented in the rich colors of my work,” she told me.

Zaurbekova’s textiles are woven over several weeks to multiple months, and the artist still works for up to 18 hours a day. The vertical threads form the foundation of a given work, she explained, while horizontal threads of different colors construct the image. Through subtle variations in their combinations, Zaurbekova achieves tonal effects that can make woven surfaces appear almost painted. She is also deft at making alasha, a traditional yet simple Kazakh carpet.

Rather than presenting national identity as a fixed collection of symbols, her compositions transform familiar motifs through color and pattern. In keeping these traditions alive, Zaurbekova said she thinks “all of my work reflects our nationality and national pride.” Kazakhstan (1977) depicts themes of agriculture and collective labor. To make it, Zaurbekova used threads sourced from a Kazakh carpet manufacturer, working within the limitations of an existing palette to achieve subtle distinctions of tone. Her exacting yet delicate manipulation of the threads’ colors gives the woven surface a gentle vibration and shimmering quality. A work like this makes visible the precision and patience necessitated by such a craft.

A centerpiece of the exhibition is Vastness (1975), a large tapestry from the museum’s collection showing a bride associated with spring and Nauryz, the celebration of the spring equinox and new year. Around her, women gather at tables and a young man on horseback appears among the birds. Elsewhere, figures emerge from the surrounding forest, creating a dense tableau that feels as abstract as it is narrative. The exhibition’s final gallery focuses on the shanyrak, the circular wooden crown at the top of a traditional Kazakh yurt. A symbol of home and family, it serves an architectural motif representing womanhood. In Mother Earth (1984), connections between generations of women evoke the continuity of life and inherited knowledge. Zauberkova’s achievement lies not only in her sheer technical mastery, but in her ability to reinterpret Kazakh textile traditions through a vision that is unmistakably her own, creating work that is deeply rooted in its cultural origins while remaining formally inventive and alive.

item.title: The Power of Photography to Shape Britain’s History - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
Photography is not a neutral witness. Every image is shaped by the conditions of its making: the photographer’s position, the subject’s visibility and the political circumstances that determine what enters the frame. In moments of protest, these considerations become charged. The camera can expose abuses of power, preserve the presence of those excluded from official histories and transform individual acts of dissent into collective visual memory. Photographs also shape how resistance is grasped, influencing which movements gain recognition and which stories remain at the margins. This complex relationship between representation, political agency and historical memory underpins Resistance – How Protest Shaped Britain and Photography Shaped Protest, a major exhibition by Steve McQueen, now on view at Leeds Art Gallery.

The distinction between photography of protest and photography as protest provides an important starting point. An image may record a demonstration, but its circulation can extend the event’s political significance, turning a local confrontation into a wider demand for accountability. Equally, the absence of certain images from public archives reveals how historical narratives are shaped by institutional priorities, editorial decisions and unequal access to representation. Spanning a century of British activism, Resistance considers these tensions through photographs documenting movements from the radical suffragette movement of 1903 to the mass demonstration against the Iraq War in 2003. Its chronology encompasses struggles for workers’ rights, racial equality, nuclear disarmament, environmental protection and social justice, connecting campaigns through their demands for dignity, representation and political accountability. By concentrating on photographs made before digital cameras became commonplace, the exhibition also considers a visual culture in which images circulated through newspapers, publications, archives and personal collections, not the instantaneous networks that now shape political visibility.

This historical perspective acquires urgency within contemporary Britain. Questions of national identity, migration, belonging and democratic expression have become increasingly prominent in public debate, while the electoral growth of right-wing populism has brought renewed attention to the histories of anti-racist organising, anti-fascist resistance and grassroots solidarity. At the 2024 general election, Reform UK received 14.3 percent of the vote and won five parliamentary seats, establishing a significant electoral presence within the first-past-the-post system. The result brought renewed attention to the changing character of British political debate and the relationship between national identity, migration and political belonging. Against this backdrop, Resistance offers an opportunity to revisit how previous generations confronted racism, inequality and political exclusion, without suggesting that historical struggles can simply be mapped onto the present. Its significance lies in recovering the experiences of individuals who challenged established structures of power, often at considerable personal cost, and reminding audiences that democratic rights and social freedoms have never been an inevitability.

Photography’s role in shaping political consciousness has also become a subject of renewed curatorial attention. At South London Gallery, Acts of Resistance: Photography, Feminisms and the Art of Protest (2024), organised in collaboration with the V&A, brought together international artists and collectives examining how the camera might challenge conventional representations of activism. Its focus on intersectionality, transnational solidarity and digital technologies explored the relationship between feminist practice and contemporary political movements. A different but related historical perspective emerged through Women in Revolt! Art and Activism in the UK 1970–1990, which toured from Tate Britain to the Whitworth in Manchester and National Galleries of Scotland. Bringing together more than 90 women artists and collectives at its Whitworth presentation, the exhibition recovered the visual culture of feminist organising, anti-racist activism, the peace movement and queer liberation, demonstrating how artistic production developed alongside wider struggles for social change. Both exhibitions established important precedents for reconsidering the relationship between cultural production and political agency, a conversation that McQueen’s project extends through the specific lens of photographic history. 

The photographic record of the 1980s offers another important point of connection. Tate Britain’s The 80s: Photographing Britain (2024–2025) assembled nearly 350 images and archival materials, tracing how photographers, collectives and independent publications responded to the social and political upheavals of the Thatcher era. Race uprisings, the miners’ strike, Section 28, the AIDS epidemic and urban transformation formed the backdrop to practices that used photography to give visibility to communities frequently misrepresented or excluded from mainstream media. Its attention to collaborative networks and independent photographic publications also challenged the idea that photographic innovation emerges exclusively through individual practitioners. The exhibition demonstrated how collective practices can create alternative visual histories, notably when established media structures fail to represent specific communal experiences. McQueen’s project develops this thinking across a longer chronology, placing photographic practices in a century of protest instead of focusing on a single decade. 

The curatorial framework is central to this ambition. Conceived by McQueen and curated with Clarrie Wallis and Emma Lewis, Resistance brings together photographs from public archives, private collections and image libraries, placing celebrated practitioners alongside lesser-known photographers whose work might otherwise remain outside established accounts of British photographic history. The exhibition encompasses more than 40 photographers, allowing different approaches to documentary practice, reportage and visual testimony to exist in dialogue. Political research by Sarah Harrison provides a historical foundation, while the exhibition’s development through Turner Contemporary in Margate and National Galleries of Scotland: Modern Two in Edinburgh reflects a collaborative approach to presenting complex histories across different institutions. Its adaptation for Leeds, undertaken with curator Liza Butakova, creates an opportunity to consider how national narratives intersect with the histories and experiences of northern communities. Instead of organising protest into a succession of isolated political events, the curatorial approach suggests a continuous history of people challenging their living conditions.

In this wider account, individual photographic practices reveal the ways resistance becomes visible. Vanley Burke’s photographs of Black British life, specifically in Birmingham’s African-Caribbean communities, offer an important counterpoint to media representations that have historically framed these communities through the language of conflict or social crisis. His attention to everyday experience makes the personal inseparable from the political, recognising family life, neighbourhoods and cultural expression as essential parts of Britain’s social history. A similarly sustained engagement with working-class experience informs Tish Murtha’s photographs of young people in Newcastle’s west end during the early 1980s. Her images challenge the reductive visual language often applied to poverty and unemployment, presenting individuals whose lives cannot be understood through statistics or political rhetoric alone. Together, these practices show that documenting a community can become an act of resistance, particularly when its members have been denied the authority to represent their own experiences.

Questions of class, labour and social visibility also run through the work of Humphrey Spender and Fay Godwin, although their approaches reveal different dimensions of documentary practice. Spender’s involvement in Mass Observation placed photography within a wider attempt to record the habits, environments and social structures of ordinary British life, questioning what should count as historically significant. His work suggests that the everyday can be as revealing as the extraordinary, particularly when viewed against the political and economic conditions that shape it. Godwin’s wider photographic practice, meanwhile, brings questions of landscape, public access and environmental responsibility into the discussion, broadening the definition of resistance beyond the familiar image of a demonstration or confrontation. Her engagement with the British landscape invites consideration of who has the right to occupy, traverse and determine the use of shared spaces. Such perspectives recognise that political agency is not confined to moments of visible dissent; it is also expressed through the defence of common resources, cultural identity and the conditions of our everyday existence.

The relationship between the photographer and the protester becomes charged in images of organised racism and public opposition. Paul Trevor’s image of anti-racists gathering to block the route of a National Front demonstration on New Cross Road in August 1977 captures a moment when the street became a contested political space. The image records more than a confrontation between opposing groups; it preserves evidence of collective opposition to the public expression of racial hatred. Its historical weight also lies in the way it makes visible those who chose to intervene, not positioning protestors solely as spectators to political events. Other photographers in the exhibition, including Edith Tudor-Hart, Christine Spengler, Andrew Testa, Henry Grant and Janine Wiedel, extend this visual history through different forms of documentary engagement, from social observation to political reportage. Their juxtaposition resists a singular definition of protest photography, suggesting that its meaning emerges through the relationship between the image, its subject, the circumstances of its production and the audience it encounters.

These histories also raise significant questions about the ethics of photographic representation. Documentary photography has long been shaped by tensions between witnessing and appropriation, particularly when images depict communities experiencing poverty, discrimination or violence. Who has the authority to tell another person’s story, and what responsibilities accompany the act of recording their struggle? By bringing established photographers into conversation with lesser-known practitioners and archival material, Resistance complicates the conventional emphasis on individual authorship and the idea of the photograph as an uncomplicated historical document. The archive itself becomes a subject of scrutiny: a space in which decisions about preservation, attribution and visibility determine which experiences survive in collective memory. This shifts the exhibition’s attention from what photographs show to how they acquire meaning, authority and historical significance.

Leeds provides a particularly meaningful setting for these conversations. As the exhibition’s North of England venue, Leeds Art Gallery offers an opportunity to encounter national histories of protest from a region with its own substantial traditions of industrial activism, labour organisation and community resistance. The arrival of Resistance is especially welcome for audiences across Yorkshire and neighbouring northern communities, where questions of class, identity, political representation and social justice remain deeply embedded in cultural life. Its presentation also contributes to a wider discussion about the geographical distribution of major exhibitions, challenging the assumption that significant artistic and intellectual conversations must remain concentrated in London and the South East. There is considerable value in bringing this material to Leeds, where visitors can consider the relationship between the histories represented in the photographs and the communities, landscapes and political experiences that surround them. The gallery becomes more than a venue for a touring exhibition; it offers a space in which national histories can be reconsidered through regional perspectives.

The exhibition’s significance lies in its insistence that photography is never simply a record of events, but an active force in shaping how they are understood. Bringing together images made across a century of political and social struggle, it invites us to consider whose experiences have been made visible, whose voices have been marginalised and how collective memory is constructed. At a time when the language of division is once again prominent in public life, these photographs carry renewed urgency. They remind us that the rights and freedoms often taken for granted were hard won through the determination of individuals and communities prepared to challenge the status quo. Resistance asks us to look again at Britain’s history, and to recognise the continuing power of images to shape how that history is told.

Steve McQueen: Resistance is at Leeds Art Gallery until 25 April.

museumsandgalleries.leeds.gov.uk
