item.title: The “Amphibian Modernist” Who Refused to Imitate - Hyperallergic
item.description:
GUANGZHOU, China — In a June 1985 article in the Venezuelan newspaper El Nacional, painter Oswaldo Vigas decried the exhibition Rauschenberg and the Third World, a traveling show organized by the Rauschenberg Overseas Culture Interchange (ROCI) program at Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Caracas. “Latin America, both in its literature and in its visual arts, has always been characterized by possessing its own languages, through which it expresses conceptions of the world and of humanity that have nothing to envy in those developed by those other societies,” the late Venezuelan artist wrote of Robert Rauschenberg’s paternalistic Cold War initiative. “If there is anything important I see in this exhibition … it is its value as an example of precisely what we Latin Americans neither should nor have any reason to imitate.” 

A giant of the Latin American avant-garde who worked between his home country and Paris, Vigas, who died in 2014, helped define a modernism that resisted Eurocentric ideals. Instead, he favored experimentation that reflected Venezuela’s Indigenous past and a hopeful vision for the future. This struggle — and fusion — between aesthetics and culture is at the center of the Guangdong Museum of Art’s survey of the artist’s work, Reality Is What I Imagine.

item.title: Rare Marie Antoinette ‘Breast Bowl’ Hammers for $2.47 M. in Paris, Surpassing Top Estimate - ARTnews.com
item.description:
One of the last known “Breast Bowls” still in private hands that once belonged to Queen Marie Antoinette has just hammered for €2.25 million ($2.47 million), or €2,945 million with fees ($3.23 million), at the Coutau-Begarie & Associés evening auction in Paris’s Hôtel Drouot, beating its high estimate of €2 million ($2.19 million).

Legend has it that this series of 18th-century porcelain bowls, made by the Royal Sèvres manufacturers, was modeled after the ill-fated French queen’s real breasts. While no documented proof of such a legend exists, the so-called “jatte-téton” or “nipple bowls,” painted in fleshy light pink with an areola and nipple at the tip, do have a surrealistic, convincingly realistic quality, despite a too-perfectly circular shape.

Made in 1787, the bowl in question was in fact inspired by ancient Greek mastos, or breast-shaped drinking cups used at banquets dating back to the 6th century BC. It is one of four highly prized jatte-tétons delivered that year and in 1788, destined for the royal “pleasure dairy” in Rambouillet, near Versailles, that King Louis XVI gifted to Marie Antoinette. There, per the fashion of the time, nobility would gather to socialize and taste an assortment of fine milk, cream, and cheese delicacies prepared for them.

The rare breast bowl comes from the collection of French dealer Claude Meyer, who passed away in November 2025. His children happened upon it while going through boxes of storage, and learned that their late father, whose Paris gallery closed in the 1990s, had never offered it for sale. It is unclear how Meyer acquired the piece, which is known to have once belonged to the French Marquise de Chanaleilles.

Three of the four breast bowls made in 1787 and 1788 for the queen’s royal dairy dishes are housed in public collections today, including two at the Musée de Sèvres and one at the Museo Duca di Martina in Naples. The bowl that sold tonight is the last of that specific series. They are “the most celebrated and the most extravagant shape of the porcelain service,” by the royal Sèvres manufactory for the queen’s dairy, notes the auction house in its description.

With the bowl comes an intricately carved tripod stand decorated with goat heads in relief, as seen above. Indeed, the breast bowls require a pedestal to hold them upside down, as it were, so as to contain the milk and cream they were meant to serve.

Speaking to Le Journal des Arts about the bowl, auctioneer Alexandre de La Forest Divonne observed: “It has become something of a symbol of the queen; it is truly a totem.”

item.title: Faurschou New York Officially Shutters Greenpoint Museum - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.

A Greenpoint Private Museum Is No Longer

Faurschou New York, a private art museum in Brooklyn's Greenpoint neighborhood, will no longer host exhibitions as its building is slated for demolition to make way for condos. The institution closed "for renovations" last year, and now its founder, collector Jens Faurschou, officially announced in a statement that the museum will not be reopening. “After forty years, my direction changes,” he wrote. “I will focus on what is essential: my family, private dealing, and working closely with artists, institutions, and collections.”

The space started as Galleri Faurschou in Copenhagen in 1986 and later expanded to Beijing. The New York outpost was opened in 2019, hosting exhibitions including Ai Weiwei's What You See Is What You See, a 2024 show that Hyperallergic's co-founder and editor-at-large Hrag Vartanian said pushed viewers “to assert our own agency in our interpretations.”

item.title: Unmaking the World With Jack Halberstam - Hyperallergic
item.description:
For decades, Jack Halberstam has been extolling the virtues of not doing what we’re supposed to — or not doing anything at all. In 2011’s The Queer Art of Failure, for instance, the pioneering gender and queer theorist posited failing as a form of creative resistance to capitalist concepts of success; in 2020’s Wild Things: The Disorder of Desire, he suggested “wildness” as a force of queer disruption to the status quo; and in 1998’s seminal Female Masculinity, he reimagined masculinity severed from maleness. His latest book, Anarchitecture After Everything: A Trans Manifesto (2026), treads further still into the terrain of queer opposition with a philosophy of unmaking and reorganizing the built environment, which he calls “unworlding,” in order to dismantle heteronormative social structures.

In contrast to “world-building,” which seeks to enact change within the parameters of these systems, Halberstam explains that “an unworld is not simply the opposite of the world we inhabit … An unworld must also unthink the logics of this world that make contemporary life under capitalism seem inevitable and right.”

The book’s thesis is summarized in its first sentence: “Anarchitecture, a set of art practices that emerged in the 1970s out of experiments with the sculpting of abandoned buildings, offers an expansive language for thinking about how bodies (and specifically trans bodies) emerge as a consequence of cutting, breaking, dismantling, and collapse.” Since space and bodies organize our daily lives and larger economic and sociopolitical sphere, “cutting” them isn’t just a symbolic act; as Halberstam writes, it’s about making “strategic cuts into the support system for our unfriendly climate and our racist world.”

item.title: Iraq Reopens and Invites You to Visit Its Museums - Hyperallergic
item.description:
After a record-high 10 million tourists visited the country in 2025, Iraq has renewed its commitment to investing in its travel and tourism sectors through cultural institutions, heritage and archaeological sites, and religious attractions.

Ali al-Dakhili, the Iraqi Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, recently announced that the Iraq Museum in Baghdad will reopen this December, while three new museums are planned for the provinces of Nineveh, Diyala, and Diwaniyah. Al-Dakhili publicized the Ministry's intentions as Iraq inaugurated its first museum devoted to Iraqi-Jewish history at the recently renovated historic Shamash Jewish School in Baghdad late last month.

item.title: At the Broad, Six Decades of Art Question the Myth of Progress - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Two weeks after the 1992 Los Angeles uprising, Los Angeles Times reporter Janny Scott published an essay confronting her own complacency toward the city’s stark inequalities. For years, she’d witnessed the chasm widen between women carrying $3,500 handbags and those wearing trash bags; from her “nice neighborhood where the helicopters don’t come,” she did little to address the disparity. Still, the unrest that followed the acquittal of four LAPD officers charged with beating Rodney King seemed to have broken through the collective apathy. Angelenos, she wrote, were suddenly talking about “things that matter”: race, guilt, poverty, urban policy, to name a few. Despite history offering little reason for optimism, Scott confessed to a sense of hope: “I’m nurturing my first illusion.”

More than three decades later, artist Guadalupe Rosales found a copy of the newspaper containing Scott’s article on eBay. The headlines “Seeing Ourselves” and “Has the Myth Been Shattered?” registered the same discrepancy she sensed between what she remembered as a child growing up in East LA and how the press perpetuated myths about the city’s seeming collectivity. Rosales was 11 years old in 1992, and she has a distinct memory of her mother rushing the family home from school as smoke stained the usually sun-drenched California sky. As an adult, Rosales has amassed an archive of clippings, photographs, and other ephemera of Chicanx youth culture—much of it crowdsourced through social media—that serves as both a bulwark against that dissonance and a counter to historical erasure and amnesia. “I’m not looking for answers,” she told ARTnews. “But for some kind of physical proof that things really happened, that they’re not just in our memories.”

Rosales’s 2024 sculpture Has the myth been shattered encases that infamous yellowed newspaper in a nearly six-foot-tall aluminum frame fitted with a two-way mirror, illuminated by colorful LED lights. Though it resembles a doorway, the work offers no passage; instead, viewers face their own reflections superimposed over the 1992 text, along with photographs of palm trees and police. The temporal distance between then and now collapses onto a single plane, leaving Scott’s question perpetually suspended in the present.

The work also lends its title to a just-opened exhibition at the Broad in downtown LA. Organized by assistant curator Jen Vanegas Rocha, the presentation brings together works by more than a dozen artists spanning six decades. Recent acquisitions by Rosales and Hank Willis Thomas appear alongside art by Andy Warhol, Barbara Kruger, Glenn Ligon, and Robert Longo, among others. Across prints, paintings, drawings, sculpture, and tapestry, artists appropriate text and images from various forms of public record, drawing attention to the ways media shapes perception of major sociopolitical events. Seen together, the works undermine the assumption that exposing injustice inevitably leads to redress. “There are echoes of the present in the past,” Willis Thomas said. “So is the past present or is the present past?”

The Broad’s founding director, Joanne Heyler, sees that unease as central to the exhibition’s timeliness. “The notion of a linear progression of change unfolding in a dependable, escalating way,” she said, is “becoming harder and harder to believe in.”

Consider the oldest work in the show, Andy Warhol’s Race Riot (1963), in which police dogs attack Black civil-rights demonstrators in Birmingham, Alabama. In 2026, the decades-old image calls to mind the police response to the 2020 protests following the murder of George Floyd, as well as the more recent pro-Palestine and anti-ICE demonstrations nationwide, in which protestors were often battered and tear-gassed. Warhol lifted the photograph directly from a visual essay by Charles Moore in Life magazine, translating the confrontation into a monochromatic silkscreen. Adopting the incendiary rhetoric of contemporary news coverage, he labeled the peaceful demonstrators “rioters.” Race Riot reflects the artist’s own reckoning with the contradictions at the heart of American life: His obsession with celebrities and mass consumption give way to the sensationalized images of death and violence that belie it, like the mangled cars and electric chairs that also feature in his “Death and Disaster” series. Viewers are left to consider whether the relentless circulation of violence sharpens public outrage or gradually dulls our empathy.

For Willis Thomas, Warhol’s Birmingham silkscreen paintings function as “postcards to the future.” By transforming them from documentation to works of art, Warhol has made a case for their continued relevance. Nearby, Willis Thomas’s photo-based Black Survival Guide, or How to Live Through a Police Riot (2018) revisits the same era to recover another history largely omitted from public memory. While researching the aftermath of Martin Luther King Jr.’s assassination, he discovered a typewritten pamphlet offering practical advice to Black residents of Wilmington, Delaware, during the nine-month National Guard occupation in 1968. Onto retroreflective vinyl, Willis Thomas printed excerpts from the pamphlet—advice on how to staunch bleeding or communicate during a power outage, for example—atop archival News Journal photographs of confrontations between armed soldiers and the city’s Black communities. Installed in a darkened gallery, the black-and-white images are invisible until a flash of light illuminates them. Rather than merely encountering the past, the audience actively aids in its recovery. “In some ways the observers become the researchers,” he said.

Histories of state-sanctioned violence and resistance movements similarly converge across a nearly eleven-foot-wide canvas in Mickalene Thomas’s 2021 mixed-media painting The Charnel House (Resist #5). Reworking Picasso’s 1944–45 masterpiece of corpses heaped beneath a table made in response to news footage of liberated Nazi concentration camps, Thomas collages photographs and placards from the Civil Rights and Black Lives Matter movements with the modernist’s fragmented anatomical forms. A poster advertising the Black Panther Party’s free breakfast program appears beside a portrait of Angela Davis and the names of Freddie Gray and Alton Sterling, both killed during encounters with police. Here, grief and trauma are paired with resistance and community building.

The language of dissent assumes a subtler register in Ligon’s Narratives (1993), a suite of nine sepia-toned etchings that mimic the ornate typography and florid prose of 19th-century slave narratives. Ligon replaces accounts of enslavement and escape with details from his early education at a predominantly white private school, his desire for other men, and the circumstances of his career as an artist. In his hands, a literary form that freed Black people used to demonstrate their humanity becomes a medium for contemporary self-portraiture and self-determination.

Museums, of course, too, play a role in shaping public records. Over the past five years, the Broad has acquired work by 26 artists previously unrepresented in its collection, many of whom are of a younger generation and, like Rosales, actively working in LA. Heyler sees these acquisitions as part of an ongoing effort to better reflect the multiplicity of the communities that surround the institution. “We’re not telling one story but many,” she said. “We’re always striving to strengthen the connective tissues between them.”

The exhibition offers an opportunity to showcase many of the newly acquired artists and to extend an art-historical conversation that Heyler traces to exhibitions like “A Forest of Signs: Art in the Crisis of Representation,” a landmark 1989 survey at the Museum of Contemporary Art, just across the street. Bringing together works by 30 American artists, from Jeff Koons to Jenny Holzer, that show examined the unstable boundaries between reality and representation in an increasingly media-saturated society. But the terrain has evolved, Heyler noted. Where artists of that period often exposed the ideologies concealed by authoritative and commercial imagery, audiences today, immersed in social media and generative AI, navigate what she called a “stew of falsehoods and truths.”

Even so, curator Vanegas Rocha hopes her exhibition inspires something more generative than cynicism, in which artists can be seen as the “architects of better futures.” She locates the potential for systemic change in the power of an individual aesthetic encounter. “It can teach you about the world, about others, about yourself,” she said. “That single moment can have a ripple effect, leading to a collective difference.” Rosales, likewise, hasn’t relinquished hope. Citing José Esteban Muñoz’s 2009 queer theory book Cruising Utopia, she described hope as an ever-receding horizon that we must continue to endeavor toward. “We are a people that don’t give up,” she said, noting that her mother also took her to protests from an early age. “Standing up for each other, even when you don’t see it right away, does pay off.” Progress, she suggests, may not be linear or inevitable, but that doesn’t make it an illusion. In her mirror, the unresolved question—“Has the Myth Been Shattered?”—is cast back onto the people who might yet determine the answer.

item.title: Juno Calypso’s Retro-Futurist World - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
Juno Calypso (b. 1989) is the protagonist of her own retro-futurist world. Her alter-ago, Joyce, is a “bored, frustrated, lonely housewife of her imagination” and often staged in surreal settings. Her sinister, alluring portraits are a critical take on modern rituals of beauty and seduction. They’ve become part of a wider cultural moment across art and literature, where audiences are leaning into media about “feminine rage.” Consider horror films like The Substance or Ready or Not, projects that are often cited as “good for her” genres. One of her images graced the cover of Eliza Clark’s She’s Always Hungry, a short story collection that explores human desire. In the shot, a discoloured, green hand pokes out of a pink bathtub, it’s nails perfectly painted and manicured. In Calypso’s work – as in Clark’s writing – there’s a disquieting sense of disillusionment with modern beauty standards and gender expectations. Immersed in a trademark palette of pastel pinks and bruising blues, the artist explores these of femininity, solitude, despair and desire. 

Empty Pleasures, set to go on display at The Print Sales Gallery at The Photographers’ Gallery, brings together highlights from previous projects with new works that incorporate collage and found imagery for the first time. Using new photographs, alongside found images from the 1970s and 1980s, Calypso cuts, mirrors and recombines fragments to create images which feel both nostalgic and uncanny. The artist describes this way of working: “Photo manipulation has always been a part of my work. I would blend two images, copying and pasting elements of each photograph together to create an illusion of perfection and harmony.” In the new forms, Calypso pushes this concept further. Her figures multiply into kaleidoscopic forms and ghostly apparitions as the pursuit of perfection begins to unravel and the distinction between physical reality and reimagining becomes increasingly blurred. 

These images feel like a natural continuation from Calypso’s earlier work. She keeps a list of dream locations to shoot in, from an underground bunker in Las Vegas to romantic hotels in Pennsylvania. Here, contemporary locations give way to historic ones, where traditional scenes of mountain ranges are overlayed with a modern kitchen. In Tuesday in Eternity, wooden structures collide with dishwashers, allowing time to crumple in on itself. Elsewhere, a snapshot of a room is disrupted by the white silhouettes of two figures, almost like ghostly apparitions. Unusual for Calpyso, they’re figures without distinct character – perhaps echoing another facet of the female experience. 

Calypso’s work really does conjure up another world. Audiences are taken through the looking glass, into an uncanny scene that echoes aesthetics we’re familiar with, without giving way to them entirely. In doing so, she reminds us that everything is not always as it seems – we just need to pay attention.

Juno Calypso: Empty Pleasures is at The Print Sales Gallery at The Photographers’ Gallery, London until 24 January: thephotographersgallery.org.uk

Words: Emma Jacob

item.title: Hoor Al Qasimi Named Curator of 2028 Venice Biennale - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Sheikha Hoor Al Qasimi has been named curator of the 2028 edition of the Venice Biennale, the world’s biggest recurring art exhibition running from April 8 to November 26, 2028. Al Qasimi is also president and director of the Sharjah Art Foundation, a member of the United Arab Emirates’s Sharjawi royal family and president of the Sharjah Museums Authority.

The board of La Biennale di Venezia said it met on November 20 to pick Al Qasimi on the recommendation of president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco. Al Qasimi will be tasked with curating the 62nd edition of the exhibition and will take on the title of director of the visual arts department.

“La Biennale di Venezia is a place where the world converges with art through its diverse visions. Throughout her career, Hoor Al Qasimi has succeeded in creating a caravanserai of geographies and the Universal, giving voice to stories and sensibilities shaped by research and the unexpected,” said Buttafuoco in a statement on Thursday. “Her work brings together a profound attentiveness to deep-rooted memory and its legacies, an open perspective on the intricate complexities of the present, and a rare ability to listen to places and their people. I also recognize in her a quality of balance and composure, namely the vibrant presence of mīzān (inner harmony), which finds its strength in relationships.”

The taking of an art biennale is nothing new to Al Qasimi. In 2024, she was appointed by the Biennale of Sydney as the artistic director of the exhibition’s 25th edition, which ran from March 7 to June 8, 2026. However, the Venice Biennale is of a larger scale on an international stage. “The international art exhibition of La Biennale di Venezia has been an important platform for many of us around the world. I first visited the 50th edition in 2003 having recently stepped into my curatorial role at Sharjah Biennial,” said Al Qasimi in a statement on Monday. “For me, La Biennale continues to be a critical space to engage with the work of influential artists and curators. I am honored to have been invited to curate this exhibition and grateful to president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, and the board for their confidence and trust.”

item.title: A New Home for LondonMuseum Opens in Smithfield - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
This weekend, London Museum marks its 50th anniversary by opening the doors of its new home, following an ambitious decade-long transformation of the historic Smithfield General Market. Visitors will enter via a converted street, filled with exhibits that reflect “the capital of today.” Known as Real Time, the opening section is populated with animated screens that explore contemporary life, including everything from the city’s pub and bee populations to Londoners’ changing moods and weekly listening habits. Here, audiences will also encounter a police sentry box by Banksy, spray-painted to resemble a tank full of piranhas. It’s an experience that sets the stage for what is to come: an electric display with its finger firmly on the pulse.

At the heart of the museum is Our Time, set across the former trading floor of the General Market. The theme of this area is human connection – with highlights including the Buckingham Palace switchboard, decommissioned in 1970 and on view for the first time. The gallery also celebrates the places where Londoners gather, featuring 20 striking signs including examples from fabric nightclub, the Galtymore Dance Club, Topshop and the original Morley’s Chicken Shop in Sydenham. This is an exciting multimedia space, incorporating the voices of London’s Generation Alpha, as well as sounds of the city – “from the rattle of city buses to the ticking of Big Ben” – which are included in a new soundscape crafted by electronic musician Scanner. Elsewhere, a powerful film from John Ogunmuyiwa brings together historic and more recent footage, documenting everything from street parties to political protests.

The next gallery, Past Time, invites audiences to venture underground. Set at Roman street level, it foregrounds the people and events that have shaped London’s “storied and sometimes turbulent” history, from prehistoric inhabitants who settled by the Thames, to today’s bustling global population. There’s a wealth of objects on view, including everything from a 2,000-year-old wall painting to Tom Daley’s London 2012 Olympic diving trunks. The multimedia experience continues here: visitors can eavesdrop on everyday dramas in Londinium as they step into a Roman shop, walk through scenes from the Great Fire, or follow an animal trail that brings London’s creatures, past and present, to life.

The museum places a significant focus on power, protest and activism, with an unparalleled collection of militant suffragette material – including Emmeline Pankhurst’s hunger strike medal. Elsewhere, photographs by contemporary artist Ajamu X represent the lost likenesses of Black abolitionists, there’s a statuette of Lady Phyll, co-founder of UK Black Pride, and audiences will encounter placards from trailblazing disabled-led group Transport for All. Beyond this, London’s status as a home for music, fashion and the arts shines through. On loan from Paul Simonon of The Clash is the smashed Fender Precision Bass guitar, immortalised on the cover of the band’s 1979 album London Calling. Further highlights include a chair owned by Charles Dickens; eye-catching stage outfits from international music hall star Kitty Lord; tablas belonging to British Bhangra pioneer Kuljit Bhamra; and Anna Pavlova’s Dying Swan costume.

This opening is a landmark moment, both for the capital and the heritage sector more broadly. London Museum holds the world’s largest collection relating to a single urban centre, and this new location reflects an ambition to continue to evolve alongside the city it documents. It embraces audience engagement and interactivity without losing sight of its historical foundations. Sharon Ament, Director of London Museum, said: “After a decade of imagining, planning, building and creating, it is extraordinary to finally throw open the doors and welcome people into our new home in Smithfield. This project has been an enormous collective endeavour, collaborating with over 100,000 people to create a museum that could only belong to London. This is the city’s story in all its grit and glitter, created together with some of the best designers, historians, curators, builders, architects, poets, writers, illustrators, photographers and shapers of the capital. There is so much to see and explore. Whether you’re a local or first-time visitor to London, we hope our museum is somewhere you can feel at home, feel inspired and find connection.”

London Museum opens its free permanent galleries in the General Market on 28 November.

londonmuseum.org.uk

Words: Eleanor Sutherland

All images: Hufton + Crow

item.title: Democrat Lawmaker Vows to Investigate Trump's Smithsonian Plan - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Democratic Representative Chellie Pingree of Maine has vowed to investigate the Trump administration's leaked overhaul plan of the Smithsonian Institution, in a letter sent to the Smithsonian's Board of Regents yesterday, November 24.

This week, photos a commuter took of a Trump staffer's laptop screen showing the so-called "Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan" were dispatched to ProPublica. The document included planned reviews of the institution's exhibition and funding strategies, new exhibitions on American nationalism, and revamped institution-wide guidelines.

If instituted, the 25 measures outlined in the plan could upend the Smithsonian's autonomous operations across its network of 21 museums, research centers, and the National Zoo.

item.title: Black Trauma and the Scars of Childhood - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The most unreasonable expression I heard as a child is now the title of Lex Marie’s solo exhibition at The Bishop Gallery. “Because I Said So,” a quote that silenced many discussions and caused a mountain of confusion for children around the world, is transformed into a site that intends to unpack the entanglement of corporal punishment and care within Black households.

Marie presents 21 works. The dominant material? Belts. In this context, their practical purpose is stripped away, and they become an emotionally charged object used to investigate cultural practices.

item.title: Smithsonian Head Assures Staff of Independence After Glimpse of White House Overhaul Plan - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Outgoing Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie G. Bunch III reasserted the institution’s independence in a letter to his staff after a leaked document from a Trump aide laid out a sweeping overhaul of its programming and personnel.

“The intended use of this list is unclear,” Bunch wrote in the letter, which the New York Times reviewed and first reported. “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programs.”

The document, titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan,” was photographed on a laptop that a Trump aide was using on the Washington Metro. As first reported by ProPublica, its 25-item action list includes plans to dismiss top curators and administrators, among them Anthea M. Hartig, director of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, whom the White House has accused of promoting “radical activist ideology.”

The plan also calls for a new permanent exhibit, “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance,” and another on “Great Families of American History.” It envisions a “Colossus Statue” of George Washington at the museum’s entrance, which would fulfill a request Trump made in September.

The plan appears to be a work in progress: Photos show the aide brainstorming additions in a notebook. One handwritten entry seems to read “No X-rated exhibition policy,” an apparent callback to a particularly contentious stretch of Hartig’s testimony, when lawmakers questioned her about images of bondage wear in an LGBTQ history exhibition. On Monday, ProPublica identified the staffer as an associate policy adviser with the Domestic Policy Council, the White House office behind a 162-page report that accused the Smithsonian of “extreme political activism that seeks to transform our country.”

A central complaint of the report was what its authors characterized as anti-white bias at the museum, which they said showed in its promotion of diversity, equity, and inclusion. The report accused one exhibition, “Many Voices, One Nation,” of trying “to convince visitors that illegal aliens are entitled to citizenship, voting rights and ‘belonging’ in America.” (Two weeks after the report’s release, Trump signed an executive order directing that signs be installed outside the museum warning visitors of its “ideological capture.”)

The document glimpsed on the staffer’s laptop laid out new interpretive guidelines for exhibits, including an explicit end to the Smithsonian’s use of a diversity style guide. The Smithsonian’s strategy for traveling exhibitions would be reviewed, and one show now on tour, “The Bias Inside Us,” would be halted. Grants to “woke third parties,” such as the American Alliance of Museums, would also be reviewed.

The Smithsonian’s online K-12 curriculum would be overhauled to “realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology.” The “Becoming US” module on immigration, for example, would be deleted and replaced with a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage.”

The Smithsonian, a network of 21 museums, is structured to operate independently of the White House. It’s governed by a 17-member Board of Regents: the Chief Justice of the United States, John G. Roberts Jr.; the Vice President, JD Vance; six members of Congress from both parties; and nine private citizens. Legally, the Smithsonian answers to Congress, not the White House, but federal money makes up about 60 percent of its budget. Trump proposed cutting that funding by roughly 12 percent for fiscal year 2026, a threat that ultimately went unrealized.

Bunch, who became secretary in 2019, has repeatedly asserted the institution’s legal independence as pressure from the White House has mounted. The administration has demanded that the Smithsonian turn over internal materials and pushed for the firing of Kim Sajet, the director of the National Portrait Gallery, whom Trump had called “highly partisan.” Sajet ultimately resigned. Bunch has drawn similar attacks: a White House aide reportedly called him a “rabid partisan.”

In a May interview with the New York Times, Bunch seemed to acknowledge that recent vacancies on the Board of Regents had weakened his position, though he still appeared to have the support of a majority of the board. In September, he announced that he would retire at the end of the year.

In his letter to staff on Tuesday, Bunch wrote, “As I have said before, we welcome scrutiny of our work, and even disagreement. The Smithsonian will continue to be driven by scholarship, research and reflection, free from outside influence and in service to the American people.”

item.title: Tate Liverpool Plans Fall 2027 Reopening With Surrealism Survey - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Tate Liverpool will reopen in fall 2027 after a £30 million transformation with the exhibition “Surrealism: Staging Dream Worlds,” a nod to the museum’s inaugural Surrealist show in 1988.

The surrealism exhibition will run from fall 2027 to spring 2028 and include works by Salvador Dalí, Eileen Agar and Man Ray. According to Tate Liverpool, the show will also explore the “important role of surrealism in the history of theater and dance” through the movement’s major commissions for stage sets and costumes. Also on view will be Dorothea Tanning’s costume designs for the ballet The Witch, photographs of Sheila Legge performing as the “Surrealist Phantom of Sex Appeal” at the opening of the 1936 International Surrealist Exhibition in London, and material from the archive of Ted Joans.

“Surrealism invites us to see the world differently and what better way to reopen Tate Liverpool. This exhibition will spark imaginations, surprise visitors and reward curiosity, offering a fresh perspective on one of art’s most celebrated movements. It also brings a wonderful echo of the surrealist exhibition that opened our gallery in 1988, while taking visitors on an exciting new journey,” said Jemima Pyne, interim director of the Tate Liverpool, in a statement.

Tate Liverpool closed in October 2023 and was scheduled to reopen in 2025, but fundraising difficulties pushed the date back to 2027. The architecture firm 6a architects is redesigning the gallery’s home, an 1846 warehouse on the Royal Albert Dock, as part of a £35 million ($46.5 million) renovation.

item.title: Shahzia Sikander Sculpture in St. Louis Generates Protests and Counterprotests - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Activists against women’s right to choose in relation to their reproductive rights protested a sculpture by Shahzia Sikander in St. Louis this week, calling for the removal of the 18-foot-tall work titled Witness (2023).

As reported by St. Louis’s First Alert 4, protesters associating the sculpture with pro-choice abortion rights gathered outside the home base of Rung for Women, a nonprofit devoted to women’s career development that hosts it. As the organization describes itself on its website, “Too many women are unfulfilled, unhappy, and underpaid in their jobs, but afraid to take the leap into the unknown. We designed a program to guide motivated women through a process to start working in exciting careers and get paid what they’re worth.”

First Alert 4 quoted an activist with a group called Students for Life America associating Sikander’s sculpture with the overturning of Roe v. Wade in 2022. “Her skirt spells Hava, which is Eve, the first female rebel, to breathe life,” said Reagan Barklage, who related the work to the late US Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg. “It’s just, you do not need to kill your children in order to breathe life. That’s actually the exact opposite of what that means.”

She continued: “We’re alarmed that this is what they’re choosing to use to represent our city. We do not stand for these pro-abortion rights. And we’re trying to stand for women and true empowerment.”

A counterprotester thought otherwise. “We’re here because this organization that’s located on this block has every right to display whatever artwork they want on their own property,” said Leslie Zacks, who spoke of the protest in the context of a recently failed amendment that would have reinstated a near-total abortion ban. “The reality of the situation is that the people in Missouri have twice had the opportunity to voice their preferences with regards to the abortion issue and have made it very, very clear with increasing majority where their preferences are.”

Rung for Women issued a statement saying the organization “respects the right of individuals to express their views about art, including those that differ from our own. We recognize that Witness has prompted strong reactions and respect the sincerely held beliefs of those who have expressed concern. We remain proud to host this work by Shahzia Sikander at Rung for Women.”

The same sculpture by Sikander was the subject of heated protest in Texas in 2024, when it was decried by a group that called it “satanic” before it was to go on view at the University of Houston. After an opening and artist talk related to the work were subsequently canceled, Sikander said, “Art should be about discourse and not censorship. Shame on those that silence artists.”

An attempt by ARTnews to reach the artist was not immediately successful.

item.title: Dead Man Is Accused of Stealing Art from Michigan Museums - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The FBI is seeking a warrant to search electronic devices belonging to a Grand Rapids man accused of stealing art from two Michigan art museums. The news was reported by multiple outlets, including MLive.

According to a federal affidavit, Mikolai Augustine Stasiulewicz, 27, allegedly stole a color lithograph by artist Ellsworth Kelly, from Western Michigan University’s (WMU) Richmond Center for the Visual Arts on June 23. A worker notified WMU police that the work was missing, and Stasiulewicz, who was caught on surveillance video carrying the framed print, was identified through facial-recognition analysis by Michigan State Police.

Stasiulewicz is also alleged to have stolen a 16th-century Albrecht Dürer print from the Grand Rapids Art Museum (GRAM) on July 2. According to the FBI, he had been seen at the museum on June 17, “in what appeared to be a pre-theft surveillance visit.” Between the two thefts, he is accused of entering nonpublic areas at the Muskegon Museum of Art on June 25; however, Muskegon police said he didn’t take anything.

The FBI, which eventually took over the case, learned during its investigations that Stasiulewicz had met with a man on July 8 at the Gun Lake Casino Resort in Wayland, Michigan. Surveillance video shows him leaving with an unknown amount of cash.

Stasiulewicz was found dead in his home on July 30. According to the Kent County Medical Examiner’s Office, he died of a morphine overdose on July 26. Although the office’s autopsy report rules the death an accident, it also notes that “the decedent is currently under investigation by the FBI for involvement in an art gallery theft,” and that a brother had told police that may have played a part in his death.

Four artworks, including the Kelly, valued at $10,000 and the Dürer, valued at $10,000–$20,000, were found at the home the next day.

On Monday, November 23, the FBI sought a warrant to search Stasiulewicz’s cellphone and laptop computer to determine if any others were involved in the thefts. “In my training and experience, and that of the Art Crime Team, phones and computers like the devices will often be used to communicate with co-conspirators,” FBI Special Agent Evan Alkema wrote in the federal affidavit. “They may contain evidence of communications about what art pieces to steal, negotiations for sale prices, and arrangements to transfer and ‘fence’ the stolen works.”

Since its inception in 2004, the FBI’s Art Crime Team, which handles cases involving the theft, forgery, and trafficking of art and cultural artifacts, has recovered more than 20,000 objects valued at $1 billion.

Stasiulewicz was an amateur artist who studied at the Interlochen Center of the Arts, the FBI said.

item.title: London’s New Museum Needs a Better Reason to Exist - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The new London Museum has been a humongous undertaking: 10 years in the making, costing £437 million in total against a budget of £337 million, and yet, after all that time and money, it’s hard to know where any of it went.

From 1976 to 2022, the city’s museum, then called the Museum of London, occupied a site on London Wall at next to the Barbican complex. It moved to Farringdon, a grittier neighbor of the City’s financial district, because the old building was hard for visitors to find and too small to display the full collection.

The new space is bright and airy, closer to an Erewhon café than a museum lobby. An on-site café, open around the clock from Thursday to Sunday, serves hot chocolate and ginger beer. The furnishings, though, feel random in such a pristine setting: a flock of large plastic sheep meant for sitting on, and shop signs from London fixtures like the Odeon cinema and Morley’s, the fried chicken chain. When was the last time any Londoner saw a sheep in the city? In theory, all of this should appeal to Londoners who have taken up early-morning run clubs, traded pints for matcha lattes and aren’t above a gimmicky bit of decor.

“People are looking for community, and they will have it in the museum,” Sharon Ament, the museum’s director, told ARTnews.

The architects, Asif Khan and Stanton Williams, working with the conservation specialists Julian Harrap Architects, have designed a space that’s inviting.

“It took people until the 21st century to realize that cultural institutions are for everyone, and that’s what we strive to make here,” Khan told ARTnews at the press preview. He wants visitors to dip in and out of the story of London without feeling as if they’re in a museum. “When we look at audiences outside of the regular museum visitors, many find it challenging and don’t feel welcome. This is a welcome for those people,” Khan said. Entry is free, there are three separate entrances, and built-in sofas with reading lights invite passersby to stop in, though few people pass through Farringdon unless they’re waiting for the nightclub Fabric or the cocktail bar Space Talk to open.

Still, London is a city of 9.1 million people and a global center for art, film, music, finance and fashion. Finding stories that capture its quirks shouldn’t be that hard.

The museum is divided into three sections. Real Time, at the main entrance, represents London today and includes Banksy’s Piranhas sentry box. (What could be more London than Banksy?) In the Linbury Hall, Our Time attempts to tie the city together through objects like the Lord Mayor’s State Coach from 1757, the Buckingham Palace switchboard and Syd’s Coffee Stall, an East End food cart that operated from 1919 to 2019. Downstairs is Past Time, perhaps the only part of the museum that feels like a museum. It’s the most educational section, with small rooms on the women’s suffrage movement and the Great Fire of London. The rest of the floor is scattered with a piece of a fatberg, Tom Daley’s diving trunks from the London 2012 Olympics, a chair owned by Charles Dickens, a 2,000-year-old Roman wall painting, Anna Pavlova’s tutu for The Dying Swan and more.

The London Museum is a work in progress and until it figures out what sets it apart from the city’s other museums, it will remain a large crèche, where parents can bring their children to roam freely. But there’s still some hope: in 2028, the museum will open two temporary exhibition spaces, perhaps the museum will finally lean into its London-ness and celebrate the cornerstones that makes the city so glamorous and gritty, from the Teddy Boys of 1950s, Mods and Rockers of the 1960s to the Sloane Rangers of the late 1970s and 1980s.

Until the London Museum gets it right, the city has the Bayeux Tapestry, on view at the British Museum through July 11, 2027, with tickets topping out at £33 ($44). At the preview, word went around that one journalist had skipped it in favor of the 950-year-old cloth. In hindsight, I should have done the same, or stayed home to play Grand Theft Auto VI.

item.title: Tending the Legacy of Cuff Annum, Ancestor of Black and Native Worcester - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The American Revolution did not begin with a “shot heard ’round the world.” Three days before the Battles of Lexington and Concord, the rebellion started with a secret. On April 16, 1775, Isaiah Thomas and Timothy Bigelow smuggled a wooden printing press across the moonlit Charles River, from Boston to Worcester, Massachusetts, the ancestral homelands of the Nipmuc people. Their clandestine mission salvaged Thomas’s patriot newspaper, The Massachusetts Spy, which published the first eyewitness accounts of the revolution. 

Soon, both men became celebrated founding fathers in New England. Bigelow sheltered the printing press and hosted Sons of Liberty meetings in his Worcester home. He commanded the 15th Massachusetts Regiment and soldiered alongside George Washington at Valley Forge. On July 14, 1776, Thomas reportedly delivered the region’s first public reading of the Declaration of Independence in Worcester. In 1812, Thomas compiled his personal collection and founded the American Antiquarian Society, the nation’s oldest and largest historical society today.  

And yet, triumphant narratives like these — particularly amid the country’s 250th anniversary this year — elide the cruel hypocrisies of American independence. As Bigelow battled alongside Black and Native soldiers, he enslaved people in private. As Thomas championed freedom, he published advertisements for the recapture of “runaways.” But this story is not about Bigelow or Thomas. There are enough monuments and collections dedicated in their honor.

This is a belated elegy for Cuff Annum — father, husband, and soldier in Bigelow’s regiment. Cuff became a common ancestor of a long, braided lineage of Black and Native families from central Massachusetts. After Cuff’s death, Hagar, his widow, became head of the largest household of color on Back Street (now Summer) in Worcester. Their daughter Dinah married twice. From one of these marriages, I am a direct descendant. Because Cuff Annum lived, I am alive today.

item.title: Nick Cave and India Pavilion Win Widely Boycotted Venice Biennale Awards - Hyperallergic
item.description:
After dozens of artists at the 61st Venice Biennale withdrew from award consideration in solidarity with the jury, which planned to omit Russia and Israel from the prizes and later resigned, the festival has announced Chicago-based artist Nick Cave and India's national pavilion as winners of its new visitors’ awards.

Nine days before the Venice Biennale opened on May 9, the women-led awards jury resigned en masse, shortly after announcing that countries facing accusations of crimes against humanity by the International Criminal Court, notably Israel and Russia, would not be eligible for prizes.

The Biennale reversed the decision soon after the jury's resignation and replaced the traditional jury-selected Golden and Silver Lion awards with the “Visitors' Lions,” voted on by ticket-holders and awarded to the most popular pavilion and artist.

item.title: What Is Internet Cinema? - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Editor’s note: This story is an edition of Link Rot, a column by Shanti Escalante-De Mattei that explores the intersections of art, technology, and the internet.

During last June’s heat wave, I found myself standing outside an unassuming office building in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, baking in the sun’s glare. The Gallery, a nomadic curatorial platform, had set up an exhibition, titled “WeWork (oralmoral)”, in one of the building’s vacant office spaces. In celebration of the show’s closing the curators were screening films, some of which fall into the category of what is being called “internet cinema,” a burgeoning movement, or method, that has been in the making since late 2020.

Once inside, I wandered around the cool, unlit space, laughing at funny paintings and sculptures until it was time to find a spot on the floor for the screening. Someone in front of me was hastily scrawling the lineup of the screenings on paper with a black marker and passing them around as fast as he produced them. One passed back to me. The first film on the list was Zarina Nares’ I am going to die (this is my sign) (2025). The projector was fiddled with and a rectangle of white with a buffer symbol appeared on the blank wall in front of the seated crowd.

A chorus of female voices rose up, all in some general distress, and while I couldn’t see these women, by the tone, I could tell they were speaking into a front-facing camera. The chorus cut out to a single voice, which spoke over dashcam footage of a car crash: “You’re having problems at work, your boyfriend broke up with you, your parents are mad at you, everything is going wrong, your car broke down – that is a good sign. Like, that is the very best sign.”

What followed was a montage of TikTok videos featuring motivational advice. One video bled into another, linked by the formulaic hooks used by podcast bros, emotional car seat influencers, clips of celebrities’ acceptance speeches, athletes in interviews, or passionate pastors, all of which was set to music. One after another these TikToks reveal ‘the one thing that you need to learn’ in a high-speed carousel of intense emotion that feels increasingly forced as it becomes clear how many of these impassioned speeches are copies of one another.

“Internet cinema isn’t necessarily about the internet or its aesthetic but about its logic, how it functions and how it makes us feel,” Zarina Nares said in a phone call. On the process of making I am going to die, she added that “Clearly, I watched enough advice videos for too long that I kept getting more. Once you watch so many you see the formula behind them, whether it’s a certain cadence of speaking or certain music.”

Internet cinema was first defined in a 2007 paper by Chuck Tryon titled “New Media Studies and the New Internet Cinema.” The technologies and formats that concerned Tryon —iPods and camera phones, software like Final Cut Pro, and home movies—are far dated, but his paper was prescient, having tapped into impulses and concerns that reflect contemporary internet cinema: a do-it-yourself ethos that blurs the line between amateur and artist; the popularization of “niche exhibition;” and a “self-reflexive style” that works “to call attention to the narrative codes and technological specs that shape cultural productions.”

Contemporary internet cinema has its roots in the COVID-era, which saw an explosion of participation in internet culture and production, that often bled out into one particular place: Dimes Square, a patch of Manhattan where Chinatown and the Lower East Side meet.

One of the most memorable dramas that played out at the time was puppeteered by a then-anonymous internet figure who went by the name Angelicism01. This figure posted creeds about extinction on Substack, and gained infamy for growing a cult-like following among young women in New York (who had never met him). With the help of various film makers, he made a three-hour long movie called Film01 which includes fast paced montages of memes, tweets, videos of natural disasters and terrorist attacks, alongside long scenes featuring the ‘it-girls’ he had recruited. Writer Madeline Cash described Film01 in the art publication Spike as “an unsophisticated collage of localized content that mimics, rather than intervenes or questions, our digital conditions,” which ultimately did nothing more than tap “into the scene’s libidinal narcissism.”

Yet, with some distance, Film01 has proven to be a productive experiment. One of Angelicism01’s collaborators, the filmmaker Dana Dawud, found internet footage to splice into the film, created short edits that became a part of the larger film, and remotely directed certain sequences. Dawud would go on to launch Open Secret, an international screening series of internet cinema that has since played a large part in consolidating disconnected artists and practices under the term.

At the same time that young women were running around Dimes Square at Angelicism01’s request, people were locked away at home with TikTok. More than ever, people around the world were subjecting themselves to hours and hours of scrolling on this relatively new video content platform.

“When you’re doom scrolling, there is, technically speaking, no specific author to this montage that you’re watching. So, it’s as if you’re exposed to radical experimental cinema all the time by a completely cynical industrial apparatus,” said 0nty, the co-author of “Dialogues on CoreCore & the Contemporary Online Avant-Garde” during a Zoom interview also attended by his co-author Mischa Dols. “The question is, how do you even begin to think about this problem? And I think internet cinema is an answer,” 0nty said.

0nty and Dols describe internet cinema as a method, rather than a genre or an aesthetic, which seeks to expose or comment on the way that the internet functions through editing found footage.

It’s worth noting that some works under the umbrella of internet cinema do feature the production of new images. Dahlia Bloomstone’s 20,000 Tokens (2025) is a screen recording of the artist chatting with men and exposing herself on the webcam site Chaturbate (the video is spliced with a glitching 3D-rendering of a blonde avatar in a black void). For The Sight is a Wound (2024), Parham Ghalamdar filmed himself burning his own paintings, as a statement on how tthe seemingly endless documentation of the genocide of Palestinians in Gaza has made images useless. Yet the particular process of editing found footage is usually highlighted in definitions of internet cinema because this method represents the folk practice that preceded internet cinema: corecore.

Core, or rather, -core, is a suffix that denotes some kind of bundle of aesthetics and moods. Cottagecore, for example, is a reference to an image universe of milkmaid tops, galoshes, a straw basket full of wildflowers, a shingled cottage, butter made with wooden tools, but also, beyond images, a wish for simple, optimistic, pastoral life. But corecore emerged not as a specific aesthetic but as a way of making video content through editing together music, clips from movies, podcasts, and other TikToks.

These videos are often melancholic ruminations of the deep and unrecognized suffering of young men, the terrible sublimity of being alone with your screen, an alienated awareness of hurtling towards extinction while scrolling on your parents’ sofa. Watching compilations of corecore I reminded me intensely of my time on Tumblr as a teenager.

On Tumblr, the practice of posting and reblogging images, fragments of text, and GIFs under an “aesthetic” was a way of cultivating and nurturing a feeling: a world of images that created a visual language for all that we thought life could be. Painful, dramatic love; intensity chased by the doom of its own ephemerality; cold, beautiful suffering. In the pivot to video platforms, corecore takes that tendency to collect images and feelings and turns it into a form much more contained and shareable than a blog: the film.

Removed from the usual logics of personal branding and sponsorship deals, it became an exciting trend for those who take internet-based cultural production seriously. Corecore, as a mass movement of people making films on the same devices they watch them on, represented the realization of an old dream of experimental cinema: film as a truly collective practice.

“Authorship gets really muddy, you have content creators and video artists making films on the same platforms. Dana [Dawud] has compared internet cinema to the way that SoundCloud functions, where people can steal your edit, steal your beat, steal a sample, and then it gets lost who put it online first, and that’s okay,” said Edison Niebla Rodriguez, a curator who also creates video art with his wife, Dayana Matasheva, under the name Demon Lovers Inc. “Obviously, it’s kind of at odds with video art which is very hard for people to see because of the way that the art market functions.”

That said, video art has been a major inspiration for artists working in internet cinema. Arthur Jafa’s Love Is the Message, the Message Is Death (2016) in particular is often cited as a kind of totem of legitimacy for internet cinema. The film is a montage of civil rights–era footage and grainy videos of Black Americans circulated online: reaction memes, women twerking, women getting slammed to the ground by police, men getting shot by police, arms raised in the air. It’s profound love and profound despair, but also a comment on how images of Black people circulate online. When I first saw it, I was struck by how internet it felt: the video was playing on a laptop, which had been filmed by a phone camera. Of course, it turned out I’d been watching a bootleg, and that extra frame wasn’t part of the original.

Dawud’s film Palcorecore (2024) can be read in Jafa’s lineage. Like Jafa, Dawud cuts together found footage in an act of memory, love, and grief. The footage shows Palestinians flying kites, breakdancing, rapping, riding horses, and playing by the sea. Children surround a tank; a mute man desperately mimes a murder he witnessed. “The internet exists to document its own martyrdom,” a computerized voice says, playing on the fact that the Arabic word for martyr comes from the root meaning “to witness.” “We are martyrs together,” the voice says: we are witnesses together.

“What interests me about internet cinema is that it creates a history of internet artists, the thoughts and languages they develop online, and the possibility of establishing a continuity between what they produce on the internet and how it can be given a temporal form through cinema,” wrote Dawud in an email. “Internet cinema doesn’t merely document an existing culture; it participates in the creation of its history. It is a way for the internet to historicize itself.”

Ultimately, internet cinema is less a practice than a name: one that gives form to a whole range of ways of making online that are often lost in the tumult of the internet’s incessant production. If there is one thing that separates the art world from online cultural production, it is that the art world is nothing if not a form of memory. In its obsession with provenance, catalogues, and archives, it is a network of stewardship. Internet cinema is a means of making an object of what is so fleeting online, by turning the internet into a film.

item.title: Five Questions for Advisors on the November Marquee Sales: Guarantees, Spotty Bidding, and a $190 M. Van Gogh - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Editor’s Note: This story originally appeared in On Balance, the ARTnews newsletter about the art market and beyond. Sign up here to receive it every Wednesday.

It’s Thanksgiving week and, for those of us who live and breathe the art market, that means only the briefest of breaks between the all-important November auction season and the year’s grand finale at Art Basel Miami Beach. But before we turn to Miami, a quick post-mortem on the marquee sales just passed.

Perhaps more than in any other industry, the health of the art market is in the eye of the beholder. Do you measure it by overall totals? By sell-through rate? By the number of bidders, or the number of guaranteed lots? By the ratio of hammer prices to estimates? Each figure tells a slightly different story, leaving plenty for our resident market whisperers to debate. But before we turn this week’s column over to the advisers, let’s set out some basic figures.

According to data from ARTDAI, the November evening sales at Christie’s, Sotheby’s, and Phillips generated $2.03 billion, a modest 7.5 percent increase over 2025, but the highest total since 2022. Sotheby’s led the pack with $1.16 billion, clearing $1 billion and taking more than half of the three houses’ combined total for the second straight year. (Its share rose to 57 percent from 53 percent. Christie’s share dropped to 38 percent from 43 percent, while Phillips’s ticked up to 5 percent from 4 percent, pushed by the $44.6 million Modigliani sculpture.)

And yes, the $384 million gap between Sotheby’s and Christie’s is roughly what the Blaquier-Arrieta collection brought in on its own: $412 million on just 12 lots. Winning those big consignments really does matter.

But for all those gaudy totals, there was a definite sense watching the week’s sales that bidding was uneven, thin, and at times absent entirely. Blame fickle collectors, sure, but it seems the auction houses pushed their estimates to the limit. Per ARTDAI, hammer prices across the various-owner sales in November 2025 came in 17 percent above the low estimates and at roughly 80 percent of the high estimates. This season, hammer prices for the same sales (i.e. excluding the Blaquier-Arrieta single-owner sale) were flat against the low estimates and just 69 percent of the highs. As Sotheby’s CEO Charles Stewart said after the Blaquier-Arrieta sale last week, “Our estimates weren’t shy.”

But does an aggressive auction house make for a weak market? Or is this the same market we’ve seen for the last few cycles—one that is choosy, blue-chip and provenance-driven, and competitive for the right objects—just approached differently by the specialists? That’s what we asked the advisers, along with their takes on everything from the spread of guarantees to that $190 million van Gogh.

Answers have been edited for clarity and concision.

item.title: Run with the Semi-Wild Yilki Horses of Anatolia in Nur Tucker’s Captivating Photos - Colossal
item.description:
Around the dusty plains and otherworldly volcanic rock formations of the historical region of Cappadocia, a millennia-old tradition continues. Here in Central Anatolia, Turkey, horses have been a part of daily life, civic programs, and military campaigns since prehistory. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, photographer Nur Tucker captures a portrait of the region’s living heritage.

Published by Hemeria, the title delves into the beauty and tenacity of the semi-wild horses while also highlighting the lifestyles of those who herd them through rugged landscapes. Tucker, who is a British-Turkish photographer based in the U.K., has long been drawn to the vigor and elegance of horses, and the yilki breed that populates Anatolia have a particularly resonant history.

“Yilki” comes from the Turkish verb yılmak, which means “to flee” or “to be set loose.” The name “has come to describe the condition of these herds that live between liberation and loss, between domestic heritage and wild abandon,” says a statement.

In a place where horses have been bred for agriculture, transportation, battle, and more for thousands of years, their role forever changed within just the past century due to mechanization and industrialization. With motorized tractors, trucks, and cars to work the fields and provide transportation, horses essentially became redundant. Released to fend for themselves, they survived harsh winters, bred on their own, and grew into sizable herds. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, Tucker composes a love letter to these striking animals, celebrating their resilience through more than 100 images.

The book is available for purchase directly from Hemeria, and it’s slated for worldwide release next October. See more on Tucker’s Instagram.

item.title: A Sculptural Playground in Shanghai Is Designed for Human-Powered Play - Colossal
item.description:
In Shanghai’s Jing’an Sculpture Park, a monumental new installation by Brooklyn’s Wade and Leta has a clear goal: to get people up and moving in the same space. Titled “Catching Feelings,” the interactive artwork doubles as an all-ages playground with the artists’ signature sculptures and geometric forms. A central tower holds a quartet of slides, while other spinning and writhing elements are designed for more unstructured interaction.

“Catching Feelings” is one of 36 projects in the ninth edition of the Jing’an International Sculpture Project, an annual project helmed by the UCCA Center for Contemporary Art. In comparison to the artists’ earlier works, the bold, kinetic playground is decidedly analog, with any movement powered by the people interacting with its components rather than embedded motors or motion generated by the wind.

“We’re interested in the life and activity around our work—the behaviors it causes, the elations it brings,” the artists say in a statement. “We watched the same grandfather return with his granddaughter to play hide and seek; an 84-year-old and his partner used the space as the backdrop for their video recordings; new friends were made on our ground spinners; we even glimpsed a man in a business suit having a go on the slide.”

“Catching Feelings” is presented alongside monumental works by Olafur Eliasson, Marshmallow Laser Feast, and many others on view through December 31. Find more from Wade and Leta on their Instagram.

item.title: Venice Biennale Awards Selected by Public Vote Go to Nick Cave, Indian Pavilion - ARTnews.com
item.description:
After a Venice Biennale of bitter controversy, the exhibition has at last revealed the winners of its top honors, which were chosen this year by public vote instead of a jury of esteemed curators because that panel resigned in protest. This time around, the awards went to the American artist Nick Cave for his participation in Koyo Kouoh’s main exhibition and India for its national pavilion.

Dubbed the Visitors’ Lions, these awards replaced the Golden Lions, which are regularly given to participants in the main exhibition and artists representing countries with pavilions in the exhibition. This time around, just two awards were given out, one for an artist in the main show and one for a national pavilion.

The Biennale was forced to instate the Visitors’ Lions after the five-person Golden Lion jury resigned in May, in advance of the show’s opening. By that point, the curators had already said that they would “refrain from considering those countries whose leaders are currently charged with crimes against humanity by the International Criminal Court,” a move that would exclude Israel and Russia from consideration. More than half of the artists in the main show said they would not accept the Visitors’ Lions in solidarity.

Cave’s contributions to the Kouoh’s show, titled “In Minor Keys,” included a decidedly major work: Amalgam (Origin), a 26-foot-tall bronze sculpture in which a person’s body sprouts branches and wildlife. The work, which appeared outdoors at the Arsenale, derived from a similar-looking proposal for a piece to replace a toppled Confederate monument.

Inside and outside the Arsenale, there were yet more large-scale Cave sculptures that composed Two Points in Time – At Once, which featured more figures whose bodies fuse with plants. Needlepointed portraits accompanied those figures. “The works address the stages of grief toward mourning, rebirth, and radical connection,” Cave wrote on social media in May, when the Biennale opened.

India’s pavilion, titled “Geographies of Distance: Remembering Home,” dealt largely with how objects act as vessels for memories and featured such grandly sized pieces as Sumakshi Singh’s Permanent Address, in which the walls of a house were remade in see-through thread, causing the domicile to appear flimsy and impermanent.

Alongside Singh, the pavilion featured works by Alwar Balasubramaniam, Ranjani Shettar, Asim Waqif, and Skarma Sonam Tashi. Organized by curator Amin Jaffer, the pavilion was the first staged by India at the Biennale since 2019.

The Biennale’s spare release unusually did not include citations for why the Indian Pavilion and Cave won, likely because neither had been selected by a jury. Instead, the release included a statement from Biennale president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, who said, “The public of the Exhibition embraced this recognition – the Visitors’ Award – as an opportunity to bring Pablo Picasso’s practice to life: a painting only comes to life through the person who looks at it. I can say without hesitation that La Biennale is brimming with ever-renewed energy thanks to the vibrant presence of everyone.”

When the Biennale opened, dozens of participants in Kouoh’s main exhibition, as well as several dozen more with national pavilions, signed a statement saying that they did not want to be considered for the Visitors’ Lions as a form of solidarity with the resigned jury. If these artists were selected as winners, they said, the Biennale could expect legal action. “Not only is this confusing for visitors, it is blatantly disrespectful towards the artists who have made the request for removal of their names,” the artists said in a statement.

Though it did not directly respond to the artists, the Biennale said in its release about the Visitors’ Lions that “all national participations” were eligible, since the exhibition is about “openness, dialogue, and the rejection of any form of closure or censorship.”

Notably, neither Cave nor the artists representing India signed the e-flux statement, which was endorsed by many of the artists with most talked-about pavilions in Venice—including Florentina Holzinger, whose Austrian Pavilion generated long lines and emerged as an early favorite during the professional preview.

The Visitors’ Lions bring to an end a tumultuous Biennale marked by protests over Israel and Russia’s pavilions, which faced an outcry both before and during the Biennale, with many calling for both countries to be ejected altogether. The Biennale sought to proclaim itself a neutral entity, saying that it cannot kick out any nation recognized as a state by the Italian government. But the logic proved unpersuasive for many, including the European Union, which said it will revoke a 2 million euro grant that it typically awards to the Biennale as a protest against the Russian Pavilion’s return this year, during a period when Russia continues to face EU sanctions over its war in Ukraine.

Lifetime achievement prizes are typically revealed ahead of the Biennale’s opening, but none were awarded this time because Kouoh, the curator of the main show, died in 2025 before she could select the winners. A Silver Lion, for a promising young artist in the main exhibition, was not awarded during this round, either, likely because that prize is given out by a jury who was not present to offer it.

The Biennale has positioned this year’s fraught edition as a resounding success. Upon its closure this past weekend, the Biennale said the show received more than 714,000 visitors, the second-highest attendance figure in the exhibition’s history. “This edition of the Biennale, so rich in events and complex developments—so immersed in the harsh affairs of the world—was pervaded by a vivid spirit, rewarded indeed by the number of visitors,” Buttafuoco, the Biennale president, said in a statement this past weekend.

The Biennale was initially expected to announce the Visitors’ Lions when the exhibition concluded its run on Sunday. Asked by ARTnews about the delay, a Biennale spokesperson said that extra time was necessary to “ensure that sufficient time is available to complete the necessary overall vote count.”

item.title: 2026 Jarman Award Winner Announced - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
For 19 years, the Jarman Award has built an enviable reputation for celebrating the practices of ground-breaking artist filmmakers in the UK. The prize, established in 2008 and run in partnership with Whitechapel Gallery, celebrates the diversity and creativity of artists working in film today. It takes its name from the radical filmmaker and artist Derek Jarman (1942 – 1994), seeking out practices that echo his bold, boundary-breaking approach. Previous winners represent some of the most ambitious and celebrated figures in moving image, redefining the genre for a new generation. They include Heather Phillipson, Imran Perretta, Lawrence Abu Hamdan, Luke Fowler and Sin Wai Kin. Now, Alia Syed joins this illustrious list, after being announced the winner of the 2026 Film London Jarman Award last night. 

Syed is an experimental filmmaker who creates poetic and textural works shaped around powerful storytelling. Across a portfolio that spans early projects made at the London Film-Makers Co-operative in the 1980s, to more recent work made in Glasgow, Syed has consistently created challenging and thought-provoking films. Oral histories and the stories she heard from her parents and grandparents are central to the artist’s practice, which often employs layered structures of image and voice to create nuanced portraits of people and places. The jury described Syed as: “A pioneer of experimental film and artists’ moving image, the beauty and compelling nature of her work which touches on questions of memory and migration among others, is combined with a deep understanding of and inventiveness with the craft of filmmaking. A master of analogue filmmaking, she continues to show a restless will to play, experiment and change.”

In her project Snow (2019), Syed uncovers hi-8 footage shot by her father, through which the artist stages a dialogue through time. Reappropriating this historic footage from a snowy day in 1995, Syed narrates her experience of viewing to reflect on temporality, distance and the elements of the past that cannot be uncovered. Snow is a mesmerising examination of the ways that the slippages of memory and decay shape family history and the unexpected ways that we discover echoes of the past in the present. Meanwhile, The Dhaba (2025) is a poetic chronicle documenting the migration of two men to Glasgow. Arriving at different historic moments from the Indian subcontinent, their testimonies shed light on the effects of ever-changing British immigration legislation. In Ka Ba Ddi: a breath, a move, a game (2025), audiences see abstracted imagery and sounds from kabaddi, an Asian contact sport of breath and movement. 

The artist was selected from a distinguished shortlist, which included Sadia Pineda Hameed, Ilona Sager and Aesthetica Art Prize alumnus Rhea Storr. Hameed brings together personal and archival footage, alongside her parent’s home movies, in a witty, playful five-channel video. Anak, Where Did We Say?, tells the story of Hameed’s mother’s migration from the Philippines to Britain. Elsewhere, Sager film shows the processes of claiming compensation for work-related illnesses, including the indignity of having your “usefulness” measured for claim, and Storr explores the in-between, translation, format and aesthetics, that depict themes such as masquerade, the performances of Black women and community space. In New Territories (spectacle is king), the artist presents a silent tableau that takes viewers to a summer of carnivals. 

Adrian Wootten, Chief Executive of Film London, sums up the impact of such Syed’s work: “In her reimagining of themes like migration and belonging, she gives her personal voice to universal experiences in a way that challenges and checks us, and so poignantly. I’m delighted that in Syed’s work, the spirit of Derek Jarman lives on.” It’s a poignant note to end on, reminding audiences that the true heart of the Jarman award is innovation, risk-taking and constant boundary pushing.

The Jarman Award 2026 shortlisted artists will be featured in an exhibition at Whitechapel Gallery 17 November – 13 December 2025: whitechapelgallery.org

For more information about the prize, visit: filmlondon.org.uk

Words: Emma Jacob

3. Alia Syed, Ka Ba Ddi- a breath, a move, a game (2025), installation view at CCA Glasgow. Photo by Diana Dumi.
