item.title: Ellie Wyatt and the Politics of Seeing Beyond Earth - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
What does it mean to photograph the unknowable? Images of distant galaxies, unidentified flying objects and imagined extraterrestrial life occupy an uncertain territory between scientific evidence and cultural mythology. Their authority rests not just on what they depict, but on the technologies and belief systems through which they are interpreted. From blurred photographs of unidentified objects to immaculate artificial intelligence renderings, representations of the cosmos expose a persistent desire to give form to what lies beyond human perception. However, as image-making technologies become increasingly sophisticated, the relationship between photography and truth grows more precarious. These tensions underpin a new research project by artist Ellie Wyatt, selected for the 2027 residency organised by The Photographers’ Gallery in partnership with The Ampersand Foundation.

The residency coincides with the 50th anniversary of the Golden Record, the collection of sounds, images and texts launched into space aboard the Voyager spacecraft in 1977 as a message to potential extraterrestrial recipients. Conceived as an introduction to humanity, the record attempted to distil life on Earth into a carefully selected cultural portrait. Its contents were shaped by decisions about which histories, achievements and forms of knowledge deserved representation, exposing the difficulty of communicating a universal identity through necessarily selective means. Half a century later, this ambitious exercise in interplanetary communication raises questions that extend beyond its original scientific purpose. Who has the authority to represent humanity, whose knowledge is preserved, and what happens when images must communicate across radically different systems of understanding?

These questions inform Wyatt’s investigation into the visual history of extraterrestrial life. Through archival research and digital image-making, she will trace representations of the interplanetary ‘other’, moving between speculative depictions of space, early astronomical photography, contemporary UFO images, AI-generated pictures and online conspiracy theories. Rather than treating these materials as separate categories, her research examines the visual conventions that connect them, particularly the ways in which images acquire credibility. Blur and pixelation can suggest the authenticity of an elusive encounter, while the technical precision of AI-generated imagery lends authority to fabricated scenes. The distinction between photographic evidence and visual persuasion becomes difficult to maintain.

Photography’s historical association with mechanical recording has established its authority as a means of documenting reality. Scientific image-making has been particularly influential, rendering otherwise inaccessible phenomena visible, from microscopic structures to distant astronomical bodies. Yet, the technologies that extend human perception also determine how the world is represented: lenses, sensors and processing techniques shape what can be seen, while systems of classification influence how visual information is interpreted. Artificial intelligence introduces another complication, producing convincing representations of events, places and beings that have never existed. As the boundary between documentation and fabrication becomes less stable, photography’s evidential status demands renewed scrutiny. Wyatt’s engagement with post-photographic practice addresses precisely this uncertainty, examining how technological authority shapes contemporary understandings of truth.

Her earlier work provides an important foundation for this enquiry. Published in 2026 by Foolscap Editions, Caress Your Vision: Observations on Gender, Representation and Power at the Final Frontier examines the politics of representation within the history of space exploration. The publication considers how narratives of scientific progress are shaped by visual languages that reproduce established hierarchies, particularly around gender, expertise and technological power. Its concerns extend beyond the representation of space to the cultural structures determining who participates in its exploration and how that participation is recorded. Similar questions inform Wyatt’s investigations into scientific image-making and conspiracy theories, where photographic detail can establish competing claims to knowledge. Her practice challenges the assumption that images offer transparent access to reality.

Space exploration itself provides an increasingly complex political context for these ideas. Once imagined primarily as a frontier for scientific discovery, outer space has become a contested arena shaped by national ambition, commercial interests and geopolitical competition. The expansion of private-sector involvement has complicated questions of ownership, access and technological authority, while unidentified aerial phenomena occupy an uneasy position between official investigation, popular entertainment and conspiracy culture. Images circulate between these contexts, detached from their original sources and invested with competing meanings. A photograph may be interpreted as evidence of technological advancement, an unexplained anomaly or deliberate fabrication. By bringing these visual histories together, Wyatt considers how representations of the cosmos reflect terrestrial anxieties.

Her constellation-based methodology also speaks to wider developments in contemporary photography, where artists increasingly move beyond the autonomous image to incorporate archival documents, moving image, text and digital processes. Such approaches challenge distinctions between documentary and fiction, asking how meaning changes when images are removed from their original contexts and placed in new relationships. Here, curation becomes more than the arrangement of visual material: juxtaposing scientific records with speculative imagery can expose the assumptions underpinning both. Rather than constructing a linear history of extraterrestrial representation, Wyatt will assemble found materials across different media, allowing connections to emerge between historical observation, contemporary fabrication and popular mythology. This approach positions photography as a means of examining how knowledge is constructed, rather than simply illustrating what is already known.

The project will extend beyond archival research through an engagement with the local community in Wirksworth, Derbyshire. On the Spring Equinox, 20 March 2027, Wyatt will invite residents and stargazers to exchange perspectives, ideas and stories about photographic representations of space. This gathering recognises that knowledge of the cosmos is not produced exclusively within scientific institutions. Stargazing involves observation, interpretation and collective imagination, bringing people together through an encounter with something that remains largely beyond human comprehension. Personal experience and cultural belief influence how the night sky is understood, creating different interpretations of the same visual phenomena. By incorporating these perspectives, Wyatt will consider how photographic images shape everyday relationships with the unknown.

The Foundation’s wider support for photographic practice provides another context for the residency. Its biennial Ampersand/Photoworks Fellowship, launched in 2021, has supported artists whose projects bring photographic practice into dialogue with wider social and technological questions. Johny Pitts, the inaugural recipient, developed Home Is Not a Place, a photographic exploration of Black British culture, identity and belonging, which subsequently toured to Graves Gallery in Sheffield, Stills in Edinburgh and The Photographers’ Gallery in London. Felicity Hammond’s fellowship produced Variations, an evolving installation examining geological extraction, data mining and machine learning, presented across four UK venues. Matthew Arthur Williams has developed an interdisciplinary practice spanning photography, moving image and sound, while Nicholas J. R. White’s 2025 fellowship has supported research into landscape, community and the nuclear submarine industry in Barrow-in-Furness. Felix Loftus, selected for the 2026 residency with The Photographers’ Gallery, explored the creative reuse of mobile devices through Waste as Resource, considering permacomputing and alternative technological infrastructures.

Wyatt’s practice is particularly resonant at a moment when the boundaries between photographic evidence and digital fabrication are becoming increasingly difficult to define. Her sustained interest in representation, scientific authority and visual belief brings a critical perspective to the ways images shape our understanding of the world, challenging assumptions about what photography can reveal and whose version of reality it supports. Alongside Caress Your Vision, her work has been presented at Soup Gallery in London, Westlicht Photo Museum in Vienna, the Finnish Museum of Photography in Helsinki, C/O Berlin and Fotomuseum Winterthur. The residency will allow her to develop these enquiries through archival research, digital experimentation and an exchange of perspectives on the cosmos. As artificial intelligence continues to complicate the relationship between images and evidence, Wyatt’s investigation takes on particular urgency. Her work invites us to look beyond what an image appears to show, and consider how it comes to mean something, and why we believe what we see.

Find out more about The Ampersand Foundation 2027 Residency: thephotographersgallery.org.uk

Words: Simon Cartwright

item.title: Art Advisor Sophia Cohen on How the Next Generation of Collectors Is Approaching the Art Market - ARTnews.com
item.description:
During during Art Week NYC, a citywide festival organized by ARTnews, Artforum, and Art in America, I was joined by art advisor Sophia Cohen to explore one of the hottest topics in the art market today: the next generation of collectors.

Cohen is the founder of Siren, an art advisory and curatorial consultancy. She started her career working for dealer Gavin Brown, who, Cohen explains, taught her about the importance of being with artists of your own generation and how an art dealer can function as an important steward for the artists they represent. When Brown’s gallery closed in 2020, Cohen pivoted to Gagosian (“the exact opposite,” in her words), where she spent six years, eventually becoming an associate director. Cohen is also one of four co-chairs leading the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Vanguard Council, an invite-only group of next-generation patrons.

At our talk on Friday, November 13, at the PMC Studio in Midtown Manhattan, Cohen spoke about the advice she gives to young collectors about when and how to buy, and why it’s sometimes important to make mistakes. She also gave insight into her own collecting, and discussed how today’s patrons are structuring their giving. Watch the video above to see the whole conversation.







.

item.title: Ireland’s Experiment in Paying Artists a Basic Income Is Working as Intended For Artists - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Life was pretty rosy for the 2,000 Irish artists who landed a spot on Ireland’s Basic Income for the Arts (BIA) pilot scheme. For three years, from 2022 to 2025, €325 arrived in their bank accounts every week. The money was intended to provide a dependable income, reduce the need to take on unrelated jobs to cover living costs, and give artists more time to concentrate on making art. Judging by the recipients I spoke earlier this month at Dublin Gallery Weekend (DGW), the pilot was a success. And since the BIA was made permanent in February, thousands more artists are hoping to reap the rewards.

“Basic Income for the Arts is a game changer, and now it is here to stay,” Ireland’s minister for culture, communications, and sport, Patrick O’Donovan, said in February.

Now in its fourth year, DGW was launched in 2023 by the city’s commercial galleries to raise the profile of its contemporary art scene. Organized by the Contemporary Art Gallery Association (CAGA), this year’s four-day program brought together galleries and cultural institutions for exhibitions, talks, screenings, and performances. A major addition was the inaugural Francis Bacon Awards for Irish Visual Arts, a €40,000 prize fund supported by Château La Coste. Painter Patrick Graham received the €25,000 Lifetime Achievement Award, while Belfast-born artist Cathy Wilkes took the €15,000 Mid-Career prize. Both will stage solo exhibitions at Château La Coste in Provence, France.

While the artists I spoke to described the BIA as a major boost to their working lives, I found little evidence that it has fundamentally changed Dublin’s contemporary art scene. None of the dealers, curators, or museum directors I spoke to suggested that its impact had been felt on a wider scale across the city’s galleries or commercial market.

Applications for the BIA’s new three-year round opened in May, with previous recipients eligible to reapply for one of the 2,000 available places. Around 10,000 artists applied, making competition fierce for a program to which the Irish government has committed €18 million.

“Over the course of the scheme, my practice flourished,” Dublin-based artist Gearóid O’Dea, who was selected for the pilot, told ARTnews. The funding allowed him to curate an exhibition based on Samuel Beckett’s work that travelled to Berlin, and collaborate with four other artists through the Glue Factory collective. He said the financial support made it possible to bring artists together and exhibit internationally without constantly having to find other jobs to make ends meet.

Cork-born Elinor O’Donovan, who is now studying for a master’s degree in Gothenburg, Sweden, also received the pilot payment. She told ARTnews that “it completely transformed my ability to work as an artist.”

Before joining the scheme, O’Donovan worked part-time as a receptionist alongside her artistic practice. The weekly payment allowed her to give up the job and concentrate on making art full-time. “Knowing the money was coming for three years was a big relief,” she said. “My psychological wellbeing improved because there was security.”

Lauren, another former recipient who is now based in London, said the payment arrived at a pivotal moment in her career. Having just completed her undergraduate degree, she had secured a graduate residency at the Royal Hibernian Academy in Dublin, where she was given a studio and access to painting classes. The BIA helped her develop her practice and take up further opportunities, including residencies and exhibitions. She has since secured funding to continue her studies in London. “There’s kind of nothing I haven’t done in the last four or five years that hasn’t, in some way, been impacted by my experience with the basic income,” she told ARTnews.

Despite the BIA’s unprecedented support for artists, not everyone is waxing lyrical about it, including some who benefited from the original pilot. Tadhg Ó Cuirrín, a visual artist who received the payment and works with the artists’ trade union Praxis, believes the government has missed an opportunity to build on its success. More than 10,000 artists applied for the new round, yet the number of places remains unchanged at 2,000. Recipients will also be limited to three years of support in every six-year period.

“It feels less like a base income per se and more like a kind of a multi-annual grant chosen by lottery,” he told ARTnews.

Although the program is now permanent, individual artists are not guaranteed support beyond three years. Artists must meet the scheme’s eligibility criteria, after which places are allocated through a lottery, with selection also taking demographic representation into account. Ó Cuirrín argued that the three-years-on, three-years-off model reinstates the financial insecurity BIA was designed to address. Artists risk losing their income just as their practices are beginning to flourish.

O’Dea has reapplied for the new round but is still waiting to hear if he’s been selected. He said the prospect of losing the regular income has brought financial anxiety back into his life.

The transition has also caused difficulties for artists who relied on other forms of state support. Michaële Cutaya, a spokesperson for Praxis, previously told The Art Newspaper that some former recipients have had to return to other work to cover their living costs. “If you have to then take on a different kind of job, it’s really disruptive,” she said.

Noel Kelly, chief executive of Visual Artists Ireland, said he welcomes the permanent scheme, but pointed to practical problems. BIA payments can affect artists receiving means-tested benefits, including disability allowance, while some applicants’ immigration status may prevent them from registering as self-employed, a requirement for participation.

Kelly also cautioned against judging the program solely on its financial return. An independent evaluation estimated that every euro invested generated €1.39 in social and economic benefits, taking into account factors including improved wellbeing. Kelly said that calculation misses much of what artists contribute to society.

“I hate that argument,” he told ARTnews. “It allows us to participate one in the local community, two in the local economy, three in the local creative ecology.”

The impact of the BIA on Ireland’s commercial art market is harder to measure. John Daly, director of Hillsboro Fine Art and chair of the Contemporary Art Gallery Association, told ARTnews that the country’s galleries continue to operate with a relatively small pool of collectors. “Success actually is survival,” he said. Daly argued the Irish art scene needs to attract younger collectors and encourage greater corporate support. Despite the presence of major international technology companies like Google in Dublin, he said corporate collecting remains limited, with companies tending to support arts initiatives such as murals and workshops. “It should be a huge opportunity, given the presence of all these multinationals, but not yet.”

item.title: Yorkshire Sculpture Park: Fifty Years of Art and Landscape - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
In 1977, taking contemporary sculpture out of the gallery and placing it in the grounds of a country estate was more than a change of setting. It challenged the assumptions governing where art belonged, who should encounter it and which institutions had the authority to define cultural life in Britain. Fifty years later, Yorkshire Sculpture Park (YSP) has become one of the most compelling examples of what happens when ambitious art is brought into sustained contact with the public realm. Its significance extends beyond the works installed across its 500 acres at Bretton Hall: it lies in the new relationships between artists, audiences and place that the institution has made possible. The landscape is never a neutral backdrop, nor is public access a simple matter of opening a gate. Both raise questions about ownership, representation and the stories through which places acquire meaning. YSP’s 2027 anniversary programme brings these questions into focus, looking back at five decades of artistic experimentation while considering the cultural and environmental responsibilities that will shape its future.

When Sir Peter Murray founded YSP, the proposition was radical in its simplicity. Contemporary sculpture could be encountered beyond the museum, in an environment where changing light, weather, distance and movement would become part of the experience. The Bretton Hall Estate, near Wakefield, provided a setting with an established history and a particular visual character, but the project also challenged the conventions attached to such places. Instead of treating sculpture as an object to be viewed at a prescribed distance, YSP made the visitor’s movement through the landscape central to the encounter. Works could be approached, circled, revisited and understood differently as the seasons changed. This expanded the possibilities of sculpture while changing the expectations placed on a public art institution.

The setting, however, carries its own complicated history. Bretton Hall’s designed landscape belongs to a tradition in which the picturesque was closely associated with private ownership, social status and the controlled experience of nature. Its carefully composed views and pathways were not created for unrestricted public use. YSP opened this environment to a much wider public, but access also brings an opportunity to look critically at the values embedded in the landscape. Who designed it? Whose histories have been preserved, and whose have been overlooked? Contemporary art can unsettle the apparent permanence of an estate, making its history visible rather than allowing it to remain an attractive but unexamined setting. In this sense, public access is not only about participation in culture; it is also about the right to interpret the places that shape collective identity.

Over five decades, YSP has developed an approach in which the relationship between artwork and environment is fundamental rather than incidental. Henry Moore’s first visit in 1979 established a connection that would become central to the park’s development; he later became a founding patron. His monumental forms found a setting in which scale, mass and the human figure could be considered against the expansive geography of the estate. The presentation of Barbara Hepworth’s work for her centenary in 2003 and Isamu Noguchi’s exhibition in 2008 further explored the relationship between modernist sculpture and its surroundings. Later, Yinka Shonibare’s FABRIC-ATION (2013) brought questions of colonial history, identity and cultural representation into the park, while Ai Weiwei’s 2014 Chapel presentation connected the historic building with an artist whose practice consistently examines power, freedom and the politics of memory. These projects demonstrated that the landscape could accommodate far more than formal responses to nature. It could become a site for difficult histories.

That ambition has helped change the cultural geography of the UK. For much of the 20th century, national artistic authority was concentrated in London, with major collections, institutions and critical networks reinforcing the capital’s position. YSP developed a different kind of cultural influence from its base in West Yorkshire, attracting international artists and audiences while remaining connected to the region in which it was founded. Its presence forms part of a wider cultural ecology that includes the Henry Moore Institute in Leeds and The Hepworth Wakefield. These institutions have distinct histories, purposes and collections; their importance lies partly in the different ways they bring sculpture and modern and contemporary art into public life. Together, they challenge the assumption that significant cultural experiences must be sought in the capital. Regional cultural authority develops through sustained investment, ambitious programming, research, partnerships and relationships with local audiences. YSP’s contribution has been to make the landscape itself a major site of that cultural activity.

The anniversary exhibition Fifty, presented in the Peter Murray Gallery will turn this history towards the present. Bringing together 50 UK-based artists born since the park’s foundation, it considers the generations whose lives and practices have unfolded alongside YSP’s development. The premise is more than a chronological celebration. Since 1977, ideas of identity, community, ecology and national belonging have undergone profound change, as have the materials and languages through which artists address them. A gathering of artists from different generations can reveal how these shifts have entered contemporary practice, and how artistic perspectives have expanded beyond definitions of British art. The exhibition also raises a question central to YSP’s own history: what does it mean for a cultural institution to represent the present, and how can it make room for the voices that will define what comes next?

Cornelia Parker’s major exhibition, opening in late November 2027, brings a particularly sharp perspective to questions of history and collective identity. Parker’s practice begins with familiar objects and materials, then subjects them to processes that expose their hidden associations and political meanings. Magna Carta (An Embroidery), made with contributions from more than 200 people, is a striking example. The work translates a foundational document of British political history into a collaborative textile, bringing together the language of constitutional authority and the labour of individual makers. Its collective authorship complicates the idea of national history as a fixed inheritance, suggesting instead that its meaning is continually produced through different voices and experiences. Presented at YSP, the work enters a landscape shaped by its own histories of ownership and privilege. The connection is productive: both the artwork and the estate invite visitors to consider how inherited structures acquire authority.

Environmental questions take a different form in Andy Goldsworthy’s Chapel Commission. Goldsworthy’ work is grounded in close attention to natural materials and the forces that transform them. His use of earth to paint the Chapel windows will bring the changing landscape into the building through colour, light and seasonal variation. The commission draws attention to its instability and constant movement, and this is an important distinction at a time when environmental art can risk turning ecological concern into spectacle. Goldsworthy’s pieces are compelling because the materials are subject to change: weather, time and the conditions of a particular site. At YSP, this approach connects the architecture of the Chapel with the surrounding land, making the boundary between built environment and natural world feel permeable.

Other anniversary projects extend the discussion of material, space and public experience. John Chamberlain’s works, presented in The Weston and outdoors from 26 March to 5 September, bring the compressed energy of his metal sculptures into dialogue with the architecture and open spaces of the park. His use of industrial materials gives sculpture a physical intensity that complicates any easy distinction between the natural and the manufactured. From June, bronzes by Henry Moore will return to the Country Park, recalling the artist’s formative relationship with YSP and the role his support played in its early development. Saroj Patel’s Dancers in the Wind, arriving in July, introduces movement and bodily presence into the landscape, while the National Art Education Association project, beginning in September, connects the anniversary with a longer history of art education and public learning. Lucy Young’s residency and presentations by Matt Johnson, Penfold Press and Kate Jenkins add further dimensions to a programme that moves between established practices and new forms of artistic enquiry.

The return of YSI from July to November 2027 extends this enquiry across West Yorkshire. Working with partners including the Henry Moore Institute, Leeds Art Gallery and The Hepworth Wakefield, the initiative connects different cultural spaces and audiences through a regional programme. Its importance lies in the possibility of making cultural participation less dependent on a single destination, allowing artistic encounters to develop across towns, cities and institutions. Such collaboration also challenges the idea that regional culture should be understood as a collection of individual attractions competing for attention. A stronger model emerges when institutions share knowledge, resources and audiences, creating a cultural network with its own intellectual character. For YSP, whose identity has always been shaped by its location, this wider reach reinforces the relationship between international artistic practice and the communities, histories and places of West Yorkshire.

The anniversary also arrives at a moment when the meaning of landscape is changing. Climate breakdown has made the relationship between human activity and the natural environment an urgent political and cultural concern. Historic estates, public parks and rural settings can no longer be viewed solely through the language of beauty, leisure or heritage; they are also places shaped by land management, ecological pressures and competing claims on resources. YSP is particularly well placed to explore these tensions because its programme has long brought artistic practice into contact with the physical conditions of the site. Sculpture can register the passage of time, expose the impact of industrial materials, question the idealisation of nature or draw attention to forms of environmental change that are difficult to comprehend.

There is, too, a continuing question about what public art institutions owe the places in which they operate. Visitor numbers and international recognition are important measures of reach, but they cannot alone describe cultural value. A meaningful institution must also consider who feels welcome, whose experiences inform its programme and how its work connects with the everyday lives of people beyond its immediate audience. YSP’s history provides a strong foundation for that conversation. Its location outside a major metropolitan centre has helped broaden access to internationally significant art, while its partnerships and educational projects extend that ambition beyond the experience of a single visit. The next stage will depend on how successfully it continues to connect global artistic debate with local knowledge.

Fifty years after its foundation, Yorkshire Sculpture Park is much more than an alternative venue for sculpture. It has helped establish the landscape as a place for serious artistic and critical engagement, widened the geography of cultural authority and changed expectations about how audiences encounter contemporary art. Its anniversary programme is strongest when understood through these achievements and the questions they leave open. Parker’s exploration of collective authorship, Goldsworthy’s attention to environmental change, Chamberlain’s engagement with industrial material and the wider network of regional partnerships all speak to an institution whose history is inseparable from the world around it. YSP’s future will be measured not only by the artists it presents or the works it commissions, but by its capacity to keep the landscape open to new interpretations and new voices. The achievement of the first 50 years is that a place once associated with the privileges of an historic estate has become a setting for shared cultural experience. The challenge now is to make that experience ever more expansive, relevant and responsive to the people and environments that will shape the next half-century.

Find out more about the Yorkshire Sculpture Park 2027 programme: ysp.org.uk

Words: Shirley Stevenson

item.title: Hail to the Squash King - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Swimming in a Peter Bradley color field. Leaping from dot to dot on a Howardena Pindell speckled canvas. A Peter Jemison horse prances toward me. A Pepsi Cherry truck pulls over as I’m having deep thoughts about authenticity.

In the morning glow, a pretty woman walks down the sidewalk with a carton of a dozen eggs. A faded black-and-white Marilyn Monroe poster greets customers at the Organic Deli. A photo in the paper shows the presidents of the United States, China, and Russia against a giant painting of the Great Wall. A Madonna song whispers, “Express yourself, express yourself.”

A well-dressed man cycling to work is nice to look at. A Hilma af Klint painting sells for $12.7 million at auction, 16 times its highest estimate. Meanwhile at the supermarket, just three small items set me back $100. How could that be? If the middle class had any guts, they’d be out there on the streets burning effigies of Adam Smith and Sigmund Freud. But they’re not; they’re waiting 40 minutes in line across the street just to buy a bagel. 

At the Ace Hotel, I read something I’ve written for the new edition of The Other Almanac. I wear my heart on my sleeve in front of strangers. The next speaker is a whale necropsy expert. At the end of the evening someone is crowned “Squash King.”

A golden sunset falls over the glass towers of Long Island City. The Kosciuszko Bridge is lit with cotton candy colors. Fog in Downtown Brooklyn, or is it smoke? I can’t really tell. In Chelsea, I follow a group of people into an art gallery just to see what they’re into. It turns out to be a big mistake.

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

Edward Said Speaks More Urgently Than Ever

In their (still brilliant) 1990 experimental film Introduction to the End of an Argument, filmmakers Jayce Salloum and Elia Suleiman splice together troves of found footage about Palestinians and Israelis. The result is an exquisite mash-up of Hollywood cartoons and political clichés, a comic pastiche illustrating the common bond between Orientalism and zombies. Both just won’t die. | Moustafa Bayoumi

item.title: Maren Hassinger Won’t Be Weighed Down - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Maren Hassinger’s retrospective at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) has a radiant warmth about it—surprisingly so, given that it’s a show made mostly of gray metal sculptures whose edges could prick you raw. This warmth owes a lot to the photographs, printed mural-sized and filling vitrines, taken by her long-term collaborator Adam Avila. Scattered throughout, they show Hassinger dancing, beaming, and/or hamming it up for the camera, often mirroring her sculpture’s forms with her body. But it owes, too, to the ways she rose to meet her career’s surprising twists and turns.

Rejected in college from Bennington’s dance department in the 1960s, Hassinger was pushed toward sculpture by a teacher who noticed her gift. “My love of motion,” she says in the catalog, carried her from one to the other. Clement Greenberg was a guest at her senior thesis critique: He had “the gift of gab, but was a bit of a bully” she remembers with accurate alliterations. He would not be her last mean man.

In graduate school, at UCLA, Hassinger was rerouted once again after finding the sculpture program to be a boys’ club. As she remembers it, not one single woman was enrolled. So she found a home in fiber, a typical tale, and made it work: “Truthfully,” she admits in the catalog, “I was just trying to get a degree so I could teach and make art.” But she found herself too impatient for the loom and uninterested in making fabric. So she gathered fibers out in the world, chancing upon a weighty rope in a shipyard. It was made of blonde hemp but discolored by oil. Playing around, she eventually unraveled some of its strands before tying segments into a series of loose, giant macrame knots that greet visitors to BAMPFA, where they lie on the ground as if waiting to be pulled tight.

Hassinger would marry craft techniques with industrial materials henceforth—a revealing portrait of women’s changing work in her time. She became such a regular at one LA wire shop that they featured her on the cover of their trade magazine. Soon, she was incorporating elevator cables—effectively wire ropes, their cords twisted together—into what would become her best known works. Leaning (1980) sees cables with frayed ends bundled in some two dozen bouquets. Only the central arrangement has a flat bottom and sits sturdily; the rest are free to lean.

Fiber meets metal in River, a 2,000-pound rope-chain Hassinger made as an ambitious graduate student in 1972. But where was a student to store such a behemoth? Recognition would not come until much later—as the title of her work Wallflower series (1975) attests—so she let River go, then finally remade it in 2011 for a Studio Museum acquisition. (Good thing she had so many photographs). A few other works at BAMPFA are recreations, too, but after school, she mainly made sculptures that could be coiled up and made compact: a resourceful response to the realities of real estate.

To see Hassinger’s work is to think about the act of making it. It shows you: Knots are blown up big so that you can see each twist and turn. Her titles are often verbs, as with Whirling (1978), Walking (1978), and Leaning (1980). “When she talks about the work, she moves” explained Margot Norton, who co-curated the show with Anthony Graham.

Hassinger met the obstacles that came her way, as a Black woman born in 1947, with poetry and practicality in equal measure. Of her turn to newspaper, which she twisted and knotted for a cascading 2008 installation, she explains that the material “is very handy and cheap [laughs].” But it also must have been cathartic to rip the headlines into strips. Her resourcefulness and resilience define the show, which sees her rethink sculpture without storage, fiber without fabric, choreography without corporeality.

Hassinger hardly did it alone. “Working alone is so antisocial” as she quips in the catalog. When Senga Nengudi first saw Hassinger’s work in 1975, she was thrilled to see another Black woman working with sculpture and performance, then looked her up. They became fast friends. With David Hammons, Nengudi then suggested that Linda Goode-Bryant show Hassinger at her gallery, Just Above Midtown (JAM). That show’s main work, Beach (1980), is installed at BAMPFA, too.

When Hassinger’s cohort of Black LA artists—known as Studio Z—lacked opportunities, they invented their own, as when Hassinger, Nengudi, Ulysses Jenkins, and others performed at the 1982 opening of “Afro-American Abstractions.” They had neither hung work on the walls nor been included in the checklist, but they did call up the Los Angeles Municipal Art Gallery to accept a nonexistent invitation: “We are so thrilled to be doing the opening performance!” they informed whoever answered the phone.

In the 1990s, Hassinger found herself without a studio. Starved for space, she turned to video. Birthright (2005) is nothing like her sculptures, but it will forever change how you see them. Onscreen, the artist interviews her uncle about her family tree. She learns that her grandmother, Puddin, had been the product both of incest and an interracial affair. Puddin’s parents hadn’t known that they were nephew and aunt, because Puddin’s father was born out of wedlock to his lover’s father who had a secret Native mistress.

Once the affair was discovered, Puddin was given away to a plantation caretaker who had been enslaved, and her father was lynched by a white mob. Puddin’s son—Hassinger’s dad—never talked about any of this: He was abandoned too by Puddin, then struggled to relate to women, cutting Hassinger out of the will and passing down patterns. “My legacy was to feel unloved,” the artist concludes in the video. But then the show keeps going.

Right next to Birthright, the curators installed Love (2008/2026), and it is here—halfway through the retrospective—that galleries of gray give way to hot pink. Plastic shopping bags filled with human breath and love notes cover the walls. Her lightness beams off the building, but look closely and you’ll find a sense of play throughout the show.

Thinking about familial lineages, Hassinger’s knots and ropes start to feel like umbilical cords severed and frayed. History is hefty, but it never weighs the work down in any sense of the word. “I always felt so good when I danced,” the artist explains, “lighter, faster.” It is easy to imagine her dancing in her studio while walking around BAMPFA, where one gets a sense of heaviness made to look light. Untitled (1972/2020) sees ropes with looped ends, noose-like, but instead of being tied into knots, strands are undone and then woven back together seamlessly. In the galleries, the ropes dangle gracefully from the ceiling and weigh heavy on the floor.

Hassinger is an artist who sees things soberly as they are and imaginatively as they might be—a gift that enables her to turn junkyard findings into elegant arrays and litter into love.

item.title: Paul McCartney: Eye of the Storm - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
In February 1964, The Beatles were in New York City. One day, they’re in the back of a limousine, moving through a city that already seems to know where they are headed. Outside, fans gather behind police lines and reporters follow their arrival in real time. Inside the car, Paul McCartney, John Lennon, George Harrison and Ringo Starr, listen as the radio turns their journey from the airport into a live update. In just twelve weeks, The Beatles had gone from regional fame to a global phenomenon. As the world turned its cameras on them, Paul McCartney began to look back, finger on the shutter. Photographs 1963-64: Eyes of the Storm, opening at Fotografiska Berlin in January, offers a rare encounter with one of music history’s most documented moments – seen not from the press line, but through the eyes of someone living it. 

Drawn from a collection of nearly 1,000 photographs rediscovered in Paul McCartney’s personal archive, the images form a visual diary of the three months between December 1963 and February 1964, illuminating both the historical and personal moments McCartney and his bandmates experienced together as their fame became something monumental that they could not outrun. This was the year of their first world tour and the reception, as The Spectator describes, was “hysterical.” From early performances in the UK to the band’s landmark appearance on The Ed Sullivan Show in New York before an audience of 73 million, the exhibition traces a cultural shift as it was happening. 

However, the show goes beyond just offering extraordinary access to a moment in time. Photographs reveal McCartney’s instinctive visual language, moving between portraiture, landscape and documentary to reflect the artistic culture of the early 1960s. Here, there are echoes of New Wave cinema, documentary filmmaking and photojournalism. McCartney’s images are best understood alongside the other creatives who captured the thrum of a society that was rapidly changing. Joel Myereowitz pioneered the use of colour in his street photography of New York City, which distilled the fast-paced, vibrant urban space. Meanwhile, film releases like Bonnie and Clyde (1967) and The Graduate (1967) signalled a different chapter for cinema under “New Hollywood.” McCartney’s photographs join this wave of creative pioneers, exploring the possibilities of the camera while navigating an unprecedented moment in cultural history. 

The exhibition also includes Beatles Touring. A Photofilm, a presentation that brings McCartney’s photographs of the band’s first trip to Miami into motion. As he later recalled in Anthology, “Miami was like paradise. We had never been anywhere where there were palm trees. We were real tourists, we had our Pentax cameras and took a lot of pictures.” Many of the shots taken there reflect a sense of temporary escape, capturing moments of leisure and spontaneity far removed from the crowds waiting outside. Using contemporary technology to animate the archive, Photofilm extends the exhibition’s central idea: not nostalgia, but a renewed encounter with memory. For the film, McCartney revisited his 2007 song 222, expanding it into a new, bespoke piece of music. 

McCartney captured the structures of public life from the inside: press conferences, police escorts, hotel rooms, rehearsal days, fans, friends, city streets and personal moments between appearances. Some of the show’s most revealing moments are also its quietest, distilling the brief interludes of rest and friendship. 

Photographs 1963–64: Eyes of the Storm is at Fotografiska Berlin from 24 January – 23 May: berlin.fotografiska.com

Words: Emma Jacob

Image Credits:

1. Paul McCartney. Self-portrait. London, 1963 © 1963 Paul McCartney under exclusive licence from MPL Archive LLP.
2. Paul McCartney. West 58th Street, crossing 6th Avenue. New York, February 1964 © 1964 Paul McCartney under exclusive licence from MPL Archive LLP.
3. Paul McCartney. Photographers in Central Park. New York, February 1964 © 1964 Paul McCartney under exclusive licence from MPL Archive LLP.
4. Paul McCartney. Welcoming scenes at Miami Airport, 1964 © 1964 Paul McCartney under exclusive licence from MPL Archive LLP.

The post Paul McCartney: <br> Eye of the Storm appeared first on Aesthetica Magazine.

item.title: Is GTA VI the Art Miami Deserves? - Hyperallergic
item.description:
“Driving at rush hour. SIGNIFICANTLY less cars on the road.” The text was from Miami-based artist, educator, and organizer misael soto, sent yesterday, November 19, a few hours after the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. We’d come full circle: The bumper-to-bumper traffic that Miami, the city I once called home, is now notorious for — in no small part due to overdevelopment, climate change, and strained infrastructure — was being alleviated by a video game that keeps people at home, inside a simulation of the same city locked in time.

The premise of GTA VI is simple on the surface. The game follows Lucía Caminos and Jason Duval in the criminal underworld of Leonida, a fictionalized state based on South Florida: Miami becomes Vice City, the Everglades are the Grassrivers. But its portrayal of real-life hardships, socioeconomic inequality, and even Lucía and Jason’s love story, among other elements, has elicited deeper reflections and responses across our increasingly blurred online and physical worlds.

To help make sense of these tensions, I got on a phone call with soto and Leo Castañeda, two Miami-based artists whose work I admire. Castañeda is an artist and video game designer exploring Latin American Surrealism in the digital age, and soto co-leads Artists for Artists: Miami, which is leading a boycott of Art Basel next month, and works in the overlapping arenas of labor rights, public infrastructure, and conceptual and social practice.

Our conversation was edited and condensed for clarity. I hope you enjoy it.

Hyperallergic: Before we even get into GTA, I was hoping each of you could tell me a little bit about your relationship to Miami — how long you've been there? How do you feel about living there now?

Leo Castañeda: I moved to Miami first when I was 11. My parents first moved to New York [from Colombia], and then they thought it was too cold, so they moved to Miami. I went to middle school and high school here, then I moved to New York for college, and I moved back in 2015. When I first moved back after college, it was mostly because of the cost of living in New York. And then, within the 10 years that I've been here, it became the same cost of living as New York, except with Florida salaries.

I do feel grateful, though, to be part of the Bakehouse Art Complex, where I have an affordable studio. I live in the North Beach area, and I was able to find a sustainable rent. Miami has a lot of arts nonprofits that help over time. I do feel that, as complicated as the Miami arts ecosystem is, it is pretty supportive — but at the same time, it is tied to all the different layers of money that have come in and dominate the arts, which are very present here.

misael soto: I moved here right after undergrad. I grew up in South Florida, originally from Puerto Rico, and Miami was always la locura, down south. We would visit my cousins and whatnot from time to time. As I became more and more interested in starting my own practice, I moved down here and have continually been sucked back in. I try to leave, and it pulls me back for whatever reason. Since COVID, everything's changed. Miami became the second most expensive city in the country. The influx was palpable: All of a sudden, there were Texas and California and New York license plates, Teslas zipping around town, and rent just started skyrocketing. There's more flooding. But at the same time, it's gorgeous, and it's special. I live in Mid-Beach. I can go to the water, I can breathe in some sea air, I can hear 10 different languages at once.

It's a really complex relationship with Miami. Especially, I think, both of us make complicated art — we both make art that is unconventional and perhaps even, you could say, difficult to collect. I don't know if you describe yourself that way, Leo, but I definitely do. And making this kind of work in a hyper market-driven neoliberal city like Miami, on the one hand, it gives me a lot of fodder, a lot of material, a lot of things to talk about, as we're doing right now. But at the same time, it can be really frustrating and alienating and lonesome, ultimately.

H: I moved from Argentina to Miami when I was little because my mom got a job there. We lived in the Doral neighborhood, where most people I knew were also from Latin America, until I left for Chicago for college at 18. I've lived in New York for over a decade now, but I still feel a strong pull to Miami, I feel seen, surrounded by people whose identities are a bit fractured the way I feel mine is.

And on the note of nostalgia, GTA is a game that was made over the last 13 years, so it chronicles a Miami that’s partly gone. For example, users say Lucía's home is based on a cute salmon-pink, 13-unit condo in Edgewater that was demolished in 2022 to build a 55-story tower, yet it lives on in the game. What does it mean for a video game to preserve a place that no longer exists?

LC: Well, a few thoughts. During that 13-year development, I would assume the map design was one of the first things they did. But there are also aspects of the chronicling of Miami, or Miami becoming this satire through the game, that have evolved in a shorter time period. For example, this morning I woke up, and there was a Miami Instagram influencer saying that in the fictional version of the Cuban coffee shop Versailles, which is called Antoinette, the bakery has a sign posted outside that says something like, “any politician must pay for all the food when they leave.” That's a reference from a few years ago, when Trump reportedly went to Versailles, ordered food for everyone, and then didn't pay and just walked out.

So it does seem like a video game takes a long time to make, and this one is probably the most ambitious one ever made — 4,500 people working really, really hard, to the point of even having the union situations that they have in the UK branch of the company. But at the same time, I feel like they studied Miami extremely well, and the integration with some local businesses and local artists in particular — I've seen a few street artists like Ahol Sniffs Glue, Soak, Tatiana Suarez, Typoe, as well as musician Nick León. One restaurant is based on Juvia on Lincoln Road, which doesn't exist anymore — they got priced out, and now there's a record of it. The game takes so long to make, but it lives in an ever-present, because it doesn't matter if you made an asset 13 years in the past, like Lucía's apartment, or now; they feel like the present. It's an interesting amalgamation. I would have to spend more time with it to really know: Does this feel like Miami in 2014 or Miami in 2026, or a hybrid?

H: To get into the politics of the conversation around GTA, I have a lot of icky feelings about one narrative that's taking hold online, which is that the game is “Woke 3.0,” and that the incels and Trump supporters are pissed about it. I only played for a few hours last night, and I went into a gun shop and bought a shotgun. That, to me, panders much more to the NRA hawks and the pro-gun community than to anything that could be considered woke, you know?

MS: Hmm. I see it the other way around, actually. To me, it's like pretending in order to pacify, in some ways. It's a very complex thing. On the one hand, I remember seeing the woman twerking on the top of a car as the sun came up over the MacArthur. Now that's in the game. And I remember the “face eater” on the MacArthur. I see a man in a thong skateboarding weekly, and now there's a character like that in the game. I teach art history, and I do a whole week on postmodernism and poststructuralism and simulacrum, and the consequences of that, which I think have led us into some really dangerous flattening territory in terms of the role of the artist in the late 20th to early 21st century. I see this game and the way that it's taken over the city in real life and in gameplay, and it makes me think about how much of this is pacifying the role of the artist, or is it pushing through to the other end and becoming a meta-modernist critique that has some gems in there, if you're willing to find them?

It ultimately makes me feel a bit sad in terms of what we deserve. I texted you yesterday, Valentina, when we were talking about having this conversation, and I said, “Well, maybe this is the kind of art the city deserves.” It's not the art that I want for Miami. But in so many ways, Miami is the perfect place. It's been the city for continual use by image makers, from Hollywood to video games.

H: There is some talk about the fact that the game does seem to have an awareness and sensitivity around identity. Cygnus, the curator at the Vice City Museum of Art, is the first non-binary character in Grand Theft Auto history. The actor cast for the role, Jesse James Rose, said that to prevent anti-trans violence, GTA made it so players would not be able to harm their character. Does this feel like an honest gesture, though?

MS: I was just talking to a friend who's been playing it, and she was like, “Where are all the Haitians?” I remembered there was this huge lawsuit against GTA and Vice City, the one set in the ’80s, from about 20 years ago. Haitian groups sued Rockstar over their portrayal. I did some research, and it seems now the company has shifted. They're saying, “We now punch up as opposed to punching down.” That feels, once again, so uncanny in comparison to the ways in which corporate America has shifted. It makes me think of the phrase, “Black faces in high places won't save us.” I don't want to be lobbing grenades at Rockstar. I think it's fantastic that these changes have been made, especially with such an influential game. But at the same time, it feels like the video game, in its attempt to replicate reality, is lagging in this area.

H: GTA has a long history of racism. We shouldn't forget that Black characters have been associated with criminality throughout all editions of the game. I haven't played enough to say whether that's the case in the latest version. There is also the question of how the company actually treats its workers, and the labor disputes that are going on behind the scenes. Nestor Uriarte, an animation programmer for Rockstar, wrote an opinion piece for the Guardian where he asked, why is it that with this game that generated billions of dollars, we are still fighting to get union recognition?

MS: I'm curious, Leo, as someone who has been playing games for as long as you have, how you feel about this. I'm a cinephile — I've been one since I was 18, and watched my first Kubrick film the summer before college. And I am dying to see Avengers: Doomsday (2026). I've been following the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) and have been consistently floored by the way they built out this world and the interconnected films. It's history, and it's been making history. But we all know how terrible Disney is. And even with the MCU, they tried to bring in more diversity, and the public didn't respond, so they backtracked on it. I don't know if that analogy holds. But it feels pertinent. It feels similar.

LC: Of course, I have to play more to fully understand it. There's the ads of the game and the game itself. I would say that the Netflix special did feel like it was perpetuating some of the stereotypes of the Haitian community. But at the same time, having played, or seen the range of minority characters so far in the first couple hours, it feels like they have a wide range of personalities, body types, and interests. It's not like they're all criminals. And I also found out that local Haitian muralist Serge Toussaint has his work featured in the game, which I think is an amazing thing. But in terms of artworks in other mediums that really relate to this, this is kind of like, let's say, South Park, or Euphoria — shows that are a mirror to the world that's very explicitly showing you both the best and the worst, and it's making fun of and critiquing everyone. But then how does it flip to show a new perspective or a solution?

I've seen a lot of people, especially women game critics and game developers, celebrating the relationship of Jason and Lucía being a central situation in the game, as opposed to a cast of different men from different backgrounds, or, in GTA IV, the Eastern European guy in the seedy underground. Having the relationship and the cultivating of the relationship be a core mechanic, almost in a Sims-like way — and even the learning of emotional labor, or doing kind things around the house, or the game having a really interesting reward mechanic for the nonviolent interactions ... At least in my experience so far, three hours in, I haven't shot a single shot.

H: Wait, how did you save Donnie in the first mission without shooting people?

LC: Oh, by hiding. It was saying, “Crouch around to make sure no one sees you.”

H: I think it's fascinating how different players can make these different decisions. I'm not very good at gaming, so I gave my husband the controller. I was like, “Get us out of here as quickly as possible. I want to get to Vice City!”

LC: Yeah, and usually my criticism of Rockstar Games and also Naughty Dog, two big companies that have these cinematic, movie-like games, is that the story missions often have a path where you fail if you don't take a violent action. The emergent gameplay — which happens just by walking around, the dynamic gameplay that's not in a story mission — is usually extremely layered and nuanced and can go in any direction, violent or not. Again, I'm only three hours in with GTA VI, but so far I appreciate that it is giving the choice of not using violence, and kind of rewarding it. There's something interesting about that. Because usually in those Rockstar games, I'm like, okay, there's this emotional tale, and now there's a mission, and I have to kill 20 minions.

MS: Leo, I'm thinking about your work and playing your pieces, immersing oneself in these worlds that you create, and there's a kind of mystery in the expansive potential that you create in your installations that at first can be a little overwhelming, but you have to just dive in. And this is the nature of games, or video games. There's a kind of trust fall. And I'm thinking about — let's just go there — the emancipatory potential of that. Because video games, to me, the potential in them as works is the building of awareness, the fostering of empathy, literally embodying someone who has a different way of life or a different body, a different perspective. Especially in our era of political correctness, and a lot of it is warranted, we're asked to speak from our own perspective and not assume things of others. And so this allowance — I wonder how you see the potential in that, especially in something like this game that is so immersive.

LC: I think games as artworks are, to a certain extent, some of the most affordably accessible. Yes, you need to have a PC or PlayStation or Switch or something, but they could be pieces of art that are globally accessible in an immediate way, and they really can affect culture. In terms of empathy, you're controlling a being that you identify as “I”: “I” drove the boat today, or in my game, “I” was camouflaging with the environment to gain energy. There's something there about the mutability of the body, or how one could shift one's self-identity into multiple beings, that is interesting in games, and also interaction and choice as a place that could be art, in a way that performance art also does, and maybe theater. And visual arts in general, maybe in a less touch-based way. But in terms of the empathy, I've been seeing a lot of reviews of GTA VI saying it's actually leading people towards that. Perhaps it is through the romantic relationship [between Jason and Lucía], or maybe by having so much freedom to do whatever you want and kill whoever you want, but then developing these characters and NPCs to a level where they feel like real people.

H: There is one moment in the game that was very emotive in a way that might provoke empathy, and it certainly did for me. At the very beginning — so this is not really a spoiler — we're shown the backstory of how Lucía gets arrested. She's been sitting at a cafe, a little Cuban cafecito, and she's just ordering ice water. The server keeps coming up to her and asking if she wants something else, and she's like, “No, no, just ice water for me.” It's clear that she just can't afford anything else. So in an act of true desperation, and from a place of deep poverty, she decides to rob a payday loan store nearby, and she gets caught. At one point, you can hear the cops saying, “She's saying she left something at the cafe.” And then we see the owners of the coffee shop taking care of her baby, who is then taken by social services.

We're not shown Tomás, her little baby, at the beginning. It's something that the game surprises us with. To me, it was such a thoughtfully articulated moment.

LC: The beginning is so strong. And then having the tutorial on how to walk and use the camera be her nine months later in prison. Out of overcapacity, the prison is letting some people who have lower sentences perhaps have probation, so she's gonna be let go, but the woman who works there says she doesn't know if or when Lucía will see her baby again. That works as a narrative tool, a teleology, giving purpose to the game beyond, “Oh, she's just a digital girlfriend.” Now there's this question of what the rewards of behavior are that the game's gonna have when one is part of the criminal underworld, but there is a child in foster care that could be taken back or not. That's gonna be so interesting if that ends up being a fork in the road within the narrative, because many of these games have multiple endings.

MS: This is so fascinating to me in regards to something we were talking about earlier — whether reality is informing the simulacrum and vice versa. It makes me think of how, living in Miami, it continuously feels like maybe the most neoliberal city I've ever lived in. But in so many ways, it oftentimes feels like when you're on the road or when you're at a cafe, you're alone. You really have to fend for yourself in this city. Of course, there are these moments where you break through, or if you're a regular at Enriqueta's, you know who to talk to, this and that. It makes me wonder how the game might change the way that we see ourselves. And, following that thread, how might it actually make us more united?

I don't know if that's a bit of a stretch, but there are just so many people playing this game. And I think over time it's really going to show, as visitors come and reflect their years of gameplay back to the city. In the same way that folks experience Paris syndrome, what will the GTA Miami syndrome be? How might that change us? I was thinking about it for the worse, but how might it change us for the better? Because I don't know a Miami where that childcare situation in the GTA story would happen. Of course, I'm not a caregiver. I'm not a parent. But I don't know that Miami — and I've been here long enough and I have a lot of family here, chosen family. So that makes me, in a weird way, hopeful.

LC: I think it's interesting, let's say with Pop art and conceptual art — if you use a urinal or a fluorescent light, you think of urinal, Duchamp; fluorescent light, Dan Flavin, etc. These artists are claiming this thing from the world. And it's interesting to have this very fluid cycle of, let's say, the Only in Dade Instagram account becoming almost a live feed of GTA, or us within Miami filtering our experience — when there's a very special or odd moment, it being a rehearsal for the game, or the game getting reflected back in the world.

If the game is marketing itself as this debauched, wild place, and that lures millions and millions of people in, but then it ends up being this profound story that actually shows how South Florida has issues of income inequality and climate change ... There's a hurricane system in the game, so there's a very strong chance that there will be flooding. Will that situation, where violence and comedy, or things that are not explicitly telling people what the values should be, actually make them more subtle and implicit? Does that create change or not?

H: We've been speaking over an hour, we could probably talk for two more hours. This feels like a beautiful note to end on. But I want to ask if there are any burning observations you want to share.

MS: I feel like we should speak about the takeover of Miami in the real world, physically. Anybody trying to do anything — F1, Art Basel, all these people who come in and take over the city, as they've done for decades — if they want to gain favor with locals, just look at what they did with GTA. Because the amount of free advertising — I mean, I went to this GTA VI-themed drag night, and it was not sponsored by them. It was at Las Rosas. They had a pool table and some neons, and they had the beer from the game available for purchase, but the event itself was fully done just to hop on the bandwagon, and everybody was lapping it up. Morphine Love Dion was playing the video game while people were dancing. It layered some uncanny feelings for me. But at the same time, I'm just very, very impressed, and scared, by the power of putting it everywhere to the point where it was inescapable. It's been inescapable for the last week. It's very impressive.

LC: Yeah. I've met at least two or three people who have been working on some of the release parties. So they're employing local artists and local musicians and local businesses, as opposed to, as misael was saying, these people arriving out of nowhere, renting a place for really exaggerated prices, and not giving back to the local community. At least through employment. We'll see over time if and how it leads to other forms of sustainability locally. I have a photographer friend who, similarly to that drag show, started doing GTA-style photos in front of one of the new signs and probably made some money through that, unofficially. So that's interesting.

MS: I think there's many ways to be a capitalist, or to do this kind of thing and take over the city in this way. And I've never seen something so thoughtful. It honestly reminds me to some degree of the first couple years of Art Basel, when they would do a lot of public programming and free concerts and they really seduced us ... But that's another conversation. I'll stop there.

H: Well, it's a perfect aperitif for Miami Art Week and the Basel boycott and everything else. And then the G20 summit hosted by Trump in Miami the following week.

MS: Wow, I forgot about that.

H: Yeah, we're going from GTA VI to G20. It's just a perfect pipeline, really.

MS: It doesn't get any more Miami surreal than that. Truly Vice City.

item.title: In a Midtown Office, Artists Sift Through the Junkspace of Capitalism - Hyperallergic
item.description:
A few hours before 260 Madison opened on September 24, I trekked to its namesake address in Midtown to meet the curators. A security guard directed me to the 14th floor of the 1950s office building, where drop ceilings, an exposed HVAC system, and two people I assumed were the exhibition organizers dressed in corporate drag greeted me. They quickly clarified they were not; they were from AmTrustRE, the real estate company that offered the derelict 23,000-square-foot office space to the artists for free while preparing it — and three other unoccupied floors — for their next corporate tenants. 

The three artists-turned-curators, Shaina Tabak, Dayana Matasheva, and Edson Niebla Rodríguez (the latter two of whom make up the duo DemonLovers Inc.), organized 260 Madison as an intergenerational, “inter-everything” show with work by over 50 artists, including self-taught and non-traditionally educated practitioners. On view through this Sunday, November 22, the show arrives just as the Whitney Museum of American Art opens artport: A History of Internet Art, signaling a new wave of institutional recognition for internet-grown art. With 260 Madison artists Maya Man, Rachel Rossin, and Eva and Franco Mattes among those included in the Whitney’s 25th-anniversary exhibition for its net art commissioning platform, the Midtown show feels especially urgent, if only because it takes place at the precipice of a paradigmatic shift within the art world.

Upon entering the first room on the left, I was immediately met with artist Jon Kessler’s towering nine-foot-tall sculpture, in which four plastic male dolls in Adidas tracksuits dangled from a weighted contraption somewhere between a carnival ride and a torture device. Titled “It Takes a Global Village Idiot” (2018) after philosopher Marshall McLuhan’s early ’60s theory that information-age technology “recreates the world in the image of a global village,” the sculpture forces viewers to confront the fact that the quick fixes of amusement proffered by technology rely on the same methods of data extraction that undergird systemic violence. It’s an unsettling introduction to a show where, even in its more humorous, delusionally conspiratorial, or enchanting moments, discomfort is always in the periphery.

“We don’t want to make a show or art that tries to be some form of escapism,” Rogríguez told Hyperallergic during an interview the week after the opening. “It’s like the [Werner Herzog] quote, ‘The poet must not avert his eyes.’ If some art in the show seems depressing, it’s because we live in what seems a depressing time.”

Rodríguez and Matasheva, who are also a couple, began making work together seven years ago while studying film in Montreal. Their video-art duo is named after Olivier Assayas’s 2002 film Demonlover, where multiple global corporations compete for a new immersive Japanese hentai company through extreme methods of espionage, exploitation, and blackmail.

“DemonLovers is about the libidinal economy and how algorithms are weaponizing our very basic instincts and desires,” Matasheva told Hyperallergic, echoing Rodríguez’s interest in what he calls “financial Freud,” or the psychoanalytic dimension of digital capital flows. 

Both DemonLovers’s own two works in the show and those they curated certainly don’t shy away from the degradation associated with extractive economies, be it of the self, physical infrastructure, or the proverbial global village. Nearby Kessler’s work, Theresa Tomi Faison’s “The Long Tail” (2026) climbs up one of the floor’s load-bearing columns. Across the curved sculpture’s six screens, images of memes, forum screenshots, and phrases ruminating on contemporary capital flow all accumulate and dissolve downstream. The river of digital spam ends at the viewer’s feet, inculcating the audience, but also the space itself, which the curators characterize as shaped by "junkspace” — architect Rem Koolhaas's term for fallout that “remains after modernization has run its course.”

Among works that are either readymades or play with the form’s history — including Anthony Discenza’s windowsill pile of unopened credit card and loan offer letters in “Offers” (2026) and Eva and Franco Mattes’s distended taxidermied cat, “Longcat” (2026) — the corporate detritus can be difficult to parse from the artistic interventions. At one point, I mistook a few square feet of wallpaper with the Champion logo for a new work. The curators clarified during a later conversation that it was actually kept from the office’s previous tenants, HanesBrands, which owns Champion. 

Having also inherited the space’s trove of gutted bathrooms, broken drywall, and stripped concrete floors (in short, its junkspace), the curators said they view 260 Madison through “layers of site responsiveness” more than anything. With some works, that connection emerged during the eleventh hour of installation. With others, the site occasioned the work itself. Ivana Dama used exposed air vents for “The Air Was Already Here” (2026), a sound work that channels air through reeds, transforming the invisible, inaudible rhythms of the space into what the artist describes as a “sculptural presence.” Pictures Generation artist Matt Mullican took a 47-foot span of unused wall space as an opportunity to reflect on his five-decade practice of constructing, deconstructing, and classifying systems of representation and perception with largely nonverbal symbols. 

“He spent three days here drawing his entire practice on the wall, right from the beginning to the end,” Matasheva said regarding Mullican’s monumental graphite piece, “Representing The Work” (2026). “He said he will give a lecture about it and that it's a very important work for him. It's kind of a conclusion of his practice.”

Meanwhile, the show’s video works are lodged into broken columns, ceiling alcoves, liminal backrooms, bathroom plumbing, abstract paintings, and even a hanging pink punching bag, a veritable reunion of the last decade of post-internet art movements. Alumni from Joshua Citarella’s publishing platform Do Not Research, the New Museum-affiliated Rhizome, and the traveling video and film screening series Open Secret, including Faison, Dana Dawud, Yehwan Song, and Ruba Al-Sweel, have contributed works. Many of them feature themes of surveillance, internet-induced conspiracy, and social media performance, as well as the technological, often AI-abetted methods of production that have come to define such enclaves.

Yet, for all the immateriality and speculative knowledge that flows through these works, 260 Madison equally plumbs an idea of technology with a long, craft-driven history. Tabak, a sculptor with a background in furniture design, is the driving force behind this facet of the show — and the currents of divination, enchantment, and even sublimity that come with it.

 “My practice is very handmade and material-focused, so I always know that that’s what I would contribute to the curatorial vision,” Tabak told Hyperallergic. “And just being in Midtown, you shouldn’t separate a show from what’s happening around it.

Tabak was particularly interested in curating works that “blur the line between the hand and technology,” inviting artists who “haven’t had a lot of chances to show in art contexts, whether it’s because they are in the design world or have nine-to-fives,” to participate in the exhibition. She explains that many of them complicate the very notion of technology and its use, citing Brian Oakes’s “Vessel 9” (2025), which gathers 3D-modeled circuit boards into a suspended “techno-Gothic” chandelier, and Ryan Decker’s “The Wavemaker Falters” (2026), which uses a motorized, rudder-like instrument to swoosh water through a raised vessel resembling a spaceship.

“We view technology not as something that has arrived in the 20th century, but something that has made humanity possible,” Matasheva said, expanding on Tabak’s comment. “Language is a technology, a chisel is a technology, everything is a technology.”

While many of the show’s craft-driven works conjure the anthropologist Alfred Gell’s idea that art is a technology that enchants, and in turn, becomes enchanted, others wield technology in the service of care. Kylie Mitchell repurposes a light-seeking solar robot and discarded electronic parts to move a found bird’s nest and egg toward a life-sustaining heat lamp. A few dozen feet away, Gregory Kalliche’s installation “Black-tailed gull nest; Ring-necked Pheasant Nest; Mallard Nest” (2016) suspends an LED light over three metal folding chairs printed with images of bird egg nests. Ben Gould’s “Ark II” (2026), on the other hand, augments a hospital gurney with eight aluminum armatures that hold fresh red roses inside coil-shaped glass vials. Doubling as a literal manifestation of Shakespeare’s “this mortal coil” phrase in Hamlet, the sculpture’s sterile infrastructure butts against the transitory visual comfort proffered by its flowers, mirroring a healthcare ecosystem wherein privatization, optimization, and tech automation have whittled medicine’s promises of care, healing, and empathy into mere aesthetic veneers.

It’s no coincidence that many of the works in 260 Madison position technology as both a pathogen and cure for today’s cultural ailments. In fact, when the real estate developers initially contacted Columbia University’s School of the Arts, it was to invite artists to “activate” a 36,000-square-foot gutted Duane Reade on the building’s ground floor. The developers eventually retracted their offer and moved the exhibition to the 14th floor, citing ongoing construction. Meanwhile, the original plan for 260 Madison to occupy the husk of the Duane Reade will be realized in a different form next month. Now serving as the building’s new temporary lobby, the former pharmacy will play host to a different group exhibition curated independently by Tabak. Opening December 3, HOW I FEEL will feature artists working across sculpture, social architecture, photography, painting, performance, and programming, including Jessica Vaughn, Quay Quinn Wolf, André Magaña, and 260 Madison’s Grayson Cox and Luke Murphy. How the forthcoming Duane Reade show contends with this moment of tech-induced economic entropy, so intense that even an entity as extractive as a real-estate company cannot commit to its own speculations, remains to be seen.

item.title: The Venice Biennale's Sham Awards Cannot Artwash Genocide - Hyperallergic
item.description:
This Sunday, the Venice Biennale will award its new “Visitors’ Lions.” But no matter who receives this poisoned chalice, the results are void. 

Stripped of the silver and gold they wore in previous iterations of the Biennale, the new Lions have been thrown to the tourists; “Best Artist” and “Best National Pavilion” will be decided by a popularity contest. Why this surprising democratic turn? The expert jury initially appointed to give these honors resigned en masse in April of this year. These resignations were, in part, the result of the Art Not Genocide Alliance’s (ANGA) nearly three years of campaigning to exclude the Israel pavilion from the art world’s most important biennial. After the jury publicly stated their intention to omit Israel and Russia from consideration for the Golden Lions, they were visited by representatives from Italy’s Ministry of Culture. The contents of the meeting are not public, but we can surmise how it went from the jury’s subsequent unanimous resignation. Shortly after, the Venice Biennale Foundation announced the Visitors’ Lions, inviting ticket-holders to cast their vote for awards to be announced at the end of the show’s run.
