item.title: Christie’s Notches a $145.9 M. Sale of 21st-Century Art, Led by a $32.9 M. Basquiat, amid Flagging Energy - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Christie’s finished out New York’s fall auction week on Thursday evening at its Rockefeller Center salesroom, bringing in $145.9 million in a 56-lot sale of 21st-century art (after works by Jeff Koons and Ed Ruscha, estimated to sell for as much as $11 million between them, were withdrawn). Leading the sale was a $32.9 million Jean-Michel Basquiat painting that fell just shy of its low estimate.

The sale included 20 works from the collection of Antonio Homem, longtime director of the storied Sonnabend Gallery, which was founded by his adoptive mother, Ileana Sonnabend. Sold to benefit their foundation, the works totaled $41.9 million. Also on offer were 10 works from the estate of beloved New York philanthropist Agnes Gund, who died last year, totaling $25.7 million.

After the withdrawals, the sale was estimated to bring between $126 million and $192 million; the hammer total on the night fell considerably shy at $117.7 million. Over the two-hour sale, the house found buyers for 51 lots, for a sell-through rate of 91 percent. Works by John Currin, William Eggleston, Wade Guyton, Gerhard Richter, and Yayoi Kusama failed to sell.

Many prominent advisors were in the room, including Erica Barrish, Amy Cappellazzo, Ralph DeLuca, and Gabriela Palmieri, as well as well-known dealers like Marianne Boesky, Jeanne Greenberg Rohatyn, and Christophe Van de Weghe. But there were a notable number of empty seats, and the atmosphere was unmistakably enervated after a long week of sales.

The sale started inauspiciously, with the first 19 lots, all from the Sonnabend collection, failing to hammer above their estimates. Bidding picked up only on the final lot of that trove, Jean Prouvé’s Table “Centrale” (“Trapèze”), petit modèle. The piece sold after five minutes of bidding between several specialists and a bidder in the room, before Sara Friedlander, Christie’s chairman of postwar and contemporary art in the Americas, nabbed it with a winning bid of $1.3 million. With fees, the total came to $1.7 million on a $700,000–$1 million estimate. But, all told, 10 of the 20 Sonnabend lots hammered below estimate. The collection hammered for $33.4 million, or $41.9 million with fees, against a pre-sale estimate of $35.25 million to $53.15 million (minus the withdrawn Koons, Wild Boy and Puppy). Not great any way you slice it.

The most notable of the Sonnabend works was Andy Warhol’s 1962 painting Campbell’s Soup Can (Turkey Noodle), tagged at $6–$8 million. The soup cans show one of Warhol’s most iconic images and are practically synonymous with Pop art. Adrien Meyer, global head of private sales and the auctioneer at Tuesday evening’s 20th-century sale, traded bids with a bidder in the room, who nailed it down with a $7.3 million bid, translating to $9 million all in.

Also from the trove was Roy Lichtenstein’s Large Spool (1963). Standing nearly six feet high, the work had been off the market since the Sonnabends bought it from Leo Castelli Gallery four years after it was painted. It has hung in museums all over the world, and its sale comes amid a major Lichtenstein retrospective at New York’s Whitney Museum of American Art. Auctioneer Yu-Ge Wang tossed out a handful of absentee bids from the rostrum before Friedlander got it for her client with a $7 million bid, for a total of $8.6 million with fees. The work’s pre-sale estimate was $10 million to $15 million.

Jeff Koons’s six-foot-high sculpture Hulk (Friends), 2004–12, also from the Sonnabend collection, shows the comic-book hero with small creatures perched on his shoulders and was estimated at $3.5–$5.5 million. It hammered after only a few bids at $3.3 million, or $4.15 million with fees, to the house’s Michael Baptist. (Koons was also a seller this week, bringing seven artworks to auction at Christie’s on Tuesday night, totaling $104 million.)

Bidding improved marginally from there, but for the most part, this was a sleepy sale. Even the biggest attraction of the night, Basquiat’s much-touted painting Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads), which dates to 1983 and measures seven feet square, failed to generate much excitement. Wang opened the bidding at $23 million, and for a few long moments it seemed there would be no bids. Then Ana Maria Celis, head of postwar and contemporary art, rescued the painting, beating out Alex Rotter, Christie’s global president and global chairman of 20th- and 21st-century art. It hammered at $28 million and sold for $32.9 million with the house’s fees.

The hammer price was just shy of the $30–$50 million estimate. But the work, inspired by a sketch by Leonardo da Vinci, had been off the market for two decades, so the seller no doubt made a tidy profit. The painter’s auction market has famously exploded in the intervening years: every one of his paintings to sell for more than $10 million, all 83 of them, has done so since then.

The large canvas, featuring the artist’s trademark scratchy messages and the titular sketchy heads against an orange background, had appreciated enormously since its previous trips to the block. It appeared at Sotheby’s London in 2000, when it fetched just above $400,000, within estimate, and again at the same house five years later, when it tripled in value to bring an above-estimate $1.3 million.

Vija Celmins’s 1990 painting Untitled (Ocean) was one of the few lots of the evening to generate a genuine bidding war. The painting came from the Gund estate; Gund bought it the year after it was painted. It drew bids from Joanna Szymkowiak, head of private sales; Arco Yu, a Christie’s Hong Kong specialist; and a woman bidding in the room. For four minutes, the three traded incremental bids until the room bidder won out. Still, that brought the hammer to only $5.75 million, just under the $6 million low estimate. With fees, the total came to $7.1 million.

The 10 Gund works fared better than those from the Sonnabend collection, hammering for $20.4 million on a $16.95 million to $24.65 million pre-sale estimate. With fees, the total squeaked past the high estimate to reach $25.7 million.

There wasn’t much rhythm to the proceedings. A 1990 Gerhard Richter Abstraktes Bild painting from the estate of legendary art dealer Marian Goodman, who long represented the artist and bought the work from him that year, carried a $6 million to $8 million estimate. It failed to sell after garnering no bids. Three lots later, another Abstraktes Bild, from 1991, measuring three feet square and dominated by red, blue, and green, sparked a short contest between Friedlander and Rotter. Rotter eventually won it with a $7.6 million bid. With fees, the total came to $9.4 million. The painting’s pre-sale estimate was $7 million to $10 million.

“The estimates were too high for this market,” Greenberg Rohatyn told ARTnews on her way out of the salesroom partway through the night. “We need to readjust, and the houses need to be at the forefront of managing expectations.”

Boesky agreed that the estimates were too high. “And the energy was low,” she said on her way out. “The lots that were estimated too high were punished, and those estimated low were rewarded.”

On a brighter note, a few records were notched: Jim Nutt ($1.1 million), Antonio Santín ($486,400), and Julia Jo ($409,600).

The Jo, a swirling, gestural abstraction of fiery oranges and yellows breaking against cool blues and teals, was the night’s final lot, estimated at $30,000–$50,000. Sold to benefit the Coalition for the Homeless, the abstraction generated arguably the most spirited bidding of the evening. Wang opened bidding at $20,000, and it quickly climbed into the hundreds of thousands as a cacophony of specialists and a bidder in the room called out bids. It eventually went to the room bidder at a hammer price of $320,000, or $403,200 with fees. That set off a hearty round of applause, at least for one lot.

The sale finished out an auction week that started Monday with a two-part $378.7 million Sotheby’s auction including works from cable television magnate Ted Baum and interior designer Ruth Baum as well as a various-owner The Now and Contemporary sale. Christie’s staged a nearly three-hour 20th-century sale on Tuesday that totaled $626.6 million, led by a record-breaking $85.8 million abstraction by Wassily Kandinsky, closely followed by an $82.3 million landscape by Gustav Klimt. The same night, Phillips sold $104.4 million in modern and contemporary art on Tuesday, led by a $44.6 million Amedeo Modigliani sculpture. On Wednesday, Sotheby’s staged a $777.8 million Impressionist and modern art sale, led by a record-breaking $190.4 million Vincent van Gogh.

item.title: Frieze Abu Dhabi Debuts to Brisk Sales and Confident Dealers - ARTnews.com
item.description:
On the morning of Frieze Abu Dhabi’s inaugural edition, Saudi Arabia’s financial center in Riyadh was reportedly attacked by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The crowd in Abu Dhabi, at least, had other things on their minds: the fair was about to open, with millions of dollars’ worth of art ready to be sold. Members of the royal family were back after getting a sneak peek yesterday, alongside politicians and celebrities including tennis star Venus Williams and architect Kulapat Yantrasast.

“It’s about time. Frieze is bringing its A-game to Abu Dhabi, where they have the best museums,” Yantrasast told ARTnews, cheekily mentioning that he’s been putting dots on artworks from The Third Line, Taymour Grahne Projects, Experimenter and Pearl Lam Projects.

The dealers were in high spirits too, as booths started to get busy an hour after the opening. At Thaddaeus Ropac, three of Imran Qureshi’s Water Bodies sold for $60,000, each to a UAE-based collection, though the gallery declined to specify whether this was a private or institutional collection.

“There is a great energy around the fair in Abu Dhabi this week. We’re having good conversations with collectors who are well-informed about the artists we are presenting, and you can feel the impact of the institutional scene here,” Xenia Geroulanos, director at Thaddaeus Ropac, told ARTnews.

The fair is under the umbrella of Frieze and has rebranded from Abu Dhabi Art fair, and attendees are noticing a difference. The exhibitor list has been streamlined to 89, down from 142 last year. Dealer Asmaa Al-Shabibi told ARTnews that when she walked through the fair’s new entrance, it felt “a little bit like going into Frieze London, and it feels like a different fair.”

Samy Ghiyati, co-founder of art advisory NG Partners, agreed. “The quality is definitely higher, and galleries made an effort to bring very good inventory. Usually fairs in the region are slower and sales happen over the course of several days,” he told ARTnews.

One of Ghiyati’s clients placed three orders on pieces ranging from $10,000 to $400,000. Within an hour of opening, dealer Sundaram Tagore had already placed two works on hold, one by Hiroshi Senju and another by Chun Kwang Young, ranging from $40,000 to $400,000. By late afternoon, Timothy Taylor had sold its entire solo presentation of paintings by Hilary Pecis to institutional and private collections in the region and internationally, to the price of $65,000-$205,000. The London-based antiquities gallery David Aaron sold a 2,000-year-old funerary stele for a seven-figure sum to a private collector, while Dubai-based Taymour Grahne Projects also sold out its booth of mosaic works depicting 70s-era architecture in Abu Dhabi.

Regional collectors reportedly spent big at Frieze Abu Dhabi. Iris Projects sold two works by Shamsa Al Omaira, a sculpture acquired by a new foundation in the UAE for $32,000 and an acrylic on canvas by Juma Al Haj for $20,400. UAE-based collectors also bought two ceramics by Eman Al Hashemi, priced at $17,000 and $15,000, an oil pastel on linen by Dhabia Al Qubaisi for $10,500, and a photograph by Ammar Al Attar for $12,500.

By then, Lawrie Shabibi had sold seven pieces by artists Hamra Abbas and Shaikha Al Mazrou, priced from $10,000 to $120,000. “People are recognizing the work when they’re coming here,” said the gallery’s cofounder Asmaa Al-Shabibi, referring to a new client who bought a work by Al Mazrou, who has a solo exhibition at the Cultural Foundation.

Rayan Ben El Mlih, sales and marketing manager at Waddington Custot, told ARTnews that a large contingent of collectors with reserves hailed from Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Qatar and Bahrain. The gallery brought works by Etel Adnan, Sophia Vari and Fabienne Verdier.

Dealers noted that local collectors, some of whom began their collections by acquiring Western artists, are now deepening their collections with more historical pieces by regional artists.

“We’ve been seeing European collectors diversifying their collections, too,” said Ghiyati. Dubai’s Carbon 12 sold a painting and a sculpture by 28-year-old artist Sarah Al Mehairi, as well as two works by Mexican artist Edgar Orlaineta, priced between $17,570 and $35,000 (€16,000-€32,000).

“We’ve engaged mostly with collectors that we’ve cultivated relationships with for a while, and this is our home fair,” Judy Karkour, associate director of Carbon 12, told ARTnews.

Collectors are branching out beyond SWANA this year, with notable interest in art from the African continent and its diaspora and Latin America. Meanwhile this year’s Frieze Masters section is dedicated to trade across the Indian Ocean, taking its cues from the Louvre Abu Dhabi’s current exhibition “Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean.” An hour into the fair, Efie Gallery had placed two works by Malian artist Abdoulaye Konaté on reserve, both priced between $45,000 to $65,000, in addition to two works by Cuban artist Maria Magdalena Campos Pons ($27,500-$55,000).

“Frieze Abu Dhabi has got off to a strong start for us with a high volume of enquiries in the first few hours from both institutions and private collections,” Kwame Mintah, cofounder of Efie Gallery, told ARTnews, which specializing in artists of African descent. “One of the more encouraging developments across the Gulf has been the gradual maturation of its collecting community, accompanied by a growing appreciation for artistic practices beyond established geographical and institutional frameworks,” he added.

At Daniel Crouch Rare Books, a private collector bought the first map to name Abu Dhabi, dated to 1832. While dealer Daniel Crouch declined to say how much the map sold for, he priced the booth’s total value between $10,073 and $1.19 million (AED 37,000 to AED 4.4 million).

“Abu Dhabi is becoming a cultural hub in the region with a lot of development,” Crouch said. “It’s the logical place to come to for dealing in the larger Indian Ocean region and the Louvre Abu Dhabi exhibition has attracted quite a lot of attention—we’ve obviously jumped into it with alacrity.” London-based antiquities gallery ArtAncient, carrying pieces ranging from $5,000 to $5 million, sold a collection of shipwreck jewels for an undisclosed sum—the gallery also had a visit from Venus Williams, who was admiring the Graeco-Roman mummy portrait Portrait L, which had recently been dubbed the “Mona Lisa of the Middle East.”

Throughout the opening, the blue-chip-leaning powerhouses, including Gagosian, Pace Gallery, Thaddaeus Ropac, and Victoria Miro, boasted crowded booths. Gagosian’s dedicated Roy Lichtenstein booth became the step and repeat for many visitors—the gallery said it “placed many” works with collectors “reputable collections” without revealing specifics.

Judging by its debut, Abu Dhabi has become a no-brainer stop on the art fair calendar. The emirate is slowly integrating into the art circuit. Earlier this month, Christie’s hosted its first fine art auction there, with Sotheby’s own version due next month, joining a colorful lineup of events that includes the Formula 1 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, Abu Dhabi Finance Week and Culture Summit Abu Dhabi.

Several dealers cited the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi’s upcoming December opening with the strong pull to participate in Frieze Abu Dhabi, characterizing the museum as a bridge between West and East.

“The Guggenheim is going to open now in the next few weeks, it’s literally where contemporary art gets space to breathe and to grow,” said Milo Gatti, fair coordinator at Galleria Continua.

item.title: Rare Hilma af Klint Painting Sells for Staggering $12.7M - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Hilma af Klint's painting “Ser III No. 5” (1920) sold for a record $12.7 million (SEK 128.9 million) at Bukowskis's modern art and design auction in Stockholm today, November 19, fetching over 16 times the upper end of its estimated price.

The first abstract painting by the Swedish artist and "mother of abstraction" to appear on the open market in 30 years, "Ser III No. 5" was one of the 85 geometric paintings the artist produced during a fervent months-long process in 1920. Theosophical symbols, triangles, and circles in "Ser III No. 5" provide insight into af Klint's last engagement with geometric abstraction before she turned to more naturalist watercolors in the last years of her life.

item.title: Benin Puts Pressure on Musée du Quai Branly in Paris to Return 35 Looted Objects - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A lot has happened between November 2021, when France formally returned 26 Benin Bronzes from its national collections to Benin, and today, when news of the West African nation’s latest request was reported by Le Monde. Namely, in May 2026, French Parliament passed a historic law designed to simplify the process by which artworks looted during the colonial era are returned to their nations of origin.

The latest request was first broached last summer and reiterated in the fall, when Beninese President Romuald Wadagni visited Paris and met with French President Emmanuel Macron. Like the 2021 repatriation, the new request is directed to the Musée du Quai Branly – Jacques Chirac, whose collection is made up of objects from Indigenous groups in Africa, Asia, and Oceania.

“We felt somewhat unsatisfied after the first return,” Alain Godonou, project manager for heritage and museums for the presidency of Benin, told Le Monde. “We drew up a second list which, in our view, meets the criteria for return under the [new] law. We are confident in our rightful claim.”

The latest request includes a divination tray and several types of weapons. But the most important object still in the French state’s collection is a hammered iron sculpture of Gou, a god of metalworking and war. This particular representation of Gou was made by Akati Ekplekendo in the mid-19th century and was taken from Benin by the French captain Eugène Fonssagrives in 1892. The 5½-foot-tall sculpture was one of 600 objects included in the 1935 exhibition “African Negro Art” at the Museum of Modern Art in New York and was also featured in the portfolio of photographs Walker Evans made in response to the show.

The new law stipulates that a joint committee—made up, in this case, of experts from France and Benin—has two years to review new claims, at which point France’s highest administrative court will make a ruling. “In France, [the Gou] sculpture has been underestimated,” said Marie-Cécile Zinsou, a French-Beninese art historian who is a member of the committee. “Whereas in Benin it will be highly valued. It is crucial for rebuilding our memory.”

item.title: The Ebullient Ecofeminism of Carolina Caycedo - Hyperallergic
item.description:
ST LOUIS, MO — A pink lake under an avalanche of digital detritus; a neon rainbow behind a man in a hazmat suit; a gilt sky above a lone wind turbine. These are among the surreal, meticulously rendered scenes in Carolina Caycedo’s series Mineral Intensive (2023–ongoing).

Caycedo’s candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy, whose production often depends on environmentally destructive mineral extraction.

Such visual beguilement — and ecological exigency — anchors Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots, an exhibition of sculpture, video, printmaking, and drawing that explores the joyous, multisensory dimensions of the artist’s activism.

Born and raised in Bogotá, Colombia, the Los Angeles-based artist devoted two years to collaborative research with botanists, plant taxonomists, and Native elders, informing her rendering of prairie and botanical life across the Mississippi River watershed. By turns bright and delicate, Caycedo’s Plant Portraits series (2021–ongoing) lends an ecofeminist bent to the larger show, merging feminine anatomy with botanical illustration.

Like a heavenly necklace, “Celestial Autonomy, the Dance of Big Dipper and North Star” (2023) dangles in the center of the gallery. Constructed of Alaskan nets, buoys, and other fishing equipment — its title honors the indigenous communities in the region.

Across the Mississippi River, another sculptural installation, “Fiesta de la Raíces” (2026), vivifies the National Building Arts Center in Sauget, Illinois. A three-dimensional “portrait” of the area’s root systems, the sculpture resembles a shaggy chandelier of rope, beads, and natural fibers — beckoning admirers to bask in its festive opulence.

At a time when ecological disaster feels ever imminent, art attuned to earthly precarity can often feel didactic or downright drab. Caycedo insists on an alternate vision: Humanity in sync with a resplendent planet — the ground beneath us trembling with riches, the sky adorned with unseen stars.

Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots continues at the Kemper Art Museum at Washington University in St. Louis (One Brookings Drive, St. Louis, Missouri) through January 4, and at the National Building Arts Center (NBAC) (2300 Falling Springs Road, Sauget, Illinois) through December 12. The exhibition was curated by Meredith Malone and James McAnally.

item.title: Laia Abril Photographs the Instruments of Rape Culture - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Editor’s Note: The following story contains mentions of sexual assault and harassment. To reach the National Sexual Assault Hotline, call 1-800-656-HOPE (4673) or visit online.rainn.org.

Some institutional rape cases create a glut of content. Recent allegations against Cornell students led to the publication of the accused’s portraits, images of their text messages, and videos of their fraternity house. Tweets and articles flooded the internet, while a journalist’s attempt to identify Jane Doe launched an entire Instagram campaign: Users posted their own pictures with the hashtag #iamjanedoe to help shield the victim. On the other side of the spectrum, reported rapes in the military, the Catholic Church, and less wealthy communities around the world may be met with silence, handled privately, or otherwise fail to galvanize the digital realm. 

Spanish photographer Laia Abril — whose larger project “A History of Misogyny” has also tackled feminicide, abortion, and endometriosis — faces a tricky mandate as she created On Rape and Institutional Failure, first shown in 2020 and now on view at the International Center for Photography. Her images have to be compelling without embracing spectacle, specific while addressing an enormous, global theme.

The artist makes two key choices, one conceptual and one formal: She shoots objects instead of people, all in black-and-white. Honing in on her palette, Abril gets at the seemingly eternal nature of misogyny; her distilled images stoke a similarly condensed rage.

item.title: A New Jean-Michel Basquiat Documentary Considers the Artist Behind the Work - Colossal
item.description:
A forthcoming documentary spotlights the life and work of luminary artist Jean-Michel Basquiat (1960-1988). Directed by Quinn Whitney Wilson and Viridiana Lieberman for Netflix, the feature film is the first project authorized by the artist’s two younger sisters, Lisane Basquiat and Jeanine Heriveaux, who helm his estate.

In a trailer, the siblings describe their brother’s energetic approach to life and how the story typically told about his meteoric rise omits so much of who he really was. Simply titled Jean-Michel Basquiat, the film features archival footage and audio, along with never-before-seen works and commentary from his family. The documentary seeks to venture beyond the mythology that’s come to surround Basquiat, who died of an accidental overdose at just 27 and whose work has continued to captivate the art world.

As one sister says in the trailer, “he was unapologetically Jean-Michel Basquiat.” The documentary will be available for streaming globally on December 11.

item.title: Art Dealer Sentenced for Falsely Claiming Native Heritage - Hyperallergic
item.description:
This month, a Las Vegas man pled guilty to a felony violation of the Indian Arts and Crafts Act of 1990 after being charged with selling counterfeit Native American art misrepresented as authentic to consumers. A United States district court judge for Nevada sentenced Jose Martinez, who adopted the name Joseph Skywolf, to two years of supervised probation and court-ordered restitution for the infraction.

A release from the US Department of the Interior's Indian Arts and Crafts Board (IACB) outlined that Martinez falsely claimed to be Chiricahua Apache, Apache, Navajo, and Native American while promoting his mobile business Skywolf's Gallery. Through the business, which was once headquartered in Jackson, Wyoming, but traveled to venues and markets across the Great Plains and Southwest, Martinez deliberately sold counterfeit artwork and handicrafts, including headdresses, jewelry, paintings, and beaded tanned hides falsely attributed to Native artists or specific tribes.

Last summer, Martinez was indicted on one count of violating the Indian Arts and Crafts Act, which prohibits the sale of products falsely marketed as authentic American Indian or Alaska Native art and craftwork. The act is intended to protect the livelihoods, cultural knowledge, and artistic traditions of recognized Native tribes, bands, and communities, as well as consumers seeking authentic cultural heritage and art objects.

item.title: Amsterdam’s Stedelijk Museum Names Krist Gruijthuijsen as Next Director - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has named the Dutch-born curator and art critic Krist Gruijthuijsen as its next director. He will succeed Rein Wolfs in July 2027.

Gruijthuijsen, a self-described “artist-driven curator,” will join the Stedelijk from EMMA – Espoo Museum of Modern Art in Finland, where he has been director since 2025, a role he holds concurrently with curator at large at Kunsthaus Zürich.

His vision for EMMA, a respected but relatively low-profile institution outside the Nordic region, included sustained support for artists through project funding, acquisitions and stipends, among more. Speaking to Frieze, he said he envisioned opening up the floor of the Brutalist building by removing its internal walls.

Prior to EMMA, Gruijthuijsen was director of the KW Institute for Contemporary Art in Berlin, beginning in 2016. His tenure there included well-received programming, with exhibitions by artists such as Hanne Lippard, Beatriz González, and Hassan Sharif. He also curated “Martin Wong: Malicious Mischief,” which the Stedelijk co-produced and hosted from November 2023 to April 2024.

His return to Amsterdam will also mark a curatorial homecoming, as Gruijthuijsen cofounded the Kunstverein Amsterdam with Maxine Kopsa and served as its director from 2009 to 2012, a role that briefly overlapped with his time heading the MA Fine Arts department at Amsterdam’s Sandberg Instituut (2011-16).

At the Stedelijk, he will oversee the institution’s modern and contemporary art and design strategy and guide collection management and public engagement.

“The [Stedelijk] has long held a special place in my personal and professional life, as it does in the history of modern and contemporary art and design,” Gruijthuijsen said in a statement. “Its remarkable collection and rich legacy carry a responsibility that extends far beyond preserving the past. Above all, they call on us to engage with the present and help shape what lies ahead, with art and artists at the heart of everything we do.”

He continued, “An essential part of my role will be to deepen the museum’s relationship with Amsterdam: to make it ever more open, engaged, and connected to the city and its communities. I want the Stedelijk not only to reflect the world we live in, but also to actively contribute to shaping its future.”

item.title: Richard Powell Unsettles Race and Color Theory - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Sometime in the 1980s, when I was still a fledgling curator of 20th-century art at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, I was invited to the studio of a rather prominent artist. During our conversation, the work of Jacob Lawrence came up somehow, and the artist mentioned that he was impressed by what he described as Lawrence’s use of “Black” colors. Did I mention this artist was White? 

I was gobsmacked by the comment. Not that I wasn’t attuned to stereotypical societal associations of color — most notably, of bright, loud colors with Black people. In the 1950s, a full three decades before Nancy Reagan practically made red her official color, my Aunt Ruth was appalled that my mother made red coats for my sister and me, rather than using more acceptable pastel colors. Then a friend who grew up in Northern Ireland told me that Protestant Irish factions associated Catholic Irish with loud and bright colors. 

But how did such racially associative ideas translate to the realm of the so-called “fine” arts? I was aware of the place of color theory in the practice of art and knew the names of important theorists, from Johann Wolfgang von Goethe to Johannes Itten to Josef Albers. But otherwise, I presumed artists’ palettes were the result of personal predilection, technical explorations (i.e., the opening up of brushstrokes and form in the 19th century and the introduction of a wall of color in the 20th century), or cultural orientation. So it was therefore with great interest that I approached reading Richard Powell’s latest publication, Colorstruck!: Painting, Pigment, Affect (2026).

item.title: ‘We’re Still Here’ Celebrates Remarkable Quilts by 15 Contemporary Black Artists - Colossal
item.description:
In the wee hours of a busy Saturday morning, on June 28, 1969, police raided The Stonewall Inn in Manhattan’s Greenwich Village, a renowned hangout for the LGBTQ+ community. During the 1950s and 1960s, few businesses openly welcomed gay people, and the legal system was against them—even two consenting adults in the privacy of their own home could face years in prison or a psychiatric institution if convicted of the crime of sodomy. Bar raids were common, but this one was particularly fraught due to the volume of people, and police quickly lost control. A riot erupted, which sparked even further protests over the coming weeks in what became known as the Stonewall uprising.

Among those on the front lines, from the raid onward, was Marsha P. Johnson—the “P” stands for Pay It No Mind—a Black transgender woman who advocated throughout the 1960s and 1970s for gay and transgender rights, LGBTQ+ youth, and those affected by HIV and AIDS. Known fondly as The Saint of Christopher Street, nodding to the well-known and welcoming area for the gay community (and home of The Stonewall Inn), she was widely known for her effervescent smile, creative clothing, and the flowers she would often wear in her hair.

For quilter Rosy Petri, Johnson proved a beautiful and vibrant personality for a large-scale textile work in We’re Still Here: Quilted Works Curated by Carolyn Mazloomi at Claire Oliver Gallery.

The works of 15 contemporary quilt artists take center stage in the expansive group exhibition. The show emphasizes work created by members of the Women of Color Quilters Network (WCQN), which historian, curator, and quilter Carolyn Mazloomi founded in 1985. Boldly pictorial and incorporating a wide range of materials, the pieces in We’re Still Here transcend the definition of quilts as stitched bed coverings; the compositions are rooted in the timeless craft of piecing and sewing, yet their portraits, stories, and collages surge into the realm of art.

L’Merchie Frazier’s “Climate Change in my Head: Afro Future Still Here,” for example, adopts a watercolor-like appearance with layers of nylon. Like many works in the show, a crucial topic is rendered front-and-center. Alita Aldridge’s “Underground Takes a Village” reflects the cooperation needed to make the Underground Railroad viable for enslaved people seeking freedom. And April Anue Shipp’s “The Oracle of Liberation” depicts abolitionist Frederick Douglass holding red and blue pills—a reference to the 1999 film The Matrix—in which we’re presented with a choice between seeing reality for what it is or remaining ignorant.

In addition to history, Black community, family, and other themes, bold portraiture recurs throughout the exhibition, such as in Viola Burley Leak’s “Maya Angelou II.” The renowned writer and civil rights activist peers over symbolic representations of her life’s work, including a bird fleeing an enclosure in a nod to her seminal memoir, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings.

“All of the work I make, and the work of my fellow quilters, deals with Black history and material culture,” Mazloomi says in a statement. Through WCQN, along with curatorial projects and in advocacy of the art form, she strives to raise critical awareness of Black quilters’ practices. “This exhibition is our way of saying that our history cannot be erased by any politician or revisionist force; our work will always showcase our triumphs, suffering, creativity, courage, bravery, and genius of my people. Black history is American history.”

We’re Still Here continues through January 7 in Harlem. You might also enjoy Chronicle Books’ recent release, Stories in the Seams: A People’s History of Black Quilts and Their Makers.

item.title: The Afterlife of Extraction:Doug Aitken’s HOWL in New York - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
The promise of progress is often measured by what an economy produces, rather than what it leaves behind. Across regions shaped by industrial expansion, the consequences of extraction persist long after the industries themselves begin to disappear. Depleted resources, abandoned infrastructure and fractured communities expose the limitations of an economic model founded on perpetual growth, raising questions about the relationship between prosperity, environmental responsibility and collective identity. For contemporary artists, these sites offer a means of examining the cultural and ecological legacies of modernity, bringing overlooked histories into conversation with an increasingly uncertain future. Doug Aitken’s HOWL examines what happens when the foundations of an entire community begin to erode.

Presented at 303 Gallery in New York,  and running until 19 December, HOWL centres on a remote desert settlement whose principal industry is oil drilling. Established in the early 20th century, the town now bears the physical evidence of industrial contraction, with boarded-up buildings and deserted storefronts interrupting its main street. Aitken’s attention extends beyond the familiar imagery of abandoned America, considering how economic systems shape collective identity and determine the possibilities available to those living within them. The settlement is a lens through which to examine the relationship between industrial ambition, environmental consequence and the uncertain prospect of social transformation.

Residents’ testimonies provide the film with a human dimension. Moving between documentary observation and cinematic abstraction, Aitken records inhabitants speaking openly about their circumstances, expectations and visions of utopia. Their accounts resist reducing dustrial communities to symbols of economic failure, revealing the emotional attachments and contradictions that persist when an industry becomes inseparable from local identity. Instead of imposing a singular narrative of decline, the artist allows individual voices to accumulate, creating a portrait in which personal experience intersects with wider structural change. The town consequently operates as a microcosm, its history reflecting questions about labour, belonging and the social consequences of an economy in transition.

Industrial machinery is a persistent visual and sonic presence throughout the film. Drilling equipment punctuates the arid terrain, its repetitive movements establishing a mechanical rhythm that gradually merges with the voices of the inhabitants. Speech, machinery and the sounds of nature are components of an evolving composition, blurring distinctions between the organic and the manufactured. This formal decision suggests that industrialisation has become embedded within the physical and psychological fabric of the settlement, altering the relationship between human activity and geological time. The desert exists in a state of tension, shaped by natural processes yet repeatedly interrupted by the rhythms of extraction.

Aitken has long explored the relationship between human experience, technology and the environments people inhabit. Working across film, photography, sculpture, sound and architectural intervention, his practice challenges linear storytelling and conventional spectatorship. Earlier projects, including electric earth (1999) and Sleepwalkers (2007), investigated the psychological dimensions of contemporary environments through fragmented narratives, multiple screens and interconnected cinematic experiences. In electric earth, the relationship between human consciousness and technological systems became a central concern, while Sleepwalkers extended moving image into the architectural fabric of New York, presenting the city through overlapping lives and activities. HOWL develops these interests through a more explicitly ecological and socially grounded investigation, introducing testimony, industrial landscapes and discarded materials to complicate his established language of immersive cinema.

The exhibition’s architecture extends this investigation into the physical environment. Visitors enter a darkened room where images are projected across skeletal wooden structures clad in screens, producing an arrangement that unsettles the conventional relationship between artwork and audience. A sculptural bus stop occupies the space, functioning as an independent object and a viewing environment for the film. Associated with waiting, departure and public infrastructure, it introduces a resonant image within a narrative concerned with communities whose futures remain uncertain. Spectators encounter a shifting environment of images, sounds and architectural references, making the act of viewing an embodied experience rather than a detached observation.

Immersion, however, carries its own critical complications. Large-scale projections and multisensory environments have become increasingly familiar within contemporary exhibition-making, prompting questions about whether spectacle can accommodate the complexity of the subjects it represents. Ecological devastation is particularly vulnerable to aestheticisation, with damaged environments frequently transformed into visually compelling images that risk distancing audiences from the conditions they depict. Aitken’s fragmented cinematic language introduces uncertainty into this relationship, resisting the coherence of a conventional documentary narrative. Overlapping voices, mechanical sounds and shifting projections complicate the viewer’s position, creating a tension between sensory experience and the social realities underpinning the images.

Materiality provides another means of examining the consequences of industrial culture. Alongside the film, sculptural works constructed from materials foraged in the urban environment introduce a vocabulary of consumption, disposal and transformation. Microplastics washed ashore, discarded motorway rubber, repurposed tyres, composted seeds and condensed organic matter are brought into new configurations, retaining traces of the systems from which they originated. These materials complicate the distinction between resource and waste, suggesting that objects discarded by industrial culture continue to participate in wider ecological processes. Their transformation into sculptural forms makes visible the environmental histories concealed within everyday commodities, drawing attention to the material consequences of contemporary consumption.

An ice machine containing a living ecosystem of cactus introduces an especially compelling contradiction. An appliance designed to regulate temperature becomes a habitat for a plant adapted to arid conditions, bringing technological intervention into contact with natural resilience. The juxtaposition raises questions about the relationship between artificial environments and ecological adaptation, without resolving the tension between them. Elsewhere, the bus stop shifts between sculpture, architectural reference and cinematic viewing structure, demonstrating how familiar objects acquire new meanings when removed from their functional contexts. These transformations recall the history of assemblage and found-object sculpture, where discarded materials have challenged established distinctions between artistic production and everyday life. Here, the emphasis falls on the environmental and cultural histories carried by matter, foregrounding the afterlife of objects within systems of production and disposal.

The exhibition’s spatial organisation brings these different registers into conversation without establishing a rigid hierarchy between them. Moving image, sculptural assemblage and architectural intervention operate as interdependent forms of inquiry, each offering a different perspective on the same subject. The darkened environment establishes continuity between the projected desert and the physical materials occupying the gallery, while the placement of the bus stop creates a point of encounter between the two. This arrangement allows the exhibition to move between the intimate scale of individual testimony and the broader implications of environmental change. The sculptural works extend the film’s concerns into the gallery, making the exhibition’s argument spatial as well as cinematic.

Aitken’s engagement with industrial environments also enters a longer history of artistic investigation into humanity’s relationship with the natural world. Land Art transformed geographical scale and geological processes into subjects of artistic inquiry, challenging the boundaries of the gallery and the autonomy of the art object. Subsequent ecological practices have increasingly addressed the consequences of human intervention, from resource extraction and pollution to the unequal distribution of environmental risk. Discussions of the Anthropocene have further complicated the idea of nature as something separate from human activity, foregrounding the extent to which industrial systems have altered the conditions of life on a planetary scale. Yet environmental change cannot be understood through universal narratives alone: its consequences are experienced unevenly, with communities dependent on extractive industries frequently caught between economic necessity and ecological damage.

The representation of these communities raises important questions about the aesthetics of industrial decline. Abandoned factories, deserted settlements and decaying infrastructure have become familiar images within contemporary visual culture, often functioning as shorthand for the failures of modernity. Their visual appeal, however, can obscure the social realities of those who continue to inhabit these environments. Industrial ruins risk becoming objects of contemplation, detached from the histories of labour, economic dependency and political decision-making that produced them. Aitken complicates this tradition by incorporating residents’ voices into the cinematic structure, allowing their aspirations and uncertainties to interrupt the familiar spectacle of abandonment. Attention shifts from the appearance of decline towards the lived experience of economic transformation.

The transition away from fossil fuels introduces further complications. Discussions of energy reform frequently prioritise technological innovation, investment and sustainable development, while the cultural consequences of industrial contraction receive comparatively less attention. Generations of employment, local knowledge and collective identity cannot be replaced through changes in energy infrastructure alone. The residents’ testimonies expose the difficulty of separating individual lives from the economic structures that sustain them, revealing how industrial dependency extends beyond employment into the organisation of everyday experience. Their visions of utopia therefore carry an ambiguity, expressing both the desire for renewal and the uncertainty of what might replace familiar systems. Environmental responsibility must also account for the communities expected to navigate the consequences of economic change.

Repetition provides a connection between the film’s formal structure and its wider political concerns. Drilling machines return to the same movements, images recur and the community remains suspended between memories of prosperity and uncertain expectations. These cycles suggest a system that continues to operate through established patterns even as the conditions supporting it begin to deteriorate. The mechanical rhythms of extraction become a metaphor for a culture organised around acceleration, consumption and perpetual production. Yet repetition also creates the possibility of recognition: once a pattern becomes visible, its continuation can be questioned. The tension between inherited systems and the capacity to disrupt them gives the film its restless energy.

Describing HOWL as a postmodern poem and an electric haiku, Aitken’s exhibition text points towards a compressed, sensory approach to meaning. Rather than presenting a comprehensive account of industrial decline, the work brings together fragmented testimony, recurring sounds and rapidly shifting images to create a portrait of contemporary life. Its restless movement reflects a world in which technological acceleration and environmental degradation increasingly occupy the same frame. The poetic register allows the film to move beyond documentary explanation while retaining the specificity of its subject. Yet the relationship between aesthetic experience and social reality remains unresolved, raising questions about how visual culture can represent ecological crisis without turning destruction into spectacle.

What happens when the economic structures that once sustained a community become the very forces responsible for its decline? HOWL approaches this question through a convergence of cinematic, sculptural and architectural languages, bringing the material afterlife of extraction into contact with the memories and aspirations of those who inhabit its consequences. Its desert setting holds the contradictions of industrial modernity in visible tension: a settlement shaped by economic dependency, an environment transformed by human ambition and a future that remains difficult to articulate. Aitken’s project insists that ecological questions cannot be separated from social histories. The challenge extends beyond finding new uses for abandoned infrastructure or imagining alternative energy systems; it concerns who gets to define progress, whose histories are preserved and who is included in determining what comes next.

Doug Aitken: HOWL is at 303 Gallery, New York, until 19 December.

303gallery.com

Words: Anna Müller

item.title: Recovering Edward Said’s Voice - Hyperallergic
item.description:
For decades, the word “Palestinian” conjured a very specific image in the minds of many intellectuals and members of the public: the commanding presence of Edward Said, credited with no less than revolutionizing our collective understanding of the dynamics of oppression. Now, as Israel’s genocide in Gaza continues, Said’s legacy is not just urgent, but also, in some spaces, the target of censorship. Today, author Moustafa Bayoumi, who studied under the late critic, activist, and professor at Columbia University, pens a thoughtful review of Edward Said: Between Worlds (2026), a new documentary by Maiken Baird whose audio consists almost entirely of Said’s own words. “To recover Said’s voice is to rediscover some of the most compelling arguments that have been made for Palestinian liberation,” Bayoumi writes.

Can contemporary art make us laugh (and not just when we’re making fun of it)? Greta Rainbow visits a New York exhibition that’s all about embracing humor in art, and somewhere between Brian Belott's absurdist fan-embedded assemblages and Ebecho Muslimova’s delightfully transgressive depictions, she learns a thing or two about her own funny bone.

—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

Edward Said Speaks More Urgently Than Ever

In their (still brilliant) 1990 experimental film Introduction to the End of an Argument, filmmakers Jayce Salloum and Elia Suleiman splice together troves of found footage about Palestinians and Israelis. The result is an exquisite mash-up of Hollywood cartoons and political clichés, a comic pastiche illustrating the common bond between Orientalism and zombies. Both just won’t die. | Moustafa Bayoumi
